comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees
Supplemental opposition comment: Further education should not reset the initial fee

I oppose the proposed OPT fee rule and request its withdrawal. This is an additional comment from the same commenter whose original submission has tracking number mvp-wb10-c5bl. It supplements that submission and should not be treated as the views of a separate person.

Sections V.A and VII.B.6 invite comment on an alternative under which the $70,000 initial fee could be required again when a student moves to a higher educational level. I specifically oppose that alternative. I understand that it is an option under consideration, rather than a description of the primary proposed fee schedule.

Completing a higher degree is not evidence of wrongdoing or a reason to presume that the student's next training opportunity imposes the same oversight burden as a first encounter with the program. A student may have an established record of lawful study and compliance. DHS should explain what additional administrative work or demonstrable risk would justify treating the next recommendation as a new $70,000 event instead of considering that existing record.

This alternative could also discourage educational progression. A university or potential employer deciding whether to support a graduate's training would have to consider another large payment. Students could face a financial penalty for investing in a master's or doctoral education, even where the later training develops substantially different skills. That would work against the educational purpose of practical training.

Before adopting any such reset, DHS should separately estimate its effects on progression between degree levels, participation in advanced training, and institutions' willingness to support graduates. The analysis should distinguish additional government processing costs from an intentional deterrent to participation and explain why less burdensome compliance measures would be insufficient.

DHS should withdraw the proposed rule and expressly reject the higher-degree reset alternative. My discussion of this alternative does not indicate support for the primary $70,000/$30,000 fee proposal.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fee rule and requests its withdrawal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees
Supplemental opposition comment: Disproportionate effects on small institutions

I oppose this proposed rule and request its withdrawal. This is a further submission by the same commenter associated with original tracking number mvp-wb10-c5bl, not an additional person's comment.

The small-entity analysis in section VII.B warrants much more attention. DHS estimates that 841 of the 1,389 small institutions examined, or 60.5 percent, would experience impacts exceeding one percent of estimated revenue. These are modeled estimates, not observed losses, but they underscore the scale of the proposal's potential consequences for institutions with limited resources.

Annual revenue alone does not measure the capacity to make a large payment for each student recommendation. DHS should examine unrestricted funds, operating margins, cash-flow timing, and the concentration of affected students within particular programs. Institutions with similar revenue can have very different financial obligations. A large upfront payment could lead a school to restrict recommendations, cut other services, or pass costs to students before any longer-term adjustment is possible.

Section VII.B.6 rejects a small-institution exemption in part because small entities account for a substantial share of regulated institutions and fraud could continue. The number of small institutions does not, by itself, establish their relative rate of noncompliance or demonstrate that a uniform fee is the best response. DHS should present evidence linking institution characteristics to actual oversight needs and evaluate targeted audits and enforcement using that evidence.

The alternatives analysis should also compare graduated charges, institutional caps, and other substantially less burdensome approaches, with transparent estimates of both compliance benefits and lost training opportunities. Any discussion of these alternatives is a request for a serious comparison, not an endorsement of a reduced version of this rule.

A fee that restricts access primarily according to an institution's financial resources does not necessarily improve compliance. DHS should withdraw the proposal and develop an evidence-based response to documented misconduct that does not impose disproportionate burdens on compliant small institutions and their students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees
Supplemental opposition comment: Financing arrangements and worker mobility

I oppose the proposed OPT fees and ask DHS to withdraw the rule. This comment supplements my original submission, tracking number mvp-wb10-c5bl, and represents the same commenter.

The proposal contemplates institutions shifting the financial burden to students or employers, even though the institution would make the required payment. DHS should analyze the consequences of those financing arrangements for students' ability to choose and leave an employer.

I recognize that section V.A states that changing employers would not itself trigger a new fee. That is a useful distinction, but it does not resolve the separate issue of who ultimately finances the existing fee. An employer willing to cover a large cost might seek repayment if a worker leaves, or seek to recover the payment through other compensation arrangements. I am identifying a foreseeable possibility that DHS should investigate, not claiming that such contracts are required by the proposal or describing any particular employer's conduct.

For a recent graduate with limited savings, a substantial repayment obligation could make it harder to leave unsuitable work, report mistreatment, or negotiate working conditions. Employers able to finance the fee could also gain a recruiting advantage unrelated to the educational quality of the training. Smaller employers and nonprofit organizations may be less able to participate even when they offer valuable supervised experience.

DHS should examine who would bear the costs under plausible financing arrangements, the likelihood and terms of repayment obligations, effects on compensation, and the consequences for mobility between employers. It should explain what safeguards would prevent the fee from undermining students' practical ability to exercise workplace rights. Simply observing that an employer change does not create another government fee is insufficient.

The proposal should be withdrawn. If DHS pursues further action, it should first assess these financing effects with evidence from students, institutions, and employers and compare targeted compliance measures that do not create a large financial dependency at the start of a training relationship.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees
Supplemental opposition comment: Students should not lose opportunities because of institutional payment errors

I oppose the proposed rule and request its withdrawal. This is a supplemental comment by the same person who submitted original tracking number mvp-wb10-c5bl.

The payment sequence described in section V.A and the proposed regulatory amendments creates a serious implementation concern. The institution would have to pay before the designated school official recommends OPT, and the proposal would prevent approval where the required fee was not paid before the recommendation or was not paid at all.

The student does not control the institution's payment systems or the government's reconciliation of those payments. DHS should examine situations in which a school intends to comply but encounters a posting delay, a transaction-matching problem, or an inadvertent sequencing error. These are hypothetical implementation risks, not allegations about current systems. Nevertheless, the consequences could fall on a student who supplied accurate information and otherwise met the applicable requirements.

The rule should explain whether and how an institution could correct a premature recommendation or demonstrate a timely payment that was recorded incorrectly. DHS should specify notice procedures, an opportunity to cure clerical errors, responsibility for resolving payment discrepancies, and a meaningful process for correcting erroneous determinations. It should analyze how those procedures would interact with existing application and training timelines. Merely telling a student to start over may not preserve the original opportunity.

DHS should also estimate the cost of reconciling payment records with recommendations, training school staff, resolving exceptions, and assisting affected students. A system that appears administratively simple at the point of collection may impose substantial work on institutions and applicants.

My primary request is withdrawal of the fee proposal. If DHS nevertheless proceeds, it should not make an otherwise eligible student's training depend on an institutional accounting error that the student cannot prevent or promptly correct. Any further proposal should include explicit correction procedures and an assessment of these operational consequences before implementation.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees
Supplemental opposition comment: The participation scenarios do not establish a reliable expected outcome

I oppose the proposed rule and request its withdrawal. This submission supplements original tracking number mvp-wb10-c5bl and comes from the same commenter. It focuses specifically on the participation forecasts in sections VII.A.3.b and VII.A.4.a.

DHS acknowledges uncertainty about how participation would respond to the fees. Its high-participation scenario assumes no participation change and uses 2024 activity. The low-participation approach uses historical averages and assumptions about institutions financing initial OPT for students eligible for a STEM extension, including a historical continuation rate. The primary fee estimate then averages the high and low results.

These scenarios may illustrate possibilities, but their arithmetic average is not automatically a statistically supported expectation. DHS should explain why those endpoints are appropriate, what evidence supports their assumptions, and why they should receive equal weight. The difference between scenarios also involves different historical reference periods. That makes it harder to distinguish the estimated effect of the fee from differences in the underlying baseline.

A more informative analysis would hold the no-rule counterfactual constant and vary clearly identified behavioral assumptions. It should test participation responses across institutions with different financial resources, students with different access to funding, and employers with different capacities to finance training. It should also test reduced STEM participation rather than presuming STEM eligibility is sufficient to secure institutional financing. Historical continuation under the existing fee environment does not establish how students and institutions would behave after a large new charge.

DHS should publish enough detail to reproduce the forecasts and show how plausible alternative assumptions change the estimated number of lost training opportunities and the distribution of costs. Sensitivity analysis should be connected to evidence, rather than treating an average of selected scenarios as a substitute for evidence.

Because the participation forecast is central to evaluating this proposal, these uncertainties require a substantive response. DHS should withdraw the rule and undertake a more transparent, behaviorally grounded analysis before considering further action.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fee rule.

OPT has long been an integral component of the F-1 student program, allowing international students to gain practical experience directly related to their fields of study. It serves important educational, economic, and workforce development purposes by connecting classroom learning with real-world training while helping U.S. employers recruit talent educated at American institutions.

The proposed fees of $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations would effectively eliminate access to OPT for many students and institutions. These amounts bear no apparent relationship to the actual cost of administering the program, maintaining SEVIS records, or investigating compliance concerns. Instead, they function as financial barriers designed to deter participation in an otherwise lawful program.

Research suggests that such fees could dramatically reduce OPT participation and international student enrollment. This would have serious consequences not only for international students but also for U.S. colleges, universities, employers, and local economies. International students contribute substantial tuition revenue that supports educational programs, research infrastructure, faculty positions, and opportunities for domestic students. A significant decline in enrollment would negatively affect these institutions and the communities they serve.

The proposal would also undermine the educational purpose of OPT. The fees would apply not only to post-graduation employment but also to pre-completion OPT used for internships and other short-term training experiences. As a result, a student seeking a brief internship could trigger a fee that far exceeds the value of the training opportunity itself. Faced with such costs, many schools would likely decline to recommend eligible students for OPT regardless of the educational merit of the experience.

The United States competes globally for talented students, researchers, and innovators. Other countries increasingly offer clear and accessible post-study work opportunities to attract highly skilled graduates. Restricting access to OPT through excessive fees would make U.S. institutions less competitive and encourage students to pursue education and careers elsewhere. This outcome would weaken, rather than strengthen, America's long-term economic and scientific leadership.

I am also concerned that DHS has not adequately demonstrated the legal or economic basis for the proposed fee amounts. The rule does not establish a clear connection between the fees and the government's actual costs of administering or enforcing the OPT program. Nor does it provide persuasive evidence that broad, punitive charges imposed on all institutions and students are a more effective solution than targeted compliance reviews, fraud investigations, and enforcement actions against specific bad actors.

Finally, the proposal contains significant ambiguities regarding when and how the $30,000 subsequent fee would apply. Such uncertainty makes it difficult for schools to evaluate potential liabilities and further undermines confidence in the proposal's economic analysis.

DHS already possesses substantial oversight tools through SEVIS, Designated School Official reporting requirements, STEM OPT training plans, employer attestations, compliance reviews, and investigations. If additional safeguards are needed, DHS should pursue targeted, evidence-based measures rather than imposing extraordinary fees that would effectively dismantle a longstanding educational training program.

For these reasons, I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and pursue alternative approaches that address compliance concerns while preserving the educational, economic, and workforce benefits of OPT.

Thank you for considering these comments.

Imposing fees of this magnitude would make practical training impossible to many of these students, regardless of their qualifications, skills, or potential contributions. This rule would force international students to leave the US in search of safer places, and if that happens, the country risks losing not only talented workers but also future researchers, entrepreneurs, businesses, and jobs. International students are not simply beneficiaries of American education. They are active contributors to its universities, laboratories, industries, and communities. They bring different perspectives, build collaborations across borders, and help strengthen the institutions in which they study and work.

I urge the Department of Homeland Security to reconsider these proposed fees and preserve meaningful access to OPT for international graduates. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am a US citizen, born and raised, who is currently enrolled in a PhD program in the US. The proposed rule introducing a $70,000 dollar fee for OPT for students on F-1 visas is frankly shortsighted and would be tantamount to shooting ourselves in the foot as a nation. The rule change appears to be intended to function as a deterrent against foreign students coming to the country and out competing domestic talent in the workforce. While this concern is understandable, this measure fails to address the core issues that face our educational institutions and the nation as a whole.

It goes without saying that a nation with the highest concentration of brilliant minds will be more competitive at a global scale than a nation of the same size with a lower concentration of equivalently capable workers. The US educational system should ideally work as a siphon, taking the most talented individuals from around the world and brings them to the US, ready to learn and ready to work, increasing our concentration of qualified workers while reducing the concentration of qualified workers in other countries. Giving our students the opportunity to surround themselves with the greatest minds from around the world, rather than just their immediate surroundings, is a part of what makes our educational system so strong. Removing the best minds from around the world would fundamentally damage our educational system.

Capability is not directly tied to the economic fortune of one's parents. At the age when most students are considering OPT, they have not had sufficient time to acquire capital of their own; rather any money they have is likely a reflection of their parents' wealth. The proposed rule change would destroy the value of a US education for most students who are worth teaching. There are plenty of wealthy foreigners who would love to send their unqualified and unruly children to the US to study at our institutions. However, these students are much less likely to recognize what a great opportunity an education in our country is, and will simply function as an anchor on our society before returning to their home countries to thrive on their parents wealth. The alternative would be foreign students taking out debts that they cannot pay back, then fleeing the country when the bill comes time to be paid. In both cases, they will have extracted value from the US without providing anything in return.

If the concern is that the number of foreign national students attending US institutions is too high, and too many people are coming to the US and out competing our own, the solution is not to place a fee on foreigners. The solution is to raise the academic bar for admission to US institutions as a foreign national so that we can be sure that we are getting only the best and brightest, perhaps placing a cap on the number of seats available at a given institution as a fraction of the student body. We should then provide this portion of students who are admitted to our institutions a clear path to citizenship, so that the effort spent on training them is not wasted by them leaving. This would ensure that we continue to reap the benefits of the US educational system without placing an anchor around our necks and without taking jobs away from qualified US born talent. A fee on entering the workforce would achieve the opposite effect.

As an employee at a higher ed institution, I strongly oppose this rule. The rule is ambiguous in both its scope and application. For instance, the proposed rule does not clarify whether the $70,000 fee is a one time, flat fee or whether it must be paid each time a student changes institutions. Moreover, the fee is directed to the Treasury rather than DHS, the department responsible for administering the OPT program. Fees are compulsory payments to offset an agency’s cost of providing a good or service. If the fee is not going to the agency providing the service, it cannot be considered a fee, but a tax. If enacted, this rule will disrupt research teams, employer partnerships, and workforce pipelines, and it would impact learning, mentorship, and career opportunities for both international and domestic students.

Crucially, the rule poses an existential threat to institutional financial stability at an exceptionally precarious moment. American higher education is currently navigating a severe "demographic cliff"—a sustained decline in the domestic college-aged population that has strained operating budgets nationwide. For years, international student enrollment has served as a critical counterweight to these domestic shortfalls. International students typically pay full non-resident tuition, providing essential revenue that supports departmental operations, student services, infrastructure, and institutional financial aid programs that directly benefit domestic students. Imposing a cost-prohibitive fee structure—whether passed on to students, shouldered by institutions, or transferred to employers—will inevitably divert international applications to competitor nations like China, European Union, Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia. The resulting decline in international enrollment will decimate institutional tuition revenue at a time when colleges and universities can least absorb the blow. For many institutions already operating under razor-thin margins, this revenue shock will force severe budget cuts, the consolidation or elimination of degree programs, faculty layoffs, and diminished course offerings, ultimately hurting the entire academic community and American students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose this proposed rule and urge DHS to withdraw it.

1. The fee raises revenue and is not a real condition of admission (Sec. IV.C). DHS says the fees would go into the general Treasury as miscellaneous receipts under 31 U.S.C. 3302, and that ICE could not use them. DHS estimates annual collections of $8.4–16.5 billion. Yet it never ties the amounts to the cost of running OPT, and it does not rely on 31 U.S.C. 9701, which requires fees to reflect the cost or value of a service. A charge this large, unrelated to cost and paid into the general fund, works as a tax. INA 214(a)’s “time and conditions” authority does not clearly give DHS the power to raise billions in new revenue.

2. The fee does not target the fraud DHS describes (Sec. IV.A). DHS’s evidence is about shell employers, staged worksites, and sold offer letters. The fee, however, is paid by the school before the DSO recommendation. DHS admits the fee is not tied to any employer, and initial OPT does not require a job offer at all. Paying $70,000 tells a school nothing about whether a future employer is real. Bad actors can pass the cost on to students, while legitimate students at schools that cannot pay lose access. Because the money goes to the Treasury, the fee also does nothing about the problem DHS itself names: compliance resources have not kept pace with the program.

3. DHS rejected targeted alternatives for its own convenience. DHS considered applying the STEM OPT safeguards (training plans, employer site visits, reporting) to all OPT. It chose a fee instead mainly because a fee needs minimal government resources. Saving agency effort is not a reasoned basis for moving billions in costs onto schools and students. Checking employers addresses the fraud DHS describes. A per-student fee does not.

4. The fee amounts are arbitrary. DHS says it picked $70,000 to match the H-1B fee and to be “on par with” one or two years of tuition. Neither benchmark measures fraud risk, harm to the labor market, or administrative cost. The same $70,000 applies to a part-time pre-completion internship, which is the form of training closest to OPT’s educational purpose. DHS itself expects pre-completion OPT to decline.

5. DHS quantifies the costs but not the benefits (Sec. VII.A). DHS estimates annualized costs of up to $8.2 billion (primary estimate $4.1 billion) and transfers of $12.8 billion per year. It gives no estimate of fraud prevented or U.S. jobs gained. It uses unpaid fees as a stand-in for lost value and does not estimate lost tuition, tax revenue, research output, or enrollment. Executive Order 12866 requires a reasoned finding that benefits justify costs, and this record cannot support one.

6. Small institutions are hit hardest (Sec. VII.B). By DHS’s own estimate, 841 of 1,389 small affected institutions would face transition-year costs above 1% of revenue, and 116 would face costs above 20%. DHS rejected a small-entity exemption because small entities make up 56% of regulated schools. That is exactly why the Regulatory Flexibility Act requires DHS to reduce the burden on them, not a reason to skip it.

7. DHS dismisses reliance interests and rushes the process (Sec. VI). Current students chose their programs, took on debt, and planned careers under the existing rules, and the fee would apply to them partway through their degrees. DHS also says schools may pass the cost to all students, which means U.S. students could end up paying for it. A rule with this much economic impact deserves the 60-day comment period that E.O. 12866 calls for, not 30 days.

8. The rule turns OPT into a privilege of wealth. Well-endowed schools and wealthy families can pay. Strong students at public, regional, and community institutions often cannot. The rule selects students by ability to pay, not by merit or integrity.

Recommendation: Withdraw the rule. To address fraud, DHS should pursue employer verification, more site visits, and enforcement against identified shell employers, and it should seek appropriations or a cost-based fee to fund SEVP oversight.

The proposed OPT fees could have consequences that extend well beyond the immigration system. They could undermine the competitiveness of American universities and research institutions, which play a critical role in the country's scientific and technological leadership.

International students are an important part of the academic and research ecosystem in the United States. They contribute to university revenues, participate in research projects, support teaching activities, and help laboratories maintain the skilled workforce needed to conduct advanced research. Their contributions do not end when they graduate. OPT provides a pathway for the knowledge and skills developed at American universities to be applied in businesses, research organizations, and other workplaces.

The proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee could discourage universities from supporting OPT participation, particularly when they have limited financial resources. Even if universities do not directly pass these costs to students, they will have to make difficult decisions about allocating institutional funds. This could affect research budgets, hiring decisions, and the ability of smaller institutions to compete for international talent.

There is also a broader concern about America's position in global higher education. International students choose where to study based not only on academic quality but also on whether they can reasonably pursue professional opportunities after graduation. If the United States becomes significantly less accessible for practical training, talented students may choose universities in other countries. Once they establish academic and professional networks elsewhere, the United States may lose opportunities for future research collaborations, business development, and innovation.

This is not simply a question of international enrollment. It concerns the long-term return on America's investment in education and research. Scientific discoveries, new technologies, and successful businesses often emerge from the collaboration between universities and industry. Policies that weaken these connections could reduce the country's ability to translate academic research into economic value.

I urge DHS to carefully evaluate the broader institutional and economic consequences of this proposal, rather than focusing primarily on the number of OPT participants. Protecting the integrity of the immigration system should not come at the expense of the universities and research institutions that help maintain America's global competitiveness.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
The proposed OPT fees appear to assume that reducing access to employment for international graduates will benefit American workers. However, this assumption overlooks how hiring decisions actually work.

Employment opportunities are not automatically transferred from one group of candidates to another. Employers hire based on qualifications, business needs, available budgets, and the expected value of a position. If an additional $70,000 fee makes hiring an international graduate financially impractical, the employer is not necessarily going to hire an American candidate instead.

In many cases, the position may simply remain unfilled. A company may cancel a planned hire, reduce its research activities, delay product development, or decide that a project is no longer financially viable. For startups and small businesses, one additional expense of this size can fundamentally change whether a hiring decision makes economic sense.

This distinction is important. A reduction in international hiring does not necessarily represent an increase in domestic employment. It could instead mean fewer jobs overall, less business investment, and reduced economic activity. American workers may ultimately lose opportunities when companies scale back or move their operations to other countries.

The proposed fee structure also raises questions about fairness and proportionality. It applies a substantial financial burden regardless of the size of the employer, the salary associated with the position, the nature of the work, or the actual risk of fraud. A small research organization and a large multinational corporation face the same fee, despite having very different financial capacities.

If the objective is to prevent fraudulent employment and protect U.S. workers, enforcement should focus on employers and arrangements that violate the rules. Stronger verification, targeted audits, and meaningful penalties for confirmed violations would address these concerns more directly.

Before adopting such a significant financial barrier, DHS should provide convincing evidence that it will actually improve employment outcomes for American workers rather than simply reduce legitimate hiring and economic activity.

I urge DHS to reconsider the proposal and evaluate its effects on total employment, business investment, and the competitiveness of American companies, not merely the number of international graduates participating in OPT.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fee harms employers, reduces jobs, and creates a heavy financial burden.

This difference could create an uneven playing field. Institutions in smaller cities and less economically developed regions often rely on international talent to support research, fill specialized positions, and contribute to local economic development. If these institutions cannot afford the proposed fees, they may become less competitive in recruiting qualified graduates.

The consequences could extend to local communities. Universities are often major economic contributors in their regions. Their research activities support local businesses, create employment, attract investment, and contribute to the development of new industries. Smaller companies also depend on access to specialized talent to grow. Making that talent significantly more expensive to employ could disproportionately affect communities that already have fewer resources and fewer alternatives.

There is also a risk that opportunities will become increasingly concentrated in large metropolitan areas and institutions with substantial financial backing. This would run counter to broader efforts to encourage innovation, entrepreneurship, and economic development across different parts of the country.

DHS should evaluate the regional distribution of these costs and consider whether the proposal would create unintended disadvantages for smaller institutions, rural communities, and emerging technology sectors.

A policy affecting a national employment and training program should account for the diversity of the U.S. economy, rather than assuming that all schools and employers have comparable financial capacity.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule. Charging schools $70,000 per student for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each later one, including STEM OPT, would weaken the American economy, strain American universities, and hand our competitors talent the U.S. has already paid to train.

I work as a scientist in the biotech sector and help hire research staff. U.S.-trained international graduates are a real part of the talent pool that keeps our research moving.

It throws away an investment America has already made. International students are educated at American universities, often in labs funded by American research dollars. OPT is how that training becomes work here, in U.S. labs, startups, hospitals, and factories. A six-figure price tag on that step means the U.S. trains scientists and engineers and then sends them to Canada, the UK, Australia, Germany, and China, all of which are actively recruiting the same graduates.

It hurts the American students it claims to protect. International tuition helps fund domestic students’ seats, financial aid, and graduate programs. DHS itself acknowledges that schools may pass the cost on to international students, to all students, or to employers. Either way, the burden lands on Americans. Lower international enrollment means lost tuition revenue, and American families, taxpayers, and the college towns that depend on these institutions absorb that loss.

It is the wrong tool for protecting workers. If the concern is that OPT undercuts American wages, the answer is wage and training standards, not a flat fee. STEM OPT already requires employers to provide a formal training plan and pay comparable to similarly situated U.S. workers. A flat fee does not distinguish a well-paid PhD researcher from a low-wage placement. It simply prices out smaller schools, students without family wealth, and startups and small businesses that cannot absorb $70,000 to $100,000 per hire. That leaves the largest companies as the only ones able to compete for this talent.
It is the wrong tool for fighting fraud. If SEVP has found abuse, the right response is targeted enforcement against the specific schools and employers involved. A blanket fee punishes thousands of legitimate institutions for the conduct of a few. And DHS would not even keep the fee revenue to fund enforcement.

The analysis contradicts itself. The rule’s claimed benefits depend on substantially reducing OPT participation: fewer participants to monitor, and more jobs for U.S. workers. Yet DHS’s economic analysis assumes schools will largely keep recommending OPT. Both cannot be true. Suppose the fee shrinks the pipeline. Then the U.S. suffers the losses to innovation, growth, and university finances that DHS waves off as too speculative to weigh. Suppose instead that it doesn’t shrink the pipeline. Then the rule delivers none of its stated benefits while imposing billions of dollars in annual costs, as DHS’s own estimates acknowledge. A rule built on contradictory assumptions should not be finalized.

It weakens U.S. competitiveness where it matters most. Leadership in AI, semiconductors, biotechnology, and advanced manufacturing depends on STEM talent, and international students make up a large share of U.S. STEM graduate programs. Many American companies, and the jobs they created, were founded by people who first came here as students. Pushing these graduates out just as they are ready to contribute hurts American competitiveness and national security.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed fee. If DHS has specific integrity concerns, it should address them through targeted enforcement, wage and training-plan compliance, and school oversight. Those measures protect American workers without dismantling a program that keeps American-trained talent working for America.

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fees. DHS has not provided a convincing economic justification for either the fee amount or its consequences.

DHS estimates that the proposal would collect approximately $12.4 billion annually. However, DHS itself classifies these payments as transfers, not new economic benefits. A recent analysis by the Institute for Progress (October 2026) estimates that the proposed fees could reduce annual U.S. GDP by approximately $362 billion after ten years under its central model. This is almost 29 times DHS's projected annual fee collections, although these are different economic measures and the GDP estimate concerns the longer-term impact.

DHS estimates only $4.1 billion in annualized economic costs under its primary scenario. But the agency assumes that the lost economic value of an OPT opportunity is no greater than the unpaid fee, instead of independently estimating the economic contribution of these workers. How can DHS conclude that the fees are reasonable when it has not properly quantified what the United States could lose?

Collecting money for the Treasury does not automatically make the country richer. If the fees discourage productive workers, reduce university enrollment, and damage American businesses, the U.S. could lose far more than the government collects.

I ask DHS to withdraw this proposal until it can provide a credible cost-benefit analysis that includes long-term economic losses.

As an international PhD student at an American university, I strongly oppose this proposal, especially its impact on students who are already studying in the United States.

The U.S. has already invested enormous resources in educating and training international students. In 2024 alone, the federal government funded $64.6 billion in university research, according to the National Science Foundation. International graduate students participate in this research, receiving specialized training while contributing to American scientific progress.

Many of these students spend five or more years completing their PhDs. By the time they graduate, they have developed specialized skills, research experience, and knowledge that American universities and companies can use.

According to NSF's 2026 report, approximately 73% of international science and engineering PhD graduates from 2017–2019 were still in the U.S. in 2023, around five years after graduation. Approximately 68% of an earlier cohort remained after ten years.

This means the U.S. has historically been able to retain much of the talent it trained. These graduates continue contributing through employment, research, innovation, and taxes.

However, the proposed $70,000 OPT fee could make it impossible for many students who are about to graduate to work in the U.S. What is the point of spending years training highly skilled researchers and then creating a financial barrier that drives them away just when they are ready to contribute?

DHS proposes only a 60-day transition period. But what about students who started their degrees three, four, or five years ago? Neither they nor their universities could have reasonably planned for a $70,000 fee when they began their education. How is 60 days sufficient to address years of educational and financial commitments?

There is also a long-term concern. Even if international students continue coming to the U.S. for education, making it difficult for them to stay afterward means they will take much of their American training and expertise back to their home countries or elsewhere.

Of course, international scientific cooperation has value. But why would the U.S. deliberately give up the opportunity to retain researchers it has already trained, especially when other countries would benefit from employing them?

OPT provides a way for the U.S. to receive a more direct return on its investment in international education. Graduates can apply their knowledge in American companies and research institutions, contribute to the economy, and help train the next generation of workers.

I don't understand how encouraging these graduates to leave would benefit the United States. It seems like an unnecessary waste of American educational resources and research investment.

I ask DHS to withdraw this proposal. At the very least, students who have already enrolled in American universities under the existing OPT rules should not be subjected to these enormous new fees.

I am an international student. I am now studying for a master's degree in computer science, and I will graduate in May 2027. I am writing to share how the proposed OPT fees would affect me and many students like me.

$100,000 is simply too much. My total cost to finish my master's degree is about $80,000, including tuition and two years of living expenses. This fee would increase my total cost of studying by 130%. If this rule had existed before, I would not have applied to universities in the US at all. I chose to study CS in the US because the job opportunities here are much better than in other countries, and the tech industry here is the best in the world. But if the OPT permission is this expensive, Europe and Singapore would be a better choice.

As far as I know, many younger Chinese students I know have already given up on applying to US universities because of the uncertain visa policies. They are now looking at Hong Kong and Singapore instead, where the visa and policy support is better. Many of them are excellent students, and most of them already have offers from top tech companies.

In my group — people who go back to school after working for about 5 years, mainly to make a breakthrough in their careers — most of us are very sensitive about budget. We have to give up our full-time jobs, pay a large amount of money for school, and take the risk of a career break. So our goals are very clear, and budget is very important. This fee would be a very important factor in our decision. I believe most people like us would simply give up the US option, because with our work experience, we can also go to work in Europe directly through employer sponsorship. Studying abroad is not a must for us. The balance is very delicate, and this fee would break that balance directly.

Not only people with career goals would give up the US. PhD students would too. To be honest, a PhD salary is only barely enough to live on, with the high cost of living. I know many PhD students need to work through summer internships, using CPT or pre-completion OPT. If both of these are restricted too, PhD students can only stay in school and do research. This is negative for both industry and research, because papers also need to be used in the real world to have value. Not being able to connect with industry is a very big disadvantage. And students who can get into US PhD programs usually have other good choices too.

One more point is the uncertainty itself. Students make their plans many years in advance. A new cost like this changes the rules after students have already started their programs. Also, even if the fee is charged to schools, schools may pass the cost to students, or become less willing to support OPT. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Tanya Maldonado
comments.commentText:
Re: Public Comment Opposing the Proposed OPT Fee Structure – DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100
I am writing to express my strong support for maintaining and protecting Optional Practical Training (OPT) opportunities for international students pursuing higher education in the US. I am deeply concerned about the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee for each F-1 international student recommended for OPT. While I recognize the government's responsibility to maintain the integrity of the immigration system and address potential misuse, I believe this proposed fee structure creates significant financial barriers, places an unreasonable burden on educational institutions, and undermines the educational and workforce-development benefits that OPT provides.
OPT is an essential bridge between academic learning and professional development. Students spend years investing in their education, developing specialized knowledge, and preparing for careers. Practical training allows them to apply classroom instruction to real-world situations, strengthen technical and professional skills, learn workplace expectations, and gain meaningful experience that cannot be fully replicated in a classroom.
Restricting access to OPT through excessive institutional fees risks creating a disconnect between academic achievement and meaningful career preparation. Students should have a reasonable opportunity to demonstrate what they have learned and develop the professional competencies necessary to succeed.
The proposed $70,000 initial fee per student creates an extraordinary financial burden for educational institutions, particularly smaller colleges, community-based institutions, and schools with limited operating budgets. Institutions could experience a financial impact that disrupts budgets, limits educational resources, and forces difficult decisions about which students they can afford to support.
A student who has successfully completed a degree and meets all eligibility requirements should not lose access to an essential career-development opportunity because their educational institution cannot absorb an extraordinary federal fee. The proposed fee also creates inequity among educational institutions. Larger, well-funded universities may have greater financial flexibility, while smaller institutions and schools will be unable to participate.
International students participating in OPT bring specialized knowledge and valuable skills to American businesses, nonprofit organizations, healthcare systems, educational institutions, and other community services. OPT participants contribute to projects, help organizations address workforce needs, and bring fresh perspectives to complex challenges. Consider the contributions of international graduates working in healthcare, technology, education, business, and scientific research. Their practical experience strengthens organizations while allowing them to apply their academic preparation in ways that benefit the broader public. In smaller communities, where employers may have difficulty attracting individuals with specialized skills, international graduates can help fill important workforce gaps.
I recognize that the federal government has a responsibility to prevent fraud, ensure compliance, and protect the interests of American workers. However, measures intended to address these concerns should be proportionate, targeted, and designed to preserve legitimate educational and professional opportunities.
A $70,000 initial fee per student is not a reasonable or sustainable mechanism for ensuring program integrity. It places the financial responsibility on educational institutions regardless of the individual student's circumstances, the quality of the educational program, or the legitimacy of the proposed employment experience.
There are more balanced approaches available, including strengthened institutional oversight, improved reporting requirements, verification of employment related to a student's field of study, and reasonable administrative fees that reflect actual oversight costs. These measures could help address legitimate government concerns without effectively pricing students and educational institutions out of the program.
The proposed fee structure threatens to turn an educational opportunity into a privilege available only to institutions with substantial financial resources and students whose employers or schools can absorb extraordinary costs.
I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to reconsider the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee. Thank you for considering this public comment and for recognizing the importance of maintaining accessible, meaningful practical training opportunities for eligible international students.
Respectfully,

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I urge DHS to withdraw the [proposed OPT fee rule](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/08/2026-20660/optional-practical-training-fees), including the fees in section V.A. Requiring schools to pay $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations, including STEM OPT extensions, would create a severe barrier to legitimate practical training. Protecting American workers and preventing fraud are valid goals, but these fees would penalize compliant students and institutions while putting America's long-term economic competitiveness at risk.

The financial burden would reach students regardless of who formally pays. DHS acknowledges that schools may pass costs to students or employers. If students pay, access would depend heavily on family wealth and borrowing capacity. If schools absorb the fees, they could restrict recommendations, raise tuition, or divert resources from teaching, research, and student services. An institution recommending 100 students for initial OPT would face $7 million in fees. A student's eligibility and academic merit should not become secondary to the size of a university's budget.

Students already enrolled deserve particular consideration. They committed years of study, tuition, and living expenses under a framework that allowed eligible students to apply for practical training. The opportunity to seek relevant training can reasonably influence educational and financial decisions. Applying a prohibitive new condition to future recommendations for these students could strand investments they cannot recover. Section V.C should give greater weight to these reliance interests.

The policy could also harm U.S. higher education exports. Students comparing countries consider the complete educational experience, including opportunities to apply classroom learning. Restricting that experience could discourage future enrollment. [NAFSA's analysis](https://www.nafsa.org/policy-and-advocacy/policy-resources/nafsa-international-student-economic-value-tool-v2) estimates that international students contributed $42.9 billion and supported 355,736 U.S. jobs in 2024-2025. These figures cover international students as a whole and show the economic activity at risk. Lower enrollment could hurt university budgets and businesses in college communities.

The longer-term cost is lost talent and innovation. America benefits when people trained in its universities can apply their skills in its laboratories and businesses. Making practical training unaffordable could encourage graduates to take those skills to competing economies. [NBER research](https://www.nber.org/papers/w30797) finds that immigrants represented 16% of inventors but accounted for 23% of patents in its sample. Although that study examines immigrants broadly, it illustrates why restricting skilled graduates' opportunities can carry consequences beyond an individual job opening. The United States risks educating talented people and then making it harder to benefit from their work.

Protecting U.S. workers requires evidence about job creation and displacement. Skilled colleagues can help teams develop products, expand operations, and support additional jobs. Some positions may go unfilled, projects may be delayed, and employers may move work elsewhere when needed talent is unavailable. Section VII.A should assess these potential outcomes. Small businesses, startups, and research organizations could be especially disadvantaged if they are asked to reimburse costs that larger employers can more readily absorb.

A large payment is also a poor substitute for verifying compliance. Ability to pay does not establish that training is legitimate, just as inability to pay does not establish fraud. DHS should target misconduct through employer verification, risk-based audits, checks that work relates to the student's degree, and meaningful penalties for fraudulent actors. If additional oversight funding is necessary, DHS should explain its costs and evaluate proportionate fees. A broad financial barrier could exclude honest participants while leaving the underlying methods of fraud insufficiently addressed.

Before imposing these fees, DHS should provide persuasive evidence that the amounts are necessary, assess effects on enrollment and research, and compare less burdensome alternatives. Fee revenue transferred to the government should not be confused with newly created economic value. The analysis must account for lost training, forgone earnings, reduced educational exports, and losses in innovation and business growth.

I respectfully request withdrawal of the $70,000 and $30,000 fees and preservation of accessible OPT for eligible students. Strong enforcement and worker protections can coexist with practical training that strengthens American universities, businesses, and long-term prosperity.

Of course, schools would be entirely unwilling to pay effectively a student's entire tuition simply to recommend them for OPT, and students would in almost all cases be unwilling or unable to pay. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Beatrice Spolidoro
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01, Optional Practical Training Fees

I am a Registered Architect, WELL Accredited Professional, and the Principal and CEO of Fisher ARCHitecture LLC, a small architecture firm in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, licensed in Pennsylvania, Ohio, and Maryland. I also teach at Carnegie Mellon University’s School of Architecture. I oppose the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fees (Sections IV.C and V.A).

My own path shows what temporary training programs are for. I came to the United States on a J-1 visa. It gave me twelve months to show an employer that I was worth investing in. I worked hard, earned that employer’s confidence, built a career here, and now run a firm that employs people and serves clients in three states. Programs like the J-1 and OPT work because merit is proven through work, and employers who value it can then choose to keep that talent here. DHS states that the fee will lead schools to recommend only “the most promising students” (Section IV.C). But a school’s willingness to pay $70,000 does not measure promise. The way to measure it is the one OPT already provides: a period of real, supervised work.

The fee does not reach the fraud DHS describes (Sections IV.A and IV.C). The rule’s evidence concerns employers: shell companies, staged worksites, and residential addresses with no employees. Yet the fee is triggered by a school’s recommendation and is not tied to any employer. A fraudulent employer pays nothing. A legitimate student at an accredited university loses access to OPT when the school cannot justify $70,000. DHS identifies roughly 10,000 students with highly suspect employers, out of more than 360,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants in 2024. A fee charged to every participant is not a proportionate response to a problem concentrated among a small share of employers.

The fee does not fund the oversight DHS says it lacks (Section IV.C). DHS states that its compliance resources have not kept pace with the program, but the proposed fees would go to the general Treasury, not to SEVP or ICE. The rule would reduce participation without adding any capacity to find fraud among those who remain.

Impact on small firms and the architecture profession (Section VII.B.6). The small-entity analysis looks at schools but not at small employers like mine. Architecture graduates must complete supervised professional experience through NCARB’s Architectural Experience Program before they can be licensed. For international graduates of U.S. architecture programs, OPT is how they earn that experience. Architecture schools will not pay $70,000 per student to recommend graduates for entry-level design positions. As a result, the rule would effectively close OPT to the profession, even though DHS has made no finding that architecture graduates or firms are involved in fraud. Small firms like mine would lose access to talented designers whom U.S. universities have already educated.

Recommendations.

Withdraw the fee. Alternatively, reduce it to the actual cost of oversight and direct the revenue to SEVP compliance.
Target employers, not schools and students. Extend the Form I-983 training plan, E-Verify, and employer attestations to post-completion OPT, and require verification that the business and worksite exist before employment begins. DHS considered this option in Section IV.C and rejected it because of the administrative effort involved. Effort aimed at the actual source of fraud is a better trade than a flat fee charged to legitimate participants.
At minimum, exempt small employers and licensure-track professions with structured, supervised experience requirements, and include small employers in the Regulatory Flexibility Act analysis.

Conclusion. I support DHS prosecuting OPT fraud. But this rule charges the wrong party, adds no enforcement capacity, and would remove the very mechanism through which people like me proved their worth and went on to contribute to the U.S. economy. I urge DHS to withdraw the fee and adopt employer-focused safeguards.

Beatrice (Bea) Spolidoro, RA, WELL AP
Principal and CEO, Fisher ARCHitecture LLC, Pittsburgh, PA
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees do not measure merit and would harm small businesses and talent retention.

I am an international graduate student who has spent several years pursuing higher education in the United States. I previously completed an undergraduate degree, completed Optional Practical Training, and am now pursuing further education in a healthcare and human services-related field.

I am deeply concerned about the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee.

Like many international students, I have invested years of my life and significant financial resources into obtaining an American education. My goal has always been to use that education to contribute meaningfully to the communities around me, particularly in fields where qualified professionals are needed.

I understand the importance of preventing fraud and protecting American workers. However, I struggle to understand how imposing fees of this magnitude accomplishes those objectives without disproportionately affecting students who have followed every immigration requirement and pursued their education in good faith.

Although these fees would technically be imposed on educational institutions, they would inevitably affect international students and their employment opportunities. Many institutions cannot reasonably be expected to pay tens of thousands of dollars for an individual student's OPT recommendation, particularly when that student is entering a profession that does not offer exceptionally high starting salaries.

What concerns me most is the uncertainty this creates for students who are already committed to completing their degrees. We made significant educational and financial decisions under an existing framework that provided a reasonable opportunity to gain professional experience after graduation. Changing that framework so dramatically risks leaving students with substantial debt and limited opportunities to use the education they worked so hard to obtain.

International students are not asking for guaranteed employment or permanent residency. We are asking for a reasonable opportunity to demonstrate our abilities, gain experience, and contribute to the country where we received our education.

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider these proposed fees and explore more targeted approaches to addressing fraud that do not effectively price legitimate students out of professional training.

Thank you for considering my perspective and for those who took the time to read.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Strong Opposition to Proposed OPT Fees – Docket ICEB-2026-0100

I strongly oppose the Department of Homeland Security's proposed rule imposing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for subsequent OPT authorization. While preventing immigration fraud and protecting American workers are legitimate objectives, these excessive fees would discourage talented international students from pursuing education in the United States, impose unrealistic financial burdens on universities, and undermine America's long-term economic competitiveness.

1. Unrealistic Financial Burden on Universities

The proposal assumes that American educational institutions will be willing and financially capable of paying $70,000 per student for OPT authorization. This assumption is fundamentally unrealistic.

Many American universities charge less than $70,000 in total tuition for an entire degree program. Expecting institutions to pay an additional $70,000 simply to recommend a student for practical training creates an unreasonable financial burden. Universities have little direct financial incentive to fund graduates' employment authorization after completing their education.

Consequently, many universities may stop recommending students for OPT altogether, regardless of their qualifications or potential contributions. Allowing institutions to pass these fees to students or employers does not resolve the problem; it merely transfers an unaffordable financial burden to another party.

2. Contradiction With President Trump's Vision of Attracting Global Talent

In a June 2024 interview, President Donald Trump suggested that international students graduating from American colleges should receive a Green Card along with their diploma. His remarks reflected an important principle: America benefits when it attracts, educates, and retains talented individuals from around the world.

The proposed OPT fees move in precisely the opposite direction.

Rather than encouraging highly educated graduates to contribute to America's economy, these restrictions would effectively force many talented individuals to leave after graduation.

The United States invests tremendous resources in building world-class universities and research institutions. Educating international students only to drive them toward competing countries after graduation would be economically counterproductive.

3. Threat to America's Leadership in Technology and Artificial Intelligence

America's leadership in technology, artificial intelligence, engineering, healthcare, and scientific research has been strengthened by generations of skilled immigrants and international graduates.

Foreign-born researchers, engineers, entrepreneurs, and technology professionals have helped build successful American companies, advance innovation, create employment opportunities, and strengthen the nation's global economic position.

At a time when countries are competing aggressively for leadership in artificial intelligence, semiconductor technology, advanced manufacturing, and scientific innovation, the United States should be attracting more exceptional talent, not creating barriers that push it away.

Countries such as Canada, Australia, and the United Kingdom actively compete to attract international graduates. These proposed fees would make America substantially less competitive as a destination for higher education and skilled professionals.

America risks educating the next generation of innovators only to see their knowledge, skills, and entrepreneurial potential benefit competing economies.

Conclusion

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee and instead adopt targeted, evidence-based measures to prevent fraud.

Protecting American workers and attracting global talent are not mutually exclusive goals. Skilled immigrants and international graduates have played an important role in making the United States a global leader in technology, innovation, and economic development.

President Trump's 2024 remarks recognized the value of retaining talented graduates educated in America. Policies should build upon that vision rather than undermine it.

America's greatest competitive advantage has always been its ability to attract the world's brightest minds. We should encourage these individuals to study, innovate, build businesses, and create jobs in the United States—not impose financial barriers that drive them toward competing nations.

I strongly urge DHS to reconsider this proposal in the interest of American economic growth, educational excellence, technological leadership, and long-term national competitiveness.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they impose unrealistic burdens and harm competitiveness.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Harsh Khot
comments.commentText:
Re: Public Comment Opposing Proposed Optional Practical Training Fees

Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 | RIN 1653-AB01

Dear Department of Homeland Security,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation.

As an international graduate of a U.S. university, I understand firsthand the significant financial, academic, and personal investment required to pursue higher education in the United States.

International students already contribute substantial tuition payments, living expenses, and valuable skills to American universities and communities. OPT provides an important opportunity to apply classroom knowledge in professional settings and contribute to the U.S. economy.

Although the proposed fees would formally be imposed on educational institutions, their magnitude raises serious concerns about whether universities could continue recommending eligible students for OPT. Institutions may be unable to absorb these costs, and students may ultimately face reduced access to practical training.

I recognize DHS’s stated objectives of preventing fraud, maintaining program integrity, and protecting American workers. However, I respectfully question whether imposing such substantial fees is a proportionate or effective approach to achieving those objectives.

I urge DHS to consider the following consequences:

1. Financial accessibility: Students from modest financial backgrounds may lose access to practical training despite meeting the same academic and immigration requirements as their peers.
2. American economic competitiveness: Restricting practical training opportunities could discourage talented international students from pursuing American degrees and limit employers’ access to graduates with specialized skills.
3. Impact on universities: Educational institutions, particularly those with limited financial resources, may face significant financial pressure or be forced to discontinue OPT recommendations.
4. Disruption to educational planning: Students who enrolled in U.S. universities with an understanding of existing OPT opportunities may face substantial changes to their post-graduation plans.
5. Availability of alternative safeguards: Targeted compliance audits, improved employer verification, enhanced reporting, and enforcement against documented violations could address program integrity concerns without imposing such substantial financial barriers.

I respectfully request that DHS reconsider the proposed fee structure, provide clear evidence supporting the necessity and proportionality of these amounts, and evaluate less burdensome alternatives.

I also urge DHS to carefully assess the effects on students who have already enrolled in or completed U.S. degree programs in reliance on existing practical training opportunities.

International graduates can contribute meaningful skills, innovation, and economic value to the United States. Immigration compliance and program integrity are important, but policies designed to achieve these objectives should also account for educational accessibility and economic consequences.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,

A U.S.-educated international graduate
comments.reason: The commenter expresses strong opposition to the proposed OPT fees, arguing they are disproportionate and harmful.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation under 8 CFR 214.13(i). As a taxpayer concerned about American workers, education, and economic competitiveness, I urge DHS to consider the costs this proposal could impose far beyond the students directly affected.

International students are an important source of tuition revenue for U.S. colleges and universities. Many pay full or nonresident tuition, and students in F-1 status generally cannot access federal student loans or grants. They and their families also spend money on housing, food, transportation, health insurance, and everyday necessities in American communities.

NAFSA (2025 economic impact analysis) estimated that international students at U.S. colleges and universities contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 jobs in the 2024-25 academic year. Those jobs include employment in higher education, accommodation, dining, retail, transportation, and other sectors.

OPT matters even before students graduate. The ability to obtain legitimate practical experience is one factor families consider when choosing where to invest years of tuition and living expenses. If that pathway becomes financially unattainable, prospective students may choose universities in other countries instead. This could also influence families making longer-term education decisions, including where their children attend secondary school before college. The proposed fees could therefore reduce future enrollment and spending, not merely the number of OPT applications.

Falling international enrollment could create a chain reaction. Schools with substantial international tuition revenue may have less funding for academic programs, laboratories, faculty, teaching assistants, student services, and financial aid. Some institutions could face program cuts, hiring freezes, layoffs, or even financial distress. American students could be affected through fewer course offerings, reduced scholarship resources, or increased pressure on tuition and institutional budgets. These effects would vary by institution, but DHS should evaluate them rather than assume the costs stop with the OPT applicant.

The impact would extend beyond campus. Local landlords, restaurants, grocery stores, coffee shops, bookstores, transportation providers, and other businesses depend in part on student spending. When enrollment declines, those businesses may lose customers and reduce hiring or hours. Communities surrounding colleges, particularly those where a university is a major employer, would feel the consequences. A policy presented as protecting American jobs should examine how many American jobs might instead be placed at risk.

There is another lost opportunity: American universities train graduates in skills and knowledge that U.S. companies can use. OPT allows graduates to apply that education in American workplaces, contribute to research and innovation, and help employers recruit qualified workers. Without an accessible practical-training pathway, some graduates will take those skills to other countries. The United States would lose the chance to benefit from expertise developed within its own educational system.

Legitimate OPT employment also occurs within a regulated framework. Authorized workers are subject to employment verification, applicable tax laws, and immigration reporting requirements. They earn documented wages and owe applicable U.S. income taxes. Maintaining clear, workable legal pathways can encourage transparent employment and compliance; imposing extraordinary financial barriers is not itself a targeted way to address unauthorized work, unreported income, or fraud.

I recognize DHS’s interest in protecting American workers and preventing program abuse. Those goals merit serious enforcement. But a $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee could punish compliant schools and students without directly identifying fraudulent conduct. DHS should consider stronger employer verification, audits, reporting, and penalties directed at proven violations, while assessing the effects of these proposed fees on university finances, scholarships, domestic tuition, local jobs, tax revenue, and the international competitiveness of American education.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee provisions and adopt proportionate, evidence-based safeguards. The United States should be able to benefit from the tuition revenue, jobs, tax contributions, and skilled workforce that its educational institutions help generate, rather than risk sending students, their spending, and their knowledge elsewhere.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Subject: Public Comment Opposing the Proposed OPT Fee Rule (Docket ICEB-2026-0100)**

To Whom It May Concern:

I am submitting this public comment in respectful but strong opposition to the proposed rule introducing substantial new fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT) and STEM OPT extensions.

As an international student, choosing to pursue higher education in the United States represents a significant academic, professional, and financial commitment. Students invest years of their lives and considerable financial resources in American universities, often with the expectation that they will have a reasonable opportunity to apply their education through practical training after graduation.

OPT is not simply an employment benefit. It is a critical bridge between academic education and professional development, particularly in engineering, science, technology, and research, where practical experience is essential to developing industry-relevant skills.

I fully recognize and respect the government's responsibility to protect American workers, safeguard employment opportunities, and ensure immigration programs serve the national interest. However, imposing extraordinarily high fees on OPT does not meaningfully address these objectives. Instead, it creates financial barriers that may ultimately harm American universities, employers, innovation, and economic competitiveness.

First, making OPT prohibitively expensive does not inherently protect American workers.A graduate's ability to participate in practical training should be based on qualifications, skills, and legitimate employment opportunities, not their ability to afford an extraordinary fee. If the objective is to prevent misuse of employment authorization programs, stronger compliance measures, wage protections, and enforcement of existing regulations would be more directly aligned with protecting American workers.

Second, these fees risk discouraging talented international students from choosing the United States. Students evaluate not only the quality of education but also the opportunities available after graduation. When practical training becomes financially inaccessible or unpredictable, talented individuals may increasingly choose countries offering more reasonable pathways from education to professional experience. The United States risks losing not only prospective students but also future researchers, engineers, entrepreneurs, and innovators.

Third, the proposal could undermine American innovation and competitiveness.American universities and industries have long benefited from attracting talented individuals from around the world. International graduates contribute to research, technological development, engineering, and specialized industries. Creating an excessive financial barrier at the transition from education to practical training risks weakening this talent pipeline and encouraging skilled graduates to contribute their knowledge and abilities elsewhere.

**Fourth, the financial impact extends beyond individual students.** International students already bear substantial tuition, living expenses, and immigration-related costs. Introducing exceptionally high fees near graduation creates financial uncertainty after years of investment. If employers are expected to absorb these costs, smaller businesses, startups, and research organizations may be disproportionately discouraged from considering qualified international graduates.

Importantly, protecting American workers and attracting international talent should not be viewed as mutually exclusive objectives. The United States can prioritize its domestic workforce while maintaining a fair, accessible, and well-regulated practical training program. A policy that discourages qualified graduates solely through financial barriers does not necessarily create better opportunities for American workers; it may instead reduce the country's ability to attract talent and compete globally.

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider the proposed fee structure, evaluate its economic and educational consequences, and pursue measures that directly address program integrity and worker protections without imposing disproportionate financial burdens on international students.

The United States has earned its reputation as a global leader in education, research, technology, and innovation partly because talented individuals from around the world have chosen to study and contribute here. Policies should strengthen that advantage rather than discourage future generations from making that choice.

Protecting American workers, supporting innovation, and attracting global talent are complementary goals. This proposal risks undermining all three without clearly demonstrating how such extraordinary fees would achieve their intended purpose.**

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw or substantially revise the proposed rule.

Respectfully submitted,

An International Student
