OPT is how F-1 students apply what they studied, and it is a large part of why international students choose U.S. schools. As I read the proposal, a school would have to pay $70,000 before it could recommend a student for initial OPT and $30,000 for each later recommendation, and USCIS would not grant work authorization until that payment is made. A fee of this size is far beyond what most colleges can absorb, especially smaller, tuition-dependent institutions. Schools may also pass the cost on to students or employers, which puts OPT out of reach for most students.
The proposal says its goal is to combat fraud and abuse. A flat fee on every recommendation does not target fraud. It penalizes honest students and the schools that follow the rules, and it does not appear tied to detecting or prosecuting abusers. DHS can pursue fraud through focused oversight of schools and employers that violate OPT rules.
The rule would also reduce international enrollment and the talent that U.S. employers rely on, while students who followed every rule lose the training they planned their studies around.
I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fee is too high, harms students and schools, and asks DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training fees in Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100.

A $70,000 initial fee, plus $30,000 for each later recommendation, bears no reasonable relationship to the administrative cost of a school official entering an OPT recommendation in SEVIS. Projections that the fees could collect roughly $8.4 to $16.5 billion a year show they would work as a revenue measure or a deterrent, not cost recovery. DHS's fee authorities, including INA § 286(m) and 8 U.S.C. § 1372, permit fees that recover the cost of services. They do not permit charges that effectively shut down a lawful program, and Congress has not delegated the power to impose what amounts to a tax.

OPT itself was upheld in Washington Alliance of Technology Workers v. DHS (D.C. Cir. 2022), and the Supreme Court declined review. DHS should not accomplish through prohibitive pricing what it has not proposed to do directly, through rescission and a full reasoned explanation.

Under the APA and DHS v. Regents (2020), DHS must also weigh serious reliance interests. By DHS's own count, roughly 290,000 students participated in OPT or STEM OPT in 2024. They enrolled, borrowed, and accepted job offers under existing rules, and employers built hiring plans around them. The proposed transition terms leave students already on OPT exposed to a new fee when they seek a STEM extension, so they do not adequately protect these interests.

Economically, Americans would bear much of the burden. International students contributed an estimated $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported about 356,000 U.S. jobs in 2024–25 (NAFSA). Their tuition also helps fund the financial aid, research, and faculty that serve domestic students.

DHS acknowledges that schools may pass these costs on to students or employers, which makes three outcomes likely:

•Many institutions, especially smaller colleges and public universities, would stop recommending OPT.
•Top students would choose the U.K., Canada, Australia, and other competitors that offer post-study work routes.
•U.S. employers would lose a pipeline of trained graduates in finance, technology, healthcare, and research, pushing that work and innovation overseas.

The rule's impact on small institutions also warrants a full Regulatory Flexibility Act analysis. Finally, a 30-day comment period is too short for a rule of this economic magnitude.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal. At minimum, DHS should tie any fee to documented processing costs, exempt students who enrolled before a final rule takes effect, and extend the comment period.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they are excessive and ignore reliance interests.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
The proposed $70,000 fee associated with Optional Practical Training (OPT) raises serious concerns about the long-term economic competitiveness of the United States, the financial stability of American universities, and the country's ability to attract and retain highly skilled talent.

The United States has spent decades establishing itself as a global leader in higher education, scientific research, technology, and innovation. Much of that success comes from attracting talented individuals from around the world who contribute to American universities, businesses, research institutions, and local economies. Introducing such an extraordinary financial burden risks undermining that competitive advantage.

A $70,000 fee is not a minor administrative adjustment. It represents a substantial financial obligation for educational institutions, many of which already face budget constraints. Universities may be forced to absorb these costs, transfer additional expenses to students, or limit their participation in OPT-related processes. Each outcome could negatively affect the American higher education system.

The broader economic implications deserve attention. International students contribute billions of dollars annually to the U.S. economy through tuition, housing, transportation, consumer spending, and other expenses. Their presence supports university employment, local businesses, and communities nationwide. If pursuing an American education becomes increasingly expensive or unpredictable, prospective students may choose countries offering more accessible post-graduation employment opportunities.

The United States would not simply lose prospective students. It could also lose tuition revenue, consumer spending, research contributions, entrepreneurial activity, and future skilled workers.

There is also a contradiction in educating talented individuals at American institutions while creating substantial financial obstacles to their participation in the American workforce. Universities provide specialized training in fields such as artificial intelligence, engineering, cybersecurity, healthcare, and data science. Restricting opportunities for these graduates to apply their education risks encouraging valuable skills and innovations to move to competing economies.

American employers, particularly startups, research organizations, and smaller technology companies, could also be affected. These organizations depend on access to specialized skills and diverse talent pools to remain competitive. Policies that reduce the availability of qualified graduates may create additional hiring challenges and limit opportunities for innovation and business expansion.

Furthermore, a fee of this magnitude raises fundamental questions about proportionality and economic justification. Administrative fees should reasonably reflect the costs of administering a program. A $70,000 charge warrants a transparent explanation of its necessity, the methodology used to calculate it, and the potential consequences for universities, students, employers, and the broader economy.

Immigration oversight and program integrity are legitimate government responsibilities. However, these objectives should be pursued through measures that are proportionate, evidence-based, and economically sustainable. Excessive financial barriers should not substitute for effective administration.

International competition for highly educated talent is intensifying. Countries around the world recognize the economic value of attracting graduates, researchers, and entrepreneurs. The United States should consider whether imposing extraordinary costs on its educational institutions will strengthen its position or encourage talented individuals to build their careers, businesses, and innovations elsewhere.

The potential consequences extend beyond immigration policy. They affect American jobs, university revenues, local economies, scientific advancement, technological leadership, and long-term economic growth.

Before implementing such a consequential fee, the Department should provide a comprehensive economic impact assessment examining its effects on university budgets, international student enrollment, OPT participation, employer access to talent, and U.S. competitiveness relative to other major education destinations.

The United States benefits when its universities remain globally competitive, its businesses have access to skilled workers, and its economy continues to attract innovation and investment. Any policy that could jeopardize these advantages deserves rigorous scrutiny, transparent justification, and consideration of less financially burdensome alternatives.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the $70,000 fee harms US competitiveness, universities, and international talent attraction.

I write in strong opposition to the proposed rule imposing a $70,000 fee for universities to recommend international students for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT), and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations.
Such a rule would place an undue financial burden on international students, universities, and employers, and would severely restrict international students' access to employment opportunities. Restricting their access to OPT would undermine the work of these institutions and the communities they serve, while discouraging employers from hiring qualified international graduates. These restrictions would also discourage talented international students from pursuing education in the U.S. and push international graduates to seek professional opportunities elsewhere, resulting in a loss of valuable talent and expertise from the national economy.
Overall, the proposed rule would place undue financial burdens on international students and American educational and research institutions, while restricting valuable employment opportunities and undermining the contributions of international workers. I strongly urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw this proposal and preserve accessible OPT pathways for international students and graduates.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 fee associated with Optional Practical Training (OPT). The fee would not ensure that employers, institutions, and students engage in appropriate practical training. Instead, it would make OPT financially inaccessible for many students and operationally unworkable for universities and employers. Students generally cannot afford a fee of this magnitude; institutions cannot absorb it on a per-student basis; and employers are unlikely to pay such a substantial amount before they have had an opportunity to assess a student’s work. Requiring payment before a designated school official can recommend OPT in SEVIS would also create serious procedural and administrative difficulties. Even where payment is possible, the proposal would increase costs for universities and for the government offices responsible for collecting and verifying the fee. In practical terms, the proposal risks ending OPT for many otherwise eligible students without meaningfully advancing program integrity.
Employers that are unable or unwilling to incur costs exceeding $100,000 for an H-1B petition are even less likely to pay $70,000 for an OPT student whose performance they have not yet had an opportunity to evaluate. The likely result is not better oversight, but fewer lawful training opportunities and reduced access to the U.S. talent pipeline.
OPT helps address critical workforce needs, particularly in science, technology, engineering, mathematics, and research. The Keep Innovators in America Act (H.R. 8013) reflects broader concerns that the United States does not currently produce enough graduates to meet demand in parts of the knowledge economy. International graduates can help fill documented skills gaps while complementing, rather than displacing, U.S. workers. A fee that effectively blocks participation in OPT would weaken this pipeline without addressing the underlying sources of program abuse.
International enrollment at U.S. institutions has already declined, creating financial pressure on colleges and universities and affecting U.S. jobs supported by international education. NAFSA reports that international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 jobs during the 2024 2025 academic year. NAFSA has also projected potential losses of $3.4 billion and 40,000 jobs in Fall 2026. A prohibitively high OPT fee would compound these economic harms by making the United States a less attractive destination for talented students.
Restricting practical training would also reduce the global competitiveness of U.S. higher education and weaken fields supported by universities, including science, technology, engineering, mathematics, and artificial intelligence. International students and scholars contribute substantially to U.S. innovation and economic vitality. According to NAFSA research cited in this comment, international student immigrants account for 25 percent of U.S. start-up companies valued at more than $1 billion, 42 percent of founders of leading artificial intelligence companies, and 40 percent of U.S. Nobel Prize winners in chemistry, medicine, and physics. The United States should retain this talent and provide lawful pathways through which international graduates can contribute. For many students, that pathway begins with OPT.
Universities share government interest in preventing fraud and protecting the integrity of the OPT program. Established public and private institutions already maintain policies for identifying and rejecting fraudulent documentation. Enforcement efforts should therefore focus on employers that exploit OPT participants; for example, by offering unpaid or underpaid work, charging students for purported employment, or providing false evidence of employment. Students may be victims of such schemes and should not be broadly penalized for misconduct committed against them.
SEVP field representatives regularly engage with universities and are positioned to assess institutional compliance within their areas of responsibility. Institutions that comply with reporting and oversight requirements should not be treated as complicit in fraud carried out by sham or abusive employers. A more targeted enforcement strategy would better protect students, preserve legitimate training opportunities, and direct government resources toward the actors responsible for misconduct.
For these reasons, I respectfully request that the agency withdraw the proposed $70,000 OPT fee and pursue narrower, evidence-based measures to prevent fraud and improve program oversight. As drafted, the proposal would impose disproportionate costs on students, institutions, employers, and the government; reduce access to lawful practical training; weaken U.S. universities; and undermine the nation’s competitiveness in STEM and other high-demand fields. The proposed fee is unlikely to achieve its stated purpose and would create substantial economic and administrative harm.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fee makes the program financially inaccessible and harms the U.S. talent pipeline.

I strongly oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees.

The United States has long stood for equal opportunity, fairness, and the belief that individuals should be judged by their abilities, contributions, and hard work—not by their nationality or financial circumstances.

This proposal fundamentally contradicts those values. Imposing fees of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT would create a deeply discriminatory barrier for international students who have studied legally, paid tuition, followed immigration regulations, and contributed to American universities and communities.

What is even more troubling is the decision to place this enormous financial burden on higher education institutions. Universities exist to educate students, advance research, and prepare graduates for meaningful careers. They should not be financially pressured into denying legitimate educational and professional opportunities to international students.

Rather than directly prohibiting OPT, this proposal risks achieving the same outcome through an unreasonable financial burden imposed on universities. This is deeply unfair to both students and educational institutions.

As an international graduate student, I find this proposal profoundly disappointing. I chose to pursue higher education in the United States because I believed in its commitment to academic excellence, opportunity, and merit. A policy that effectively makes practical training dependent on an institution’s ability to pay extraordinary fees undermines those principles.

If the government’s goal is to prevent fraud or protect workers, it should pursue targeted enforcement rather than impose sweeping financial barriers on students and universities acting in good faith.

I strongly urge DHS to withdraw this proposal. America should be strengthening its universities and attracting talented students from around the world, not placing extraordinary financial pressure on educational institutions to exclude them.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Dear Department of Homeland Security,

I am writing as an international master's student currently pursuing my education in the United States, coming from a developing country where opportunities like this are not easily available.

For students like me, studying in the United States is much more than earning a degree. It is a dream that takes years of hard work, financial sacrifices, and immense courage to pursue. Many of us leave behind our families, our homes, and everything familiar to us in the hope of building a better future. Our families often spend their lifelong savings or take on significant financial burdens just to give us this opportunity.

When I came to the United States, I came with the hope of receiving a quality education, learning valuable skills, and gaining practical experience that would help me grow professionally. I understood that the journey would not be easy, but I believed that if I studied hard, followed the rules, and worked honestly, I would at least have a fair chance to succeed.

The proposed $70,000 OPT recommendation fee makes that hope feel increasingly uncertain.

For someone coming from a developing country, $70,000 is not just a large amount of money. It can represent years of a family's earnings. Even though the proposed fee would be charged to universities, the possibility of schools passing these costs on to students or being unable to offer OPT recommendations is deeply concerning.

OPT is not simply about earning money. It is an opportunity to apply what we have spent years learning, gain meaningful professional experience, and contribute our knowledge and skills to American companies and communities. Without that opportunity, many international students could finish their degrees with substantial financial burdens and little chance to gain the practical experience they came here hoping to achieve.

I understand the importance of protecting American workers, preventing fraud, and maintaining the integrity of the immigration system. I respect those goals. But I sincerely believe that students who have followed the rules and invested so much in their education should not face barriers so financially overwhelming that their opportunities disappear before they even begin.

We are not asking for guaranteed jobs, special privileges, or shortcuts. We are simply asking for a fair chance to work hard, prove our abilities, and make meaningful contributions.

Behind every international student is a personal story, a family that believes in them, and years of effort that cannot be measured only in dollars. Policies like this affect real people, their futures, and the sacrifices their loved ones have made.

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider and withdraw this proposed fee structure and explore more reasonable, affordable approaches to strengthening the OPT program without making opportunities inaccessible to students from ordinary financial backgrounds.

As an international student currently pursuing higher education in the United States, I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and the additional $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation.

1. Undermining America's Global Competitiveness

OPT provides international graduates with an opportunity to apply their academic knowledge in real-world professional settings. The United States attracts talented students from around the world partly because of its educational and career opportunities. Making OPT prohibitively expensive could push talented graduates toward countries such as Canada, the UK, and Australia, weakening America's ability to attract and retain global talent.

2. Negative Impact on the U.S. Economy

International graduates contribute to the American economy through employment, taxes, research, innovation, and consumer spending. The proposed fees could discourage employers from hiring international graduates due to additional costs, even when those candidates are highly qualified. This would hurt both American businesses seeking skilled talent and the broader economy.

3. An Ineffective Approach to Preventing Fraud

If the government's objective is to prevent OPT abuse, imposing excessive fees on all participants is an overly broad and unfair approach. Legitimate international students who comply with immigration regulations should not be penalized for misconduct by unrelated individuals or organizations. The government should instead focus on targeted investigations and stronger enforcement against fraudulent employers and institutions.

4. Unreasonable Financial Burden on International Students

International students already face substantial financial challenges, including higher tuition costs and limited access to financial aid. Although the proposed fees would technically be paid by universities, these costs could ultimately be passed on to students or employers. This would create an unreasonable financial barrier for graduates who have already invested significant time and money in their American education.

Conclusion

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider and withdraw this proposal. I support reasonable oversight of the OPT program, but such oversight should not come at the expense of legitimate international students and American economic competitiveness. International students are not merely recipients of American education; they are contributors to its universities, businesses, and communities. Preserving reasonable opportunities for them to work after graduation benefits not only international students but also the United States as a whole.

Dear Department of Homeland Security,

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation.

I understand the importance of preventing fraud, maintaining immigration system integrity, and protecting American workers. However, these goals should be pursued through targeted, evidence-based enforcement rather than extraordinary financial barriers that may harm students who follow the law.

First, legitimate F-1 students should not bear the consequences of others' misconduct. International students comply with immigration rules, invest substantial resources in their education, and contribute to universities and local communities. Fraud should be addressed through investigations, employer verification, and enforcement against those responsible. DHS should explain, with evidence, why these particular fees would prevent fraud more effectively than targeted oversight. Reducing OPT participation is not the same as identifying fraudulent activity.

Second, access to practical training should not depend on wealth. Many students and their families make significant financial sacrifices to study in the United States. Although the proposed fees would be charged to educational institutions, schools could pass the costs on to students or limit OPT recommendations. A $70,000 barrier could deny qualified graduates opportunities because of financial circumstances rather than academic performance, professional ability, or compliance with the law.

Third, the proposal would create uncertainty for students who made educational and financial commitments under the current system. Many chose U.S. universities partly because they understood they might qualify for a limited period of lawful, degree-related practical training. Imposing a drastic new financial barrier after students have already enrolled could undermine confidence in the predictability of U.S. education and immigration policies. DHS should specifically assess the effects on currently enrolled students and those approaching graduation.

Fourth, OPT participants can contribute valuable skills and perspectives to American employers and communities. Small businesses, in particular, may lack the resources to absorb substantial additional costs. DHS should examine whether the proposal could discourage future international enrollment or prevent graduates from applying skills developed at U.S. institutions, while also evaluating its claimed benefits for American workers.

Finally, I ask DHS to consider proportionate alternatives: stronger verification of genuine employment, better oversight of institutions and employers with documented compliance issues, improved reporting, and focused enforcement against proven fraud. Any fee should be reasonable, transparent, and justified by evidence of its costs and expected effects. DHS should also evaluate whether the proposal would disproportionately burden students from lower-income backgrounds.

International students are not asking for special treatment. They are asking for a fair opportunity to use the education they worked hard to earn, without facing disproportionate barriers because of others' misconduct.

Please withdraw the proposed fee structure and pursue measures that protect program integrity while preserving fair access for law-abiding F-1 students.

Thank you for considering this comment.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Member of the Public

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Tingyu Wu
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security:

I am writing as an international undergraduate student at a U.S. university to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule, Optional Practical Training Fees, particularly Sections V.A, VI, and VII concerning the proposed fees, reliance interests, and economic impacts.

1. The proposed fees are financially disproportionate and create serious barriers to legitimate practical training.
The proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee are extraordinarily high relative to the purpose of Optional Practical Training. Although the proposal formally requires educational institutions to make these payments, DHS explicitly acknowledges that institutions may transfer the costs to international students, other students, or employers.
This raises a fundamental question: who can realistically afford these fees?
Many international graduates pursue entry-level positions, research assistantships, internships, or other early-career opportunities that provide valuable training but do not offer the financial resources necessary to absorb such substantial costs. Universities, particularly public institutions, may also be unable or unwilling to pay tens of thousands of dollars for each eligible student.
As a result, otherwise qualified students could lose access to practical training solely because they or their institutions cannot afford the fees.

2. Financial capacity is not a reliable measure of immigration compliance or educational legitimacy.
DHS identifies fraud prevention and program integrity as central justifications for the proposal. These are legitimate regulatory objectives. However, the proposed fee structure does not meaningfully distinguish compliant students and employers from those engaging in misconduct.
A student who has maintained lawful F-1 status, completed a legitimate degree, and obtained a training opportunity directly related to their field of study should not be presumed less deserving of OPT authorization because their university or employer cannot afford a $70,000 payment.
Conversely, the ability to pay a substantial fee does not establish that a training opportunity is legitimate.
DHS should provide evidence demonstrating that these specific fee amounts would reduce fraudulent participation more effectively than targeted verification, employer oversight, reporting requirements, or enforcement against documented violations.

3. The proposal would undermine academic research and the development of early-career talent.
As a mathematics student interested in research and graduate study, I am particularly concerned about the impact on research-oriented graduates.
OPT provides an opportunity for international students to apply their academic training in university laboratories, research groups, and other professional environments. Some of these opportunities offer modest compensation or depend on limited research funding.
A fee of $70,000 per student could make such positions financially infeasible, even when the research is legitimate, academically valuable, and directly related to the student's degree.
This would harm not only international graduates but also universities and research groups that benefit from their contributions.

4. The proposal inadequately addresses the reliance interests of students who have already invested in U.S. education.
International students make substantial academic, financial, and personal commitments when pursuing degrees in the United States. Many reasonably incorporate the existing OPT framework into their educational and career planning.
The proposed transition period does not adequately address the situation of currently enrolled students who made these commitments years before the proposed rule was announced but have not yet received an OPT recommendation.
Such students cannot simply reverse years of educational investment or fundamentally restructure their professional plans within a short transition period.

5. DHS should reconsider the proposed fee structure and evaluate less restrictive alternatives.
I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fees.
If DHS determines that additional program-integrity measures are necessary, it should evaluate targeted oversight, improved verification, and proportionate administrative fees supported by documented regulatory costs.
At a minimum, DHS should provide a transparent justification for the proposed amounts, assess the financial burden on students and public universities, evaluate impacts on research and early-career employment, and establish meaningful protections for students already enrolled in U.S. institutions.
OPT should remain a legitimate educational training opportunity governed by compliance with immigration regulations, not by the financial capacity of individual students, universities, or employers.

Thank you for considering my comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and ask DHS to withdraw the rule.

1. DHS lacks authority for what is functionally a tax. The fees would go to the general Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, ICE would not keep them, and DHS set the amount by reference to the H-1B fee rather than any cost (NPRM § IV.C). INA 214(a) lets DHS set the "time and conditions" of a student's stay; it does not authorize a $109 billion, ten-year revenue charge on schools. When Congress wanted an anti-fraud fee for a skilled-worker program, it set one itself: $500, earmarked for fraud detection (INA 214(c)(12)). A federal court has already vacated the H-1B fee policy this fee is modeled on, holding among other things that such a payment needs clear authorization from Congress (California v. Mullin, D. Mass. 2026).

2. A student visa has never ended at graduation. Post-graduation practical training dates to 1947. Congress re-enacted the student-visa language in 1952 and has amended the statute many times without disturbing it, and the D.C. Circuit upheld OPT in 2022. In applied fields, supervised practice is part of education, just as residency is for physicians.

3. OPT does not take American jobs. The 360,078 OPT and STEM OPT participants in 2024 (§ IV.B) are about 0.2% of a 170.8 million-person labor force. DHS's own figure puts 2025 unemployment in computer occupations at 3.02%, below the 4.3% national rate. The two most recent studies of the 2016 STEM OPT extension found higher native employment and wages. A large Stanford payroll study links part of the recent decline in entry-level software jobs to AI, which the NPRM never mentions.

4. Restricting OPT sends jobs abroad. When H-1B visas were restricted in 2004, U.S. multinationals expanded hiring at foreign offices, particularly in China, India and Canada (Glennon, Management Science, 2024). India's 2,117 corporate "global capability centers" already employ 2.36 million people. The NPRM assumes lost OPT jobs go to Americans and never considers offshoring.

5. The fee misses the fraud. Most fraud DHS describes involves employers (shell companies, staged worksites), yet employers pay nothing, and the fee is paid before any employer is known. DHS's largest investigation flagged about 2.8% of participants; the fee hits all of them and selects for ability to pay, not merit.

6. DHS's math does not hold up. It projects up to $8.2 billion a year in costs and quantifies no benefits. Its method values a lost 24-month STEM extension at no more than the $30,000 fee, or $15,000 a year, less than a full-time federal minimum-wage job ($15,080). It compares 165,524 STEM OPT participants, a two-year group, with the 85,000 annual H-1B cap; its own annual figure, 95,384, is 12% above the cap, not "nearly double."

7. It breaks reliance. Under proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(3), schools would owe $70,000, not $30,000, for graduates already working on OPT who apply for the STEM extension, as DHS's own Year 1 assumption confirms (§ VII.A.4.a).

8. The process is deficient. An economically significant rule received only a 30-day comment period, key fraud evidence is cited to a YouTube video rather than docketed data, and the UMRA and federalism analyses contradict themselves.

Fraud should be fought with employer verification, enforcement of existing unemployment limits, and a cost-based fee spent on oversight. I ask DHS to withdraw this rule or, at minimum, extend the comment period to 60 days, docket its underlying data, and protect students already enrolled or on OPT.

Additional point: an "anti-fraud" fee that funds no anti-fraud work is a tax. DHS justifies the fee as fraud prevention, yet concedes the money funds none: it goes to the general Treasury as miscellaneous receipts (31 U.S.C. 3302), ICE "would not maintain or use" it, and DHS says only that Congress "could later" appropriate it (§ IV.C). No cost study supports the amount; DHS chose it to be "comparable to the fee for H-1B visas." A charge that pays for no service, ignores cost, and is designed to change behavior is a tax (see National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 1974), and taxing power belongs to Congress. Congress knows how to fund fraud prevention: for H-1B and L petitions it set a $500 fee and directed it to a fraud prevention and detection account (8 U.S.C. 1184(c)(12), 1356(v)). DHS proposes a charge 140 times larger that funds no detection at all. Even when the Supreme Court upheld an agency-collected charge in FCC v. Consumers' Research (2025), it relied on the statute limiting collections to what the program needs; INA 214(a) sets no amount, purpose or ceiling. If fraud is the concern, the logical remedy is enforcement paid for by a cost-based fee, not a revenue measure DHS cannot even spend.

I have attached as a PDF, a much more detailed analysis of these arguments, I urge this analysis be taken into consideration as it covers the effects this fee could have.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for subsequent OPT. DHS should withdraw this excessive proposal. Imposing these charges on educational institutions would discourage legitimate participation, undermine American higher education, and weaken our ability to retain talent. [1]
International students are an economic asset. NAFSA estimates that international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 jobs in 2024–2025. These figures cover international education overall, rather than OPT alone, but demonstrate the economic interests threatened by policies that discourage studying here. American businesses and communities share these benefits. [2]
OPT helps turn education at American universities into skills available to American employers. Research published in the Journal of Public Economics found that international graduates contribute to the U.S. skilled labor supply and that transitions into employment were higher for STEM graduates following the 2008 OPT expansion. [3] Making practical training prohibitively expensive risks sending that talent elsewhere.
The stakes for technological leadership are substantial. NSF reports that temporary visa holders earned 62% of U.S. research doctorates in computer and information sciences, 56% in engineering, and 53% in mathematics and statistics in 2023. [4] NSF also found that 73% of temporary visa holders who earned U.S. science and engineering doctorates during 2017–2019 remained here in 2023. These are not estimates of OPT’s independent effect, but they demonstrate the lasting value of retaining internationally educated talent. [5]
DHS’s fraud rationale does not justify a blanket financial barrier. Documented misconduct deserves enforcement. However, Section IV.A’s criminal cases and investigations—including students associated with highly suspect employers—do not themselves establish a representative, adjudicated program-wide fraud rate. Suspicions, charges, and proven violations are different categories. [1]
“Fraud, waste, and abuse” cannot substitute for measurement. DHS should identify substantiated violations, relevant time periods and populations, actual losses, and the harm these particular fees would prevent. Available evidence does not establish that fraud is nonexistent or necessarily nominal. Equally, individual cases cannot establish that the entire program warrants prohibitive charges.
GAO’s 2014 OPT review identified weaknesses in risk assessment, employment information, and monitoring. Those findings support better oversight and reliable data. They do not establish that charging compliant institutions tens of thousands of dollars per participant is an effective remedy. [6]
A payment is not a verification system. Wealth does not establish compliance, and limited resources do not establish wrongdoing. An institution recommending initial OPT for 100 students would face $7 million in proposed fees alone. That arithmetic illustrates the proposal’s extraordinary scale; it does not demonstrate any corresponding enforcement benefit.
If DHS needs additional oversight resources, it should publish a transparent cost analysis and explain why targeted investigations, employer verification, improved reporting, and sanctions against proven violators would be insufficient. It should also distinguish fees collected from genuine net economic benefits: money transferred to the government does not automatically offset lost education, research, innovation, or productive employment.
I urge DHS to:
Withdraw the proposed fees.
Publish a transparent assessment of substantiated OPT violations and their prevalence.
Compare targeted enforcement alternatives with the proposed blanket charges.
Assess effects on enrollment, research, local jobs, talent retention, and competitiveness.
Support any alternative administrative fee with demonstrated costs and a proportionate justification.
America should enforce its rules while preserving a valuable training pathway. This proposal fails to demonstrate why its extraordinary charges are necessary or why their benefits would outweigh the damage. Pricing legitimate participation out of reach would surrender American economic advantages without establishing that misconduct will be prevented.
Sources:

[1] DHS proposed rule, especially Section IV.A:
https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-10-08/html/2026-20660.htm

[2] NAFSA economic impact estimates:
https://www.nafsa.org/policy-and-advocacy/policy-resources/nafsa-international-student-economic-value-tool-v2

[3] Beine, Peri, and Raux, 2023:
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpubeco.2023.104917

[4] NSF doctorate data:
https://ncses.nsf.gov/pubs/nsf25300/figure/A

[5] NSF graduate retention:
https://ncses.nsf.gov/pubs/nsf25325/table/1

[6] GAO OPT oversight report:
https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-14-356
Federal Register, Volume 91 Issue 194 (Thursday, October 8, 2026)

comments.commentText:
Re: Docket ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees
I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule. I write as a former F-1 student from Kenya who completed my degree in the United States, worked on OPT, and now works and pays taxes in New York.
1. The fee is larger than a graduate's salary. My first full-time job on OPT paid $70,000 a year before taxes. The proposed $70,000 fee for a first OPT period equals my entire first-year gross pay, and with a later OPT period the total would reach $100,000. Even if schools are billed, most cannot absorb these amounts. They would pass the cost to students or stop supporting OPT. Either way, the practical result is the same: only the wealthiest students could use a benefit that has always been tied to their field of study, not their family's bank account.
2. OPT is now the only path to work experience. With Curricular Practical Training currently restricted, OPT is often the only way an international student can gain any US work experience connected to their degree. Practical training is part of how a US education works. Putting it out of reach removes a core part of the education students were admitted to receive.
3. Students on OPT follow the rules closely, because the rules are strict. When I arrived, I quickly learned there are rules at every corner. I followed each one. I never fell out of status, and I reported every required update to SEVIS on time. That is typical, not exceptional: students on OPT know that losing status or employment can mean leaving the country, so we are careful, law-abiding members of our communities.
4. OPT is short, limited, and works for both sides. OPT lasts 12 months, and up to 36 months only for eligible STEM graduates with employers that use E-Verify. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Subject: Public Comment Opposing the Proposed OPT Fee Rule (Docket ICEB-2026-0100)**

To Whom It May Concern:

I am submitting this public comment in respectful but strong opposition to the proposed rule introducing substantial new fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT) and STEM OPT extensions.

As an international student, choosing to pursue higher education in the United States represents a significant academic, professional, and financial commitment. Students invest years of their lives and considerable financial resources in American universities, often with the expectation that they will have a reasonable opportunity to apply their education through practical training after graduation.

OPT is not simply an employment benefit. It is a critical bridge between academic education and professional development, particularly in engineering, science, technology, and research, where practical experience is essential to developing industry-relevant skills.

I fully recognize and respect the government's responsibility to protect American workers, safeguard employment opportunities, and ensure immigration programs serve the national interest. However, imposing extraordinarily high fees on OPT does not meaningfully address these objectives. Instead, it creates financial barriers that may ultimately harm American universities, employers, innovation, and economic competitiveness.

First, making OPT prohibitively expensive does not inherently protect American workers.A graduate's ability to participate in practical training should be based on qualifications, skills, and legitimate employment opportunities, not their ability to afford an extraordinary fee. If the objective is to prevent misuse of employment authorization programs, stronger compliance measures, wage protections, and enforcement of existing regulations would be more directly aligned with protecting American workers.

Second, these fees risk discouraging talented international students from choosing the United States. Students evaluate not only the quality of education but also the opportunities available after graduation. When practical training becomes financially inaccessible or unpredictable, talented individuals may increasingly choose countries offering more reasonable pathways from education to professional experience. The United States risks losing not only prospective students but also future researchers, engineers, entrepreneurs, and innovators.

Third, the proposal could undermine American innovation and competitiveness.American universities and industries have long benefited from attracting talented individuals from around the world. International graduates contribute to research, technological development, engineering, and specialized industries. Creating an excessive financial barrier at the transition from education to practical training risks weakening this talent pipeline and encouraging skilled graduates to contribute their knowledge and abilities elsewhere.

**Fourth, the financial impact extends beyond individual students.** International students already bear substantial tuition, living expenses, and immigration-related costs. Introducing exceptionally high fees near graduation creates financial uncertainty after years of investment. If employers are expected to absorb these costs, smaller businesses, startups, and research organizations may be disproportionately discouraged from considering qualified international graduates.

Importantly, protecting American workers and attracting international talent should not be viewed as mutually exclusive objectives. The United States can prioritize its domestic workforce while maintaining a fair, accessible, and well-regulated practical training program. A policy that discourages qualified graduates solely through financial barriers does not necessarily create better opportunities for American workers; it may instead reduce the country's ability to attract talent and compete globally.

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider the proposed fee structure, evaluate its economic and educational consequences, and pursue measures that directly address program integrity and worker protections without imposing disproportionate financial burdens on international students.

The United States has earned its reputation as a global leader in education, research, technology, and innovation partly because talented individuals from around the world have chosen to study and contribute here. Policies should strengthen that advantage rather than discourage future generations from making that choice.

Protecting American workers, supporting innovation, and attracting global talent are complementary goals. This proposal risks undermining all three without clearly demonstrating how such extraordinary fees would achieve their intended purpose.**

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw or substantially revise the proposed rule.

Respectfully submitted,

An International Student

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ethan Baxter
comments.commentText: I write to oppose the proposed fees totaling $100,000 for STEM Optional Practical Training (OPT).  These exorbitant fees will obviously discourage if not outright prevent international scholars - in whom American institutions will already have invested - from staying in the United States after graduation to continue work.  As a professor and associate dean at an R-1 institution, I see how many outstanding international scholars come to American universities for their PhD.  We admit them because they meet our qualifications and because they can help power our research during their PhD.  We invest in them by providing classes, advising, mentoring, and research experiences.  We encourage all of our PhD students to develop a broad network, including international partners, because that is how science progresses most effectively.  This rule does nothing to prevent international scholars from coming to our universities for their PhD in the first place (if it did, I would oppose that as well).  Rather, it prevents those international PhD students from staying in the USA after they get their PhD.  This is simply foolish.  We will already have made the significant investment in them during their PhD.  Why would we then prevent them from staying in the USA where we could all continue to benefit from their training, skills, and knowledge?  It would be like Microsoft investing in an employee development program for their top up and coming employees and then forcing all of them to go to Apple after they finish the program.  This proposed OPT rule makes no sense and should be stopped.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by St. Jude Children's Research Hospital
comments.commentText:
As a leading pediatric research and treatment institution, St. Jude relies on a highly specialized, skilled, and nationally and globally sourced workforce to advance scientific discovery and improve outcomes for children with catastrophic diseases, many of which are rare or poorly understood. To make progress, we need to recruit researchers and physician-scientists with focused experience and niche expertise and training that are capable of advancing our understanding of these diseases and developing cures. International students graduating from U.S. universities are an essential component of that workforce. This includes OPT participants.

We are deeply concerned that the proposed fee structure, consisting of a $70,000 fee for initial OPT authorization and a $30,000 fee for STEM OPT extension, would create significant barriers that would undermine the purpose of the OPT program and reduce our and other U.S. institutions’ ability to recruit and retain highly qualified research and scientific talent. The proposal would also adversely affect employers that depend on international graduates to fill other specialized positions. For St. Jude, the STEM OPT program serves as a critical bridge that enables graduates to gain practical experience and contribute to the science that is providing life-saving cures for Americans, while employers and employees pursue longer-term immigration options. The proposed $30,000 STEM OPT fee would significantly increase employment costs and could force us and other employers to alter longstanding workforce and immigration strategies that support both employee success and institutional needs. This will harm our ability to achieve new cures and means of prevention for the devastating childhood illnesses our institution studies and treats. Policies that discourage highly educated research and healthcare professionals from contributing their talents in the United States may more generally have unintended consequences for the pace of scientific discovery and medical innovation across academia and the healthcare sector that would save lives. We ask that DHS consider the downstream impact of these proposed fees on research institutions and the patients whose lives depend on continued advances in medicine, treatment and care before finalizing this rule.

The proposed fees are unprecedented in magnitude and would likely discourage many international students from pursuing employment opportunities in the United States after graduation, or even pursing an education in the US at all. For recent graduates, a $70,000 fee represents a substantial financial burden that is out of proportion to the benefit received and is beyond the means of most individuals beginning their professional careers. As a result, many talented graduates may choose to leave the United States rather than participate in the OPT program.

In the biomedical research field, workforce development often requires several years of post-graduate training and experience before an individual is prepared to pursue permanent residence or longer-term employment-based immigration pathways. OPT and STEM OPT provide a valuable period during which researchers can strengthen their credentials, contribute to critical scientific innovation and research, and establish themselves professionally. The proposed fees would disrupt this pathway and diminish the United States’ ability to attract and retain top global scientific and research talent. The United States has long benefited from welcoming highly educated international graduates who contribute to innovation, research, healthcare, and economic growth. Policies that create substantial financial barriers to participation in OPT risk driving talent to other countries competing for the same individuals. Such an outcome would be detrimental to U.S. research institutions, universities, employers, and the broader economy.

For these reasons, St. Jude respectfully urges DHS to withdraw the proposed fee increases, or, at a minimum, substantially reduce the fees to levels that are reasonably related to the administrative costs of operating the OPT program, or, exempt US academic medical centers from this proposed fee increase. We also encourage DHS to carefully evaluate the impact of the proposed fees on U.S. competitiveness, scientific research and discovery, healthcare innovation, and workforce development before moving forward with any final rule.

Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on this important matter.

Respectfully submitted,
St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an international graduate student in a STEM master's program at a U.S. public university, and I am writing to oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent fees for Optional Practical Training.

OPT was one of the main reasons why I chose to study in the United States. I had other options, including staying in my home country and studying online or studying in some other countries. I chose a U.S. program and accepted much higher costs because OPT and the STEM extension would let me apply my training in real work after graduation. Without a realistic path to OPT, the cost of a U.S. degree would have been hard to justify, and I likely would not have enrolled. Many of my international classmates made the same decision for the same reason.

The fee is effectively a ban. The rule places the fee on schools, but schools can pass it on to students or employers. Few students can pay $70,000 at graduation, especially after paying out-of-state tuition and living costs with limited ability to work during school. An initial OPT period plus the STEM extension could total $100,000, more than most master's programs cost. Many universities and employers will not pay this either. In practice, the proposal would end OPT for nearly everyone except the wealthiest students, without Congress or DHS openly deciding to eliminate the program.

It would hurt U.S. universities and communities. International graduate students pay substantial tuition that helps fund programs, research, and teaching for domestic students. Many of us also work as teaching and research assistants, grading, running labs, and supporting faculty research. If OPT becomes unaffordable, prospective students will choose Canada, the UK, Australia, Germany, and other countries that offer post-study work paths. U.S. universities will lose enrollment and revenue, and graduate programs in STEM fields that depend on international students could shrink.

It would weaken U.S. competitiveness. OPT lets employers keep talent trained in this country, often in fields with real shortages. Charging a fee this large would push graduates trained at U.S. universities to bring their skills to competing economies. The United States would pay for part of their education and then lose the benefit.

Some specific concerns I have with this proposal

- Charging $70,000 plus $30,000 when a student uses both pre- and post-completion OPT would effectively remove pre-completion OPT, which many students rely on for internships tied to their studies.
- I strongly oppose the alternative of charging $70,000 again at each higher degree level. It would penalize students for pursuing advanced education in the United States.
- Current students enrolled based on the rules in place when they applied. Applying these fees to students who are already partway through their programs, or who are about to move from OPT to the STEM extension, is unfair and disrupts plans they made in good faith.
- If DHS is concerned about misuse of OPT, targeted compliance measures such as stronger reporting, employer verification, and enforcement against bad actors would address it without pricing out legitimate students.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees. If it does not, I ask that the amounts be lowered to a level that reflects actual administrative cost, that current students be exempt, and that DHS drop the alternative to re-charge at each degree level.

Thank you for considering this comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
While supportive of reducing fraud and abuse of government programs, my comment is submitted in opposition Proposed Rule, Optional Practical Training Fees, 91 FR 64566, Cock N. ICEB-2026-0100. My opposition is based on the exorbitant level of the fee, failure to address the stated problem, internal inconsistencies within the proposed rule, and lack of legal authority for the fee.

The proposed rule does not explain the logic behind the fee amount or adequately address the fee’s impact on educational institutions. At my institution, a small school with fewer than 100 students in F-1 status, the published cost of attendance is approximately $65,000 and our average discount rate is 60%, so almost no students pay the full cost of attendance, including international students. This places the fee well above what most students are paying for a single year of education.

As many schools will be unable or unwilling to make payments in the amount of $70,000 for even the most promising international student’s OPT request, the cost will likely be passed to the student, should they recommend OPT at all. My entire office budget dedicated to international students is less than $15,000, making it impossible to pay such fees from the institution. I am not aware of any student in my current cohort that could pay an additional $70,000 to apply for OPT authorization.

Each year, my small institution graduates 15-20 international students. Approximately 5-6 of them apply for OPT, often in healthcare roles with staffing shortages and in the business world. These students each meet the regulatory eligibility requirements for OPT and diligently report their employment. The proposed rule would require DSOs to discriminate between their students submitting OPT requests. Nowhere do the regulations provide for prioritizing students based on financial resources, employment prospects, or other criteria to discriminate between eligible students.

The proposed rule does not address the problem DHS is trying to solve. This failure happens in three places:
1)There is no evidence provided that students with fewer financial resources are more likely to engage in fraud. A student or school’s financial resources has no direct relationship to compliance in external employment. Such financial barriers may actually exclude students from participating in legitimate and valuable opportunities.
2)More effective means of countering fraud and abuse would be to increase employer checks, site visits, and training plans, all of which have been rejected without explanation by DHS. The anecdotal accounts of fraud cited by DHS all involved employers. There is no explanation of how placing an exorbitant fee on schools would reduce actions by fraudulent actors in the employment sector.
3)The goal of lessening DHS’s oversight burden is in direct conflict with the proposed rule’s fees being deposited into the Treasury. Fees levied by DHS should be used for oversight and such fees are not available if they are deposited in the Treasury.

The proposed rule also raises internal inconsistencies about implementation. As the proposed rule attaches the fee to the institution rather than the student, there is no way to determine if the $70,000 is to be paid once or twice should a student transfer between institutions. Additionally, the proposed fee is ambiguous regarding how many times the $30,000 would be paid; once for a second OPT application or multiple times at a rate of $30,000 for each additional application.

The administrative and record keeping burden for both schools and DHS would be extremely high under the proposed rule. As noted, schools would likely pass these fees onto students. Therefore, DSOs and colleagues would need to build and maintain internal systems to process and make such large payments, collect funds from students, create liability and risk assessments, and develop ways to prioritize and weigh student OPT request applications. As the fees in the proposed rule are attached to the school rather than the student, DHS has not provided systems to tie fees to SEVIS records to prevent schools from having to pay the same fee multiple times. With the funds being directed to the Treasury, it seems this would be more difficult for DHS to track relative to SEVIS records.

Finally, the proposed fee itself lacks legal justification. With funds to be deposited into the Treasury, such payments become a tax rather than a fee. DHS does not have the legal authority to levy a tax on international students.

I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee and instead pursue targeted measured to reduce fraudulent instances of employment that in such a way as to not undermine the benefits of the OPT program.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule due to exorbitant fee levels and negative impacts on students and schools.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by University of Nebraska at Omaha
comments.commentText:
The University of Nebraska Omaha (UNO) opposes the proposed fees of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT.

1.OPT gives international students the same hands-on experience as their domestic peers. Experiential learning is central to a modern university education. OPT lets international students apply their learning in U.S. workplaces, as domestic students do through internships and early-career roles. Fees of this size would put that experience out of reach for most students and the institutions that support them, creating an unequal educational experience.

2.OPT builds connections that advance mutual understanding and diplomacy. Through OPT, international students form lasting professional and personal relationships with U.S. colleagues, employers, and communities. These relationships continue long after students leave the U.S. They strengthen the people-to-people ties that benefit Americans and our partners worldwide.

3.The fee would burden students, employers, and universities. Whether the cost falls on students, employers, or institutions, the amounts are prohibitive. The proposal anticipates that schools will pay the fee before recommending a student for OPT, and students can apply for OPT without having an employer, which make it impossible for the institution to immediately pass the fee on to an employer. A public metropolitan university like UNO cannot absorb costs on this scale. Students would struggle to cover them, and employers, particularly small and mid-sized employers, would likely hesitate to hire OPT participants. The result would be fewer students gaining U.S. work experience and fewer employers able to draw on their skills.

4.The premise that a fee will reduce fraud is not supported by evidence of existing fraud. The proposal asserts that a fee will deter fraud and “visa mill” activity. It does not show that fraud is widespread among students at SEVP-certified institutions in good standing. A flat fee penalizes the many compliant students and institutions without targeting the few bad actors. Existing safeguards, including SEVIS reporting, designated school official oversight, SEVP certification and site reviews, STEM OPT reporting requirements, and employer obligations under STEM OPT training plans, are better tools. We urge DHS to strengthen enforcement against specific violators instead.

5.The rule would add significant workload for International Student and Scholar Services offices. Our ISSS staff would need new systems to track, collect, and reconcile fees, along with new training, new procedures, and expanded advising for students and employers. DHS has not accounted for these costs, and offices would have to absorb them without additional resources.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are prohibitive and harms students, employers, and universities.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an international student, and I respectfully oppose this proposed rule. I ask DHS to withdraw it.

Personal impact (Section VI, Reliance Interests)

International students plan for years before coming to the United States. I am from India and am studying for a Master's. Students like me prepare for English proficiency exams and the GRE, apply to universities, and sometimes wait months or longer for a visa appointment. Many take out loans to pay for their education. We make these sacrifices for a quality education and the practical experience that OPT provides.

After all this work, while meeting tight university deadlines, we learned of a proposed $70,000 fee for OPT and an additional $30,000 for STEM OPT. I feel trapped. The plans I made in good faith are now in doubt, and this uncertainty causes real stress and anxiety for students.

Section VI calls the expectation of OPT speculative. It also notes that only about 20 percent of F1 students participated in OPT in 2024. That is a one-year snapshot, and many students who plan to use OPT are still in their studies, so it does not show how many relied on OPT when choosing a U.S. school. Footnote 124 also acknowledges that current students, who have already moved here, are in a different position from prospective students.

The fee does not target fraud (Sections IV.A and IV.C)

DHS should investigate and punish fraud wherever it exists, but a fee charged to every participant punishes honest students along with bad actors. Section IV.A cites about 10,000 students working for highly suspect employers. Even if every case were confirmed, that is only about 3 to 4 percent of the 289,938 OPT and STEM OPT authorizations reported for 2024 in Table 2.

The fee also does nothing to detect fraud:

The money does not fund enforcement: Section IV.C states that the fees would go to the Treasury and would not be earmarked for SEVP or immigration enforcement.
Ability to pay does not demonstrate legitimacy: A fee indicates who can afford OPT, not whether a job or employer is legitimate. Students with strong academic records but limited means could be shut out.
Better tools were set aside: DHS considered site visits and additional reporting, but largely rejected them because a fee is quicker and easier to administer. Speed does not justify burdening every student for the misconduct of a few.

The costs are high, and the benefits are not measured (Section VII)

Table 1 lists monetized benefits as "Not Estimated," while the primary estimate of annualized costs is about $4.1 billion. DHS also admits that schools may pass the fee to students. Students already carrying loans could not absorb it.

Table 17 estimates that 116 small institutions would face impacts above 20 percent of annual revenue in the transition year.

Harm to universities and the U.S. economy

New international enrollment fell 17 percent in fall 2025, according to the Institute of International Education. NAFSA reports that international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 jobs in 20242025. It also projects that the expected fall 2026 decline could cost $3.4 billion and nearly 40,000 jobs. Taking away practical experience would make the United States less attractive at the worst possible time, hurting universities and the communities around them.

Requested action

1. Withdraw the proposed fees.
2. Address fraud through targeted investigations, employer site visits, and penalties for those who actually commit it.
3. If DHS finalizes any fee, exempt all students who were enrolled or admitted before the final rule is published, because they made their decisions under the current rules.

Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule and asks DHS to withdraw the costly OPT fees.

comments.commentText:
Subject: Strong Opposition to Proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) Fees – Docket ICEB-2026-0100

I strongly oppose the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed rule imposing a $70,000 initial fee and an additional $30,000 subsequent fee for Optional Practical Training (OPT).

This proposal creates an unreasonable financial burden on international students, educational institutions, and American employers. It also risks undermining the United States’ position as a leading destination for global talent.

1. Excessive Financial Burden

A $70,000 initial fee is disproportionate and unreasonable. International students already invest substantial amounts in tuition, living expenses, and other educational costs. Although the proposed fee is technically imposed on educational institutions, those costs could ultimately be passed on to students or employers, creating additional financial hardship.

2. Unfair Treatment of Legitimate Students

International students enter the United States legally, comply with immigration requirements, pay significant tuition, and contribute to American universities. OPT provides an opportunity to gain practical experience directly related to their academic qualifications. Imposing excessive fees on this legitimate pathway unfairly penalizes students who follow the rules.

3. Negative Impact on American Competitiveness

International students contribute significantly to American research, innovation, technology, healthcare, and economic growth. Excessive OPT fees could discourage talented students from pursuing education in the United States and push them toward countries offering more accessible post-graduation employment opportunities.

4. Harm to American Employers

American companies benefit from hiring highly educated graduates in specialized fields, including science, technology, engineering, and healthcare. Excessive OPT fees could discourage employers from hiring international graduates, increase operational costs, and reduce access to qualified talent.

5. Disproportionate Approach to Preventing Fraud

If the objective is to prevent fraud and abuse, DHS should focus on targeted enforcement, improved verification, institutional oversight, and penalties for organizations that violate regulations. Imposing a massive fee on every legitimate OPT applicant is neither a proportionate nor an effective solution.

6. Request for Reconsideration

I respectfully urge DHS to:

* Withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee.
* Avoid transferring excessive financial obligations to legitimate international students and their families.
* Implement targeted measures to address actual fraud and regulatory violations.
* Conduct a comprehensive economic and educational impact assessment before introducing additional OPT fees.
* Ensure that any future fee structure is reasonable, transparent, and proportionate to actual administrative costs.

OPT is an important bridge between American higher education and the U.S. workforce. It allows qualified graduates to apply their knowledge, contribute to American businesses, and strengthen the nation’s global competitiveness.

Combating fraud is a legitimate government responsibility, but it should not come at the expense of thousands of law-abiding international students and their families who have invested their time, money, and future in an American education.

I strongly urge DHS to reject this proposed rule in its current form and protect legitimate international students, American educational institutions, and the long-term interests of the United States.

Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees

I am writing as a parent to strongly oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training fees of $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation.

My child has been studying in the United States since first grade and has grown up with the dream of becoming a doctor. Our family has planned, sacrificed, and worked for many years toward that goal. My child has been educated alongside American classmates, has learned the same values of service and responsibility, and hopes to use that education to care for patients and contribute to this country.

The proposed fees would create an overwhelming financial barrier unrelated to a student's talent, honesty, academic performance, or commitment to public service. A fee of this size does not identify fraud or measure merit. It primarily separates students and institutions by their ability to pay. DHS itself recognizes that schools may pass these costs to students, employers, or other students. Families already facing the high costs of college, medical education, examinations, and training cannot reasonably absorb tens of thousands of dollars in additional fees.

This proposal is especially damaging to students pursuing medicine and other healthcare professions. Becoming a physician requires many years of education and supervised training. Practical experience is not a shortcut to employment; it is an essential bridge between education and professional service. Placing an extraordinary charge at that bridge could prevent qualified future doctors, researchers, and healthcare professionals from completing their training and serving patients.

The proposal would also unfairly disrupt the reasonable expectations of families whose children have spent most of their lives in the United States. My child has followed the rules and built an educational future under the existing system. A sudden fee of this magnitude would change that future after years of study and investment. Students raised and educated here should not see their professional dreams become impossible merely because of their immigration classification or their family's financial resources.

I understand the government's responsibility to prevent fraud and protect workers. However, broad and punitive fees imposed on lawful students and educational institutions are not a properly targeted solution. Fraud should be addressed through focused investigations, audits, verification, employer oversight, and enforcement against people or organizations that actually violate the law. Honest students should not be priced out of practical training because of misconduct attributed to others.

The proposal may also produce harmful consequences for American universities, hospitals, laboratories, and communities. Schools may decline to recommend deserving students because they cannot afford the fee. Smaller and public institutions may be particularly disadvantaged. Hospitals, research programs, and other employers may lose access to highly trained graduates who could otherwise contribute their knowledge and skills in the United States.

I respectfully request that DHS:

Withdraw the proposed rule and retain reasonable access to OPT.
Reject the alternative of charging another $70,000 fee whenever a student advances to a higher degree level.
Use targeted enforcement measures against documented fraud rather than imposing extraordinary fees on all participating schools and students.
If DHS proceeds with any fee, conduct a complete analysis of its effects on long-term U.S.-educated students, healthcare education, small institutions, families, and underserved communities, and establish reasonable fees, hardship waivers, and appropriate transition protections.
My child is not seeking an unfair advantage. My child is asking for the opportunity to complete an education, receive lawful practical training, and pursue a lifelong dream of becoming a doctor and serving patients in United States. Please do not allow a student's future to depend on whether a family or school can pay $70,000 for access to practical training.

For these reasons, I strongly oppose the proposed rule and respectfully urge DHS to withdraw it.
