comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ashley Albrinck
comments.commentText:
Ambiguity surrounding the subsequent $30,000 fee further illustrates the proposal's deficiencies.
A. DHS must clarify whether the $30,000 OPT fee applies only to the first subsequent OPT recommendation or to every subsequent recommendation.
Under the proposal, the initial $70,000 fee would be triggered by the first OPT recommendation for a particular student by a DSO at a particular SEVP-certified school following the final rule's effective date. See proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1).
Proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(2) then provides that a school that has paid the initial $70,000 fee for a particular student must pay $30,000 before "a subsequent recommendation" for that student for whom it has already paid the initial $70,000 fee.
But proposed 8 CFR 214.12(i)(3) then says that “any subsequent DSO recommendations for OPT issued for any F-1 student who has previously participated in OPT, and for which the $70,000 OPT fee has been paid, will be subject to the subsequent OPT fee of $30,000 per alien.”
Using the singular “a subsequent recommendation” and the plural “any subsequent DSO recommendations” in the same paragraph (i) creates ambiguity and uncertainty as to whether DHS intends a single $30,000 payment for the first subsequent OPT recommendation or $30,000 payments for each subsequent recommendation.
Two interpretations are possible.
Under the first interpretation, a particular school would pay $70,000 for the student's initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for the first subsequent recommendation, with no further fee for additional OPT recommendations for that student at that school. Total liability would be limited to $100,000. This interpretation appears consistent with a notice distributed on October 8, 2026 by SEVP to DSOs, which describes a $70,000 initial charge and a $30,000 charge for the “second year” of practicaltraining, with no additional fees in subsequent years. DHS also uses a $100,000 total in portions of its economic analysis included in the proposed rule.
Under the second interpretation, the school would pay $70,000 for the initial recommendation and an additional $30,000 each time it subsequently recommends OPT for the same student. Total liability could therefore exceed $100,000. Statements in the proposed rule preamble support this second interpretation. The preamble summary describes the subsequent fee as applicable to "any subsequent OPT." Elsewhere in the preamble DHS expressly describes the proposed charge as applying "each time there is a subsequent OPT recommendation for that student." These statements are difficult to reconcile with a single second-payment interpretation.
The distinction is illustrated by the following examples.
Example. Consider a Master of Engineering student who seeks three months of pre-completion OPT for a summer internship, followed by nine months of post-completion OPT and a subsequent 24-month STEM OPT extension.
•
This student's school would first pay $70,000 before recommending the pre-completion OPT. It would then pay $30,000 before recommending post-completion OPT.
•
If DHS intends a maximum of one subsequent fee, the school would owe no additional amount when recommending the STEM extension, and total liability would be $100,000.
•
If DHS intends to assess the fee for each subsequent recommendation, the STEM extension would trigger another $30,000 payment, bringing total liability to $130,000.
Example. The same ambiguity could also affect students pursuing post-completion OPT following successively higher degrees at the same school, for example, a student who obtains a bachelor’s degree, then a master’s degree, and then a doctoral degree at the same school, each followed by a period of post-completion OPT permitted.
•
Under the first interpretation ($100,000 limit), the school would have to pay a total of $100,000 for the three OPT recommendations ($70,000 for the first, $30,000 for the second, and $0 for the third).
•

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ashley Albrinck
comments.commentText:
International students and graduates contribute substantially to the nation's scientific and technological capacity. OPT provides an important bridge between American higher education and the U.S. workforce, enabling employers to recruit individuals already educated at U.S. institutions.
The Institute of International Education (IIE)’s Fall 2025 International Student Enrollment Snapshot Survey posits institutions will continue to place significant value on the OPT program, with 76 percent of institutions responding it was important for recruiting international students, and 92 percent reporting that, without OPT, many international students would likely choose to study in other countries.
Research from Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology illustrates the importance of international educational pathways to American innovation. Its September 2026 report, How Global Talent Pathways Shape U.S. STEM Award Achievement, examines 550 recipients of major STEM awards between 2014 and 2024. Of the 471 awardees who had studied, worked, or lived in the United States, 47 percent were foreign-born. Among foreign-born U.S. awardees whose initial educational or professional activity could be identified, approximately two-thirds first came to the United States as students.
Although these findings do not establish that OPT itself caused these achievements, they demonstrate the importance of maintaining educational and early-career pathways through which international talent contributes to American science and technology.
The OPT Observatory, developed by IFP using detailed SEVIS microdata obtained through the Freedom of Information Act, provides further evidence of the importance and breadth of these pathways. Its data document international student participation across institutions, degree levels, academic fields, and employment sectors. These data, together with DHS's own SEVIS by the Numbers reports, provide a substantial empirical foundation for examining the proposal's effects on different student populations and institutions. DHS should use these resources to evaluate whether the proposal would disproportionately affect STEM graduates, smaller institutions, rural institutions, regional universities, and employers that lack the financial resources to support excessively large fees.
The effects would also extend to American workers. International students attending U.S. colleges and universities contribute tuition revenue that supports academic programs, faculty positions, research infrastructure, and educational opportunities for domestic students. International graduates also contribute specialized skills to businesses, laboratories, and research teams. Reducing these contributions could undermine, rather than advance, the interests of U.S. workers.
A key finding of The 2026 US Talent Report, Benchmarking America’s STEM Pipeline Amid the Great Talent Competition, produced by the Hoover Institution and the Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence at Stanford University and written by Emerson Johnston and Amy Zegart, is that “[i]nternational talent powers American research and industry after graduation. International graduates constitute majorities of postdoctoral researchers in several STEM fields, work in STEM at higher rates than US-born graduates with comparable degrees, and have founded or co-founded a large share of the country’s leading AI firms.” (Ibid, page 7).
The report also found that while the United States has abruptly changing policies that create uncertainty about opportunities after graduation, “Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, Germany, and Singapore have moved in the opposite direction, offering skilled migrants clearer criteria, faster decisions, or more direct routes to permanent residence.” (Ibid, page 159). Considering competition among countries, the researchers state, “America is no longer competing only on the quality of its universities and laboratories. It is competing on the predictability of the path that follows them.” (Ibid, page 159).
This change in demand is evidenced in the most recent Global Enrolment Benchmark survey (January to March 2026 Intake) that indicates sharp declines in international enrollments in the U.S. and Canada while many European and Asian institutions reported growth. Restrictive government policies and visa restrictions were cited as the biggest negative impact for those institutions experiencing enrollment declines.
Imposing charges of this magnitude would create a substantial competitive disadvantage for American institutions and employers, particularly when other countries offer more accessible post-study work opportunities.
comments.reason: The commenter emphasizes the value of OPT and international talent, arguing against changes that harm pathways.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ashley Albrinck
comments.commentText:
DHS identifies fraud prevention, immigration system integrity, protection of U.S. workers, and the costs of OPT investigations as principal justifications for the proposal. These are legitimate areas of governmental concern. They do not, however, establish that fees of $70,000 and $30,000 are necessary, appropriate, or authorized.
The proposal does not adequately demonstrate why these particular amounts are required. Nor does it establish that charging educational institutions extraordinary amounts for making otherwise permissible OPT recommendations is a proportionate response to identified compliance problems.
The distinction between a regulatory fee and a revenue-raising or deterrent charge is particularly important. Congress has established statutory frameworks governing immigration-related fees, including 8 U.S.C. 1356(m) and 8 U.S.C. 1372. DHS must identify statutory authority supporting the charges it proposes and explain how that authority permits fees designed to discourage participation rather than recover the costs of providing governmental services or administering a program.
General authority to administer and enforce immigration laws does not, without further explanation, resolve whether DHS may impose charges of this magnitude for the purpose of changing institutional, student, and employer behavior.
DHS should provide a transparent accounting of the governmental costs that the proposed fees are intended to recover, including the extent to which those costs are attributable to individual OPT recommendations. It should also distinguish administrative cost recovery from any intended deterrent effect.
If the objective is to encourage greater institutional review of OPT recommendations, DHS should explain why targeted documentation requirements, enhanced compliance reviews, and enforcement against identified violations would be insufficient. If the objective is to deter fraudulent employment arrangements, DHS should demonstrate how imposing the same substantial charges on compliant institutions and students would more effectively accomplish that purpose than targeted investigations and enforcement.
The proposal also warrants closer examination under the Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980 (5 U.S.C. 601-612, as amended) and the principles governing reasoned agency decision-making. Its effects on small educational institutions, students, employers, and other affected entities cannot be adequately evaluated without accounting for the likelihood that institutions will decline to make OPT recommendations rather than incur the proposed fees.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that the proposed OPT fees are disproportionate, lack statutory justification, and are excessively high.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ashley Albrinck
comments.commentText:
DHS says in the proposed rule preamble that its authority to impose the proposed OPT fees rests on "multiple, independent, and mutually reinforcing statutory sources." However, the authorities identified concern DHS's general responsibility to administer immigration laws, regulate nonimmigrant status and employment, and oversee educational institutions certified by the Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP) and tracked in SEVIS. [DHS states in the preamble, “The Secretary has authority under Section 102 of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (HSA) (Pub. L. 107-296, 116 Stat. 2135), 6 U.S.C. 112,and section 103(a)(1) and (3) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), 8 U.S.C. 1103(a)(1), (3), to administer and enforce the immigration and naturalization laws of the United States, to include the issuance of regulations that he deems necessary. Section 214(a) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1184(a), authorizes the Secretary to prescribe the time and conditions of admission of any alien as a nonimmigrant.”] None of these provisions expressly authorizes DHS to impose the extraordinary charges contemplated by this proposal. DHS's reliance on these provisions raises substantial questions about whether it is attempting to exercise taxing authority that Congress has not delegated.
DHS's proposal to deposit OPT “fees” into the general Treasury as miscellaneous receipts under 31 U.S.C. 3302, rather than retain or earmark them for SEVP administration or immigration enforcement, raises further questions not only about their characterization as regulatory fees. DHS acknowledges that ICE would not receive the revenue and that any subsequent appropriation for immigration enforcement would depend on congressional action. And so there is no assurance that the substantial amounts DHS seeks to collect from educational institutions would be used to address the very program vulnerabilities DHS invokes to justify the charges. DHS dismisses this concern by asserting that the charges would retain their deterrent effect regardless of whether Congress ever appropriates the revenue for immigration enforcement. Although depositing revenue into the general Treasury does not itself invalidate a regulatory fee, the absence of any dedicated use for the funds, coupled with the lack of a demonstrated relationship between the amounts charged and the costs of administering or enforcing OPT requirements, strengthens the argument that these assessments function primarily as deterrent taxes on lawful activity rather than fees to recover costs for governmental services. DHS has not identified clear statutory authority to impose charges of this nature.
DHS identifies deterring fraud and other misconduct involving OPT as a principal justification for the proposed fees yet offers no systematic evidence establishing the prevalence of such misconduct, relying instead on anecdotal accounts. Rather than targeting demonstrated abuses, the proposal would arbitrarily impose substantial charges on all institutions and students seeking to participate in a longstanding, lawful immigration benefit, regardless of any evidence of wrongdoing. In this respect, the proposed charges more closely resemble an arbitrary excise tax designed to discourage otherwise lawful activity than a regulatory fee intended to recover the costs of administering or enforcing the program.
The power to issue regulations necessary to administer a statutory program cannot be interpreted as authority to impose taxes or high fees on participation in that program. Broad regulatory discretion is not a substitute for the clear congressional delegation required to exercise Congress's taxing power.
DHS also relies on INA section 214(a), 8 U.S.C. 1184(a), which authorizes the Secretary to generally prescribe the time and conditions of nonimmigrant admission, as well as other provisions granting DHS the authority to implement programs. But the authority to prescribe conditions governing optional practical training does not necessarily include authority to tax institutions or charge them exorbitant fees for making otherwise lawful OPT recommendations.
As mentioned above, the proposed charges exhibit characteristics that support their treatment as taxes rather than ordinary regulatory fees. They would apply to otherwise lawful activity, would not depend on a finding of misconduct (as would a fine), and do not correspond to the governmental cost of processing an OPT recommendation or administering the associated regulatory requirements. DHS instead emphasizes their intended deterrent effects, which, although ostensibly targeting bad behavior, will instead indiscriminately deter all use of the OPT benefit.
comments.reason: The commenter argues DHS lacks statutory authority to impose such high OPT fees, effectively acting as an undelegated tax.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ashley Albrinck
comments.commentText:
DHS tangentially references section 641 of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996, 8 U.S.C. 1372, which authorizes the collection of information concerning nonimmigrant students and exchange visitors and provides a statutory framework for SEVIS. This statute contains specific provisions at 8 U.S.C. 1372(e) addressing fees associated with the student and exchange visitor monitoring program. Those provisions demonstrate that Congress knows how to authorize fees for the administration of this program and to define their purposes. DHS does not explain how the proposed OPT charges, which are designed in substantial part to deter participation and address broader immigration policy concerns, fall within that specific statutory fee framework. Nor does DHS establish that the proposed amounts are related to the costs Congress authorized the agency to recover. The existence of express, purpose-limited fee authority weighs against interpreting more general immigration provisions as granting an additional, unrestricted power to impose exorbitant monetary assessments.
Absent a persuasive statutory justification, the proposed charges would exceed DHS's delegated authority. Therefore, DHS should withdraw the proposal.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fees exceed DHS's statutory authority and requests that the proposal be withdrawn.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my opposition to Optional Practical Training Fees Docket (ICEB-2026-0100)

The proposed regulation is inadequate and contradicts regulation that it is not attempting to change.

Historically, SEVP has taken the position that institutions may not charge students a separate fee for processing OPT recommendation I-20s (or other SEVIS authorizations), as eligible students are entitled to those immigration benefits and schools certify to SEVP that they possess the personnel, facilities, and financial resources necessary to administer SEVIS and meet regulatory obligations. This proposal appears carefully drafted to avoid directly addressing whether institutions could recover the new OPT fee through a student-specific charge. In addition, SEVP has continually emphasized that I-20s are the property of DHS and not the institution and that school DSOs are in the position of reporting information. Through issuance of the OPT recommendation I-20 the DSO is reporting certain objective information such as the student is completing their studies, the student met the 1 year of studies requirement, the student submitted for I-983.

SEVP field representatives continue to remind schools that they “cannot hold I-20s hostage” to require students to pay bills or fees and MUST issue OPT recommendation I-20s to students who meet the criteria. This proposed regulation does not change those portions of current regulation.

Lastly, this proposed regulation does not change the standards for which a student is entitled to the OPT other than including a receipt for the school payment. Nor does the proposed regulation include any mention of institutions granting OPT recommendation I-20s based on merit. The only addition would be submission of receipt for payment of the “OPT fee”.

Thus, DHS is unable to provide any documentation of merit as the standards for “selection” of who is eligible for OPT recommend I-20 is not changed.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states opposition to the proposed Optional Practical Training Fees rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ashley Albrinck
comments.commentText:
B. DHS must clarify whether the payment history of a particular school for a particular student persists after a break in study when the student returns in the future to pursue additional study at the same school.
Example. It is possible that a student pursues OPT following completion of a degree at one school, returns home for more than a temporary absence (or otherwise has a lawful break in the continuity of F-1 status as in a change of status to H-1B), and then returns to the same school to pursue another degree at a higher educational level. For example, a student completes a bachelor’s degree at a school, does 12 months of post-completion OPT, returns home to work in that country (let us say for two years in this example), and then returns to the same school to pursue a master’s degree, finishes the master’s degree, and then plans for a period of 12 months of post-completion OPT following the master’s.
•
In this case, the school would have paid a $70,000 fee before making the OPT recommendation following the bachelor’s degree.
•
If the payment history persists, the school would pay a $30,000 fee before making the OPT recommendation following the master’s degree.
•
If the payment history does not persist following a lawful break in F status, the school would have to pay another $70,000 fee for the same student.
DHS must clarify this in any final regulatory wording.
C. DHS Must Clarify How the Rule Would Work When OPT is Recommended by Different Schools.
There is also ambiguity as to whether payment history and obligation is school-specific or follows the student across institutions, although the regulatory wording is best interpreted as OPT fee payment liability being school-specific. For example, consider this scenario under that interpretation:
•
Student at School A wants to apply for 12 months of OPT eligibility as post-completion OPT, following completion of the master’s degree.
o
Before recommending the post-completion OPT, the DSO at School A must ensure that School A has paid the $70,000 amount, since this is the first OPT being recommended for that student by that school.
•
After completing the 12 months of OPT based on the master’s degree earned at School A, student transfers to School B for a PhD in engineering.
•
Student wants to apply for 12 months of OPT eligibility as post-completion OPT, following completion of the PhD degree at School B.
o
Before recommending the post-completion OPT, the DSO at School B must ensure that School B has paid the $70,000 amount, since this is the first OPT being recommended for that student by that school (i.e., a different school).
•
Student wants to apply for STEM OPT
o
Before recommending the STEM OPT, the DSO at School B must ensure that School B has paid the $30,000 amount.
In the event that DHS proceeds with any form of this proposed rule, DHS must clarify these fee payment ambiguities in the regulatory wording. The proposal's financial analysis cannot be considered reliable unless DHS clearly identifies the circumstances triggering each fee and models the resulting liabilities. An analysis based on a fee maximum would understate costs if institutions could incur additional charges.
comments.reason: The comment asks for administrative clarification on fee application rules without expressing support or opposition.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ashley Albrinck
comments.commentText:
DHS can address legitimate concerns about fraud, program integrity, and worker protections without imposing financial barriers that would effectively eliminate OPT opportunities for large numbers of otherwise eligible students.
The existing regulatory framework and SEVIS already provide DHS with substantial tools and information to identify potential fraud and noncompliance in OPT. DSOs must determine student eligibility and enter OPT recommendations in SEVIS, while students must report changes in employment and other required information. For STEM OPT, additional safeguards include employer participation in E-Verify, individualized Form I-983 training plans, employer attestations, periodic student evaluations, reportingobligations, and DHS authority to conduct employer site visits. SEVIS maintains information on students' academic programs, immigration status, OPT authorization periods, and reported employment, enabling DHS to identify potentially suspicious patterns across students, employers, and institutions. These existing data and oversight mechanisms provide a substantial foundation for targeted, risk-based compliance reviews and enforcement against actual misconduct, without imposing extraordinary fees on institutions making otherwise lawful OPT recommendations.
Potential alternatives include improved use of SEVIS data to identify unusual employment patterns, risk-based compliance reviews, clearer institutional reporting requirements, enhanced enforcement against fraudulent employers or institutions, and additional guidance concerning DSO responsibilities. Any proposed administrative fees should be supported by a documented cost analysis and proportionate to the governmental services or regulatory activities involved.
DHS should also meaningfully evaluate the effects of the proposal on students already enrolled in U.S. institutions who made educational and financial decisions in reliance on the availability of OPT. Even prospective application of the proposed fees would substantially disrupt the expectations of these students and their institutions.
The economic studies and administrative data identified in these comments provide a basis for a more comprehensive assessment of the proposal's costs and alternatives. DHS should incorporate these resources into its analysis, address their findings, and provide the public with an adequate opportunity to evaluate any substantially revised proposal.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the fees create financial barriers that eliminate OPT opportunities and suggests alternatives.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ashley Albrinck
comments.commentText:
The proposed OPT fees that function as a tax would impose extraordinary costs on American educational institutions and threaten an established pathway through which international students gain practical experience and contribute to the U.S. economy. DHS has not adequately demonstrated that the proposed amounts are necessary to achieve its stated objectives, that the fees are supported by the statutory authorities cited, or that their likely consequences for students, institutions, employers, and American workers have been fully evaluated. Existing regulatory mechanisms already provide for school certification, DSO oversight, student and school reporting, employer obligations under STEM OPT, and investigations of suspected violations. DHS should instead better assess whether these mechanisms can be strengthened through more targeted measures. The ambiguity surrounding the subsequent $30,000 fee further illustrates the proposal's deficiencies.
For these reasons, we urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and pursue targeted, evidence-based measures that address identifiable compliance concerns while preserving the educational and economic benefits of OPT.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the fees impose extraordinary costs and urges DHS to withdraw the proposed rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
DHS docket # CEB-2026-0100

This is a deeply flawed proposal, and I urge DHS to withdraw it in its entirety.

It is hard to find data to confirm the level of fraud in OPT as news reports quote DHS sources to provide their numbers, and DHS doesn’t say where these numbers come from. We have no way to verify their accuracy. Sharing a YouTube clip where someone makes a comment or states a number doesn’t make it true. Is there fraud in OPT? Yes, probably. But when imposing something as drastic as an $100,000 fee it’s important to ask how much fraud is really there to be found. DHS really needs to justify a change of this magnitude.

One recent article from The National Law Review from May 2026 (https://natlawreview.com/article/opt-under-scrutiny-what-increased-ice-enforcement-means-employers) says that ICE claims the number is potentially around 10,000 cases. No time frame is given for this number: is it per year, or over the last couple of years? Decades? It is unclear. According to DHS’s own data, as cited by the Center for Immigration Studies (https://cis.org/Jacobs/DHSs-Crackdown-OPT-Fraud-Will-Not-Fix-Programs-Biggest-Problems), 505,590 international students participated in OPT and STEM OPT in FY 2024.

Imagining for a moment that the number of cases quoted is 10,000 cases per year, this gives a fraud rate of 1.9%. That means that 98.1% of OPT students are NOT fraudulent.

Therefore, 98% of OPT holders are working legitimately. They pay taxes, consume food and entertainment, pay rent to landlords etc. They contribute to our communities and to the US economy. This ridiculous plan to penalize everyone for 1.9% of wrongdoers seems like a great example of cutting your nose to spite your face and will do nothing but hurt American businesses and communities.

The same article from The National Law Review referenced above indicates that the fraud on the part of employers (note: not universities) was uncovered by DHS investigations. DHS already reviews every single OPT and STEM OPT application for fraud, and clearly occasionally finds something. The current processes work. Students must report employment through SEVIS, so mechanisms to detect fraud already exist: DHS is successfully using them already.

Also, by DHS’s own admission, the funds raised through these fees will not actually go to fraud prevention but to a miscellaneous fund at the US Treasury. By confirming that they will not actually receive the funds raised, DHS is confirming that they don’t need the money to fight fraud. The logic doesn’t hold together at all: “we need funds to fight fraud, but we wont actually use the funds to fight fraud”. Saying funds raised will be used for one thing and then not actually using them for that thing: isn’t that committing fraud?

If DHS is so convinced that the OPT process is comprehensively fraudulent, surely it would make more sense to punish the employers who hire fraudulently, not universities? If DHS was serious about looking for more fraud there would be investment in site visits, increased reporting requirements, additional and updated processes etc. Not a ridiculous fee. Financial payments don’t verify anything. Any fraud that takes place is at the employer level per DHS own data. It is not perpetuated by universities or DSOs, so how will making a university pay an exorbitant fee prevent fraud from taking place?

This fee will not possibly achieve its stated goal of stopping fraud. It is a deeply flawed proposal and should be entirely withdrawn.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fee is drastically high and urges DHS to withdraw it in its entirety.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: I strongly oppose the proposed rule under Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, which would impose a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation. As an international student at the University of Southern California (USC), I find this proposal deeply unfair, economically damaging, and contradictory to the values that make American higher education exceptional. International students make enormous financial, academic, and personal sacrifices to study in the United States. We pay substantial tuition, contribute to local economies, support American businesses, and invest years pursuing an American education. We choose institutions like USC for their academic excellence and opportunities to apply our education professionally. Imposing a $70,000 fee would make OPT inaccessible for countless hardworking, law-abiding students. First, this proposal punishes legitimate students for the misconduct of a minority. DHS cites fraud and abuse as justification. Fraud should be prosecuted, but imposing enormous financial burdens on every international student fails to distinguish between fraudulent participants and those who follow immigration rules and earn legitimate degrees. A student's wealth or their university's willingness to pay $70,000 does not determine academic merit, professional qualifications, or immigration compliance. This proposal risks transforming OPT into a privilege reserved for the wealthy. Second, the proposal disregards students already enrolled in American universities. Many of us committed to studying in the United States years before this proposal appeared. Our families invested significantly in tuition, housing, and living expenses with an understanding of the opportunities available, including OPT. Although the rule would apply prospectively, it would still affect enrolled students without an OPT recommendation. We cannot simply reverse years of financial commitments or educational decisions. The proposal inadequately addresses these legitimate reliance interests. Third, this rule threatens America's competitiveness in attracting global talent. Universities like USC attract ambitious students, researchers, and innovators worldwide. If post-graduation training becomes financially inaccessible, talented students will increasingly consider other countries. American universities could experience declining international enrollment, reduced tuition revenue, and diminished contributions to research and innovation. Local economies would also suffer. Fourth, the proposal could harm American employers, particularly startups, small businesses, and nonprofit organizations. OPT allows employers to recruit graduates educated at American institutions who possess valuable skills. Requiring a $70,000 payment, potentially passed to employers or students, creates an enormous barrier to accessing this talent. Professional opportunities should depend on qualifications and merit rather than financial capacity. Fifth, these fees are disproportionate and lack a convincing connection to fraud prevention. Making OPT prohibitively expensive does not necessarily make it more secure. Financial barriers cannot replace employer verification, targeted investigations, compliance audits, and enforcement against fraudulent organizations. The proposal acknowledges that collected fees would enter the U.S. Treasury rather than be specifically allocated to OPT enforcement. DHS should prioritize stronger employer verification, penalties for fraudulent organizations, and investigations of suspicious employment arrangements instead of imposing billions of dollars in financial burdens. Finally, the proposal risks creating an inequitable system. A talented international graduate from a modest financial background deserves the same opportunity to gain practical experience as someone from a wealthy family. Financial capacity should never replace academic achievement, professional qualifications, or lawful compliance. I support protecting American workers and strengthening immigration integrity. However, these objectives should be pursued through proportionate, evidence-based policies rather than sweeping financial restrictions. As a USC student, I see international students contributing to classrooms, campus organizations, research, local businesses, and the broader Los Angeles community. We came to the United States to learn, develop our skills, and contribute meaningfully. Policies like this undermine the opportunities that attracted us here. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule and pursue targeted reforms addressing genuine fraud without unfairly penalizing law-abiding students. The United States should continue attracting global talent, not discourage it through financial barriers that undermine its educational excellence. Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule, arguing the high OPT fees are unfair and make the program inaccessible.

I write in strong opposition to the proposed rule imposing a $70,000 fee for universities to recommend international students for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT), and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations.

America has long aspired to be a shining city on a hill, a country where people from around the world can pursue opportunity, work hard, and contribute to society. This ideal has helped make the United States a global leader in education, research, and technological advancement. A policy that welcomes talented international students into our universities, only to impose exorbitant fees that prevent them from putting their education to work here, betrays that promise. It makes opportunity a question of wealth rather than merit, contrary to the American values of fairness and opportunity. Such a policy is fundamentally un-American.

These proposed fees would place an extraordinary financial burden on universities, international students, and employers. Universities may be forced to pass these costs onto students or discontinue OPT recommendations altogether. For many international graduates, this would effectively eliminate their opportunity to gain professional experience in the country where they earned their degrees.

International students contribute enormously to American universities and research institutions through their work in research and teaching. Their contributions extend beyond campus, strengthening American industries and the communities in which they live. Discouraging these students from remaining in the United States after graduation would undermine our universities, weaken American competitiveness, and drive talented graduates to countries more willing to welcome them.

America should aspire to live up to its promise as a shining city on a hill. We should welcome those who come here to learn, work, and contribute, rather than erect financial barriers that shut them out. I urge the agency to withdraw these proposed fees and preserve OPT as a meaningful opportunity for international graduates.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw its proposal to charge $70,000 for an initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation, including for a STEM OPT extension.

OPT gives international students a chance to apply what they learned at a U.S. college or university through work related to their degree. The proposed fees would put that opportunity out of reach for many otherwise eligible students. Although schools would be responsible for paying, they could pass the cost on to students or employers, or stop recommending students for OPT altogether. A student could lose access to training because their school could not absorb the fee or because a small employer could not afford to cover it. Students already enrolled may have committed years of study and substantial tuition based in part on the opportunity to pursue practical training after graduation.

The proposed fees are also poorly matched to DHS’s goals of preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers. The ability to pay $70,000 tells DHS little about whether an employer is legitimate, whether a job relates to a student’s degree, or whether workplace protections are being followed. DHS can address those concerns more directly by verifying employers and training placements, auditing cases with signs of abuse, and enforcing existing requirements when it finds violations.

I ask DHS to withdraw both fees. Before considering any replacement fee, DHS should publish the costs it seeks to recover and assess how schools, students, and employers would actually respond, including how many schools might stop recommending students for OPT. Students who follow the rules should have a realistic opportunity to use the education they earned in the United States.
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposed exorbitant OPT fees, arguing they harm students and employers.

The CEOs of Alphabet (Google), Microsoft, Nvidia, Tesla, Intel, AMD, Broadcom, Qualcomm, and countless other high-tech firms are first-generation immigrants. Their employees are likewise very immigrant-heavy. They aren't taking jobs away from Americans; they're _creating_ jobs for Americans. This measure needs to be abandoned immediately.

For context, I am a recently-retired American-born computer scientist. I am the author or co-author of 170 refereed technical papers, five patents, and two textbooks, including the #1 text in the field of programming languages. I am a Fellow of the Association for Computing Machinery, a Life Fellow of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, and a Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01 — Optional Practical Training Fees

I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee.

I am a postdoctoral researcher in theoretical physics working in the United States under F-1 post-completion OPT, and I expect to apply for a STEM OPT extension in 2027. I came to the United States for scientific training and research and made long-term educational and professional decisions based on the existing F-1 and OPT framework.

My principal concern is that the proposed fee is not well targeted to the fraud and program-integrity problems DHS identifies.

DHS states that the fee is intended in substantial part to deter participation, and the collected funds would be deposited into the U.S. Treasury rather than retained by ICE specifically to increase OPT enforcement. A fee of $70,000 therefore does not appear closely connected to the administrative cost of reviewing an individual student's participation.

If fraud is the concern, more targeted approaches are available: increased audits of employers or institutions presenting compliance risks, expanded site visits, stronger enforcement of existing STEM OPT training-plan requirements, or fees reasonably connected to the cost of additional oversight. These measures would address misconduct more directly without imposing the same extraordinary cost on legitimate participants.

The proposal may also have unintended consequences for U.S. scientific research. Many STEM graduates work in universities, research institutes, nonprofit organizations, start-ups, and laboratories that do not have the resources of large corporations. A cost of tens of thousands of dollars per researcher could make continued employment impossible even when the training arrangement is legitimate and scientifically valuable.

DHS itself acknowledges substantial uncertainty about how institutions, students, and employers will respond to these fees. That uncertainty is important. Before imposing fees large enough to change whether institutions participate in OPT at all, DHS should more fully evaluate their effects on universities, scientific research, small employers, and the ability of the United States to attract and retain international STEM talent.

I am also particularly concerned about current F-1 students and OPT participants. People already in the United States have spent years pursuing degrees, conducting research, paying tuition and living expenses, and planning careers under the existing OPT framework. For a person already participating in post-completion OPT, introducing a fee of this magnitude before a planned STEM extension changes the economic conditions of a decision that was made years earlier.

If DHS nevertheless proceeds with a new fee, I strongly urge it to grandfather students who are already in F-1 status, and particularly those who are already participating in post-completion OPT and later seek a STEM OPT extension.

I support reasonable enforcement measures to protect the integrity of OPT. But those measures should target actual misconduct and compliance risk rather than use an exceptionally large uniform financial barrier as a proxy for enforcement.

I therefore respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 fee structure. Alternatively, DHS should adopt substantially lower, cost-justified fees, more targeted enforcement mechanisms, and meaningful grandfathering protections for current F-1 students and OPT participants.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they are overly burdensome and not targeted to fraud.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees

I am an F-1 graduate student at a university in California, and I write to oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation. I ask DHS to withdraw this proposal.

I came to the United States to study, and like many international students, I have invested years of work and substantial tuition in my education. OPT is the reason many of us can apply what we learned and contribute to the American economy after graduation. A $70,000 fee, more than 130 times the current $520 application cost, would destroy that path. DHS itself acknowledges that schools may pass this cost on to students or stop recommending students for OPT altogether. For students who followed every rule and studied seriously, this proposal replaces a clear, lawful path with deep uncertainty about whether we will be allowed to work in our field at all. That loss of security is itself a serious harm.

The fee would also harm American interests. International graduates do not only fill jobs, they create them. A high school classmate of mine came to the United States to study and later founded a startup in Silicon Valley. That company has generated at least $300 million in revenue in the United States and created more than 80 new jobs. Those positions were senior technical and creative roles, new jobs created by a new company, not jobs taken from American workers. If OPT had been priced out of reach, that company, its revenue, and those jobs might never have existed here.

This pattern is not unusual. Research by the Niskanen Center and the National Foundation for American Policy has found that OPT does not displace American workers, and international students and their families contribute tens of billions of dollars to the United States economy each year. OPT also fills shortages in high demand STEM fields. A fee of this size would push talented graduates to Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and other countries that welcome them, and the United States would lose the companies, jobs, and tax revenue they would have created here.

Finally, the fee bears no relation to the cost of administering the program. The current OPT application fee is $520. A $70,000 charge is not cost recovery. It is a barrier designed to shrink the program, and it falls hardest on students and schools, not on any party responsible for fraud.

For these reasons, I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and preserve OPT as a lawful, affordable path for international students who study and contribute in the United States.

Respectfully submitted,
An F-1 graduate student in California
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed high OPT fees will harm students and the U.S. economy, and asks DHS to withdraw it.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Phillip Tsurkan
comments.commentText:
My name is Phillip Tsurkan and I am a U.S. citizen enrolled in a graduate program at the University of Connecticut, currently pursuing a PhD in Materials Science and Engineering. I am in my fifth year of study, and I have completed the requirements to be a PhD candidate. Throughout my program, I have collaborated within my institution, with outside universities, as well as with national laboratories on experimental and computational research regarding Materials Science, Physics, Biomedical Engineering, and Mechanical Engineering. I have attended and presented at relevant conferences, published in peer reviewed journals, completed summer schools/programs, and taught as an instructor. Through these experiences, I have observed firsthand how the insight, knowledge, perspective, and vigor of international students strengthen U.S. institutions and laboratories.
The diverse learning environments that exist throughout the world foster generations of scientists, engineers, academics, and scholars that advance the current state of the art in STEM-relevant fields. Currently, the brightest students seek education here in the U.S., with national students such as myself continuing education here rather than abroad, and international students leaving their home countries to take part in advancing the leader in scientific innovation. This raises two concerns with the proposed fees on Optional Practical Training (OPT) in DHS Docket No. ICEB–2026–0100: 1) U.S. educated talent will be lost after international students finish their respective degrees, and 2) international student enrollment/acceptance will decline, slowing our advancement as a nation in STEM fields.
The technical and academic capabilities of international students grow during their studies within the U.S., which is attributed to the expertise that already exists here, as well as to that which forms through interactions with top students and professors on the world scale. It is therefore paramount that this U.S.-enhanced talent remains within the country of which it was fostered. The OPT program serves as a pathway for international students to find a permanent place in advancing the STEM-relevant capabilities of the U.S., whether this occurs through academic institutions, national laboratories, and especially industry, which STEM-majors often pursue. Adding any hindrance into the OPT program will deter international students from staying within the U.S., thereby exporting U.S.-educated talent.
International student enrollment in higher (graduate) education programs at U.S. institutions relies largely on confidence on the part of the student and the institution itself. An available (and attainable) OPT program boosts confidence in students to seek education in foreign institutions, as a possibility to continue working in a nation at the frontier of scientific research and innovation supports their commitment to starting a new life abroad. Similarly, U.S. institutions take the prospective future of their students into account, ensuring they find positions that progress their careers after graduation. The proposed fees on OPT programs discourage both international students from applying and U.S. institutions from making offers. Scaling back enrollments due to a lack of confidence will immediately affect international students and further spread to the broader graduate body. This will ultimately limit opportunities for national students to obtain higher education in this country, thereby eroding our country’s lead in STEM innovation.
Alongside the decreased growth and integration of talent within U.S. academia and industry, paying the proposed fees raises multiple concerns. The cost of OPT fees paid by universities would largely fall onto research grants and tuition paid by undergraduate students. This results in less funding for the research itself, as well as raising cost of college education for Americans. Both aspects stretch well beyond the realm of international students within the U.S. by choking the funding supporting current research and depleting the pipeline of domestic talent pertinent to the future of this country.
For these reasons, I urge DHS to reject the proposed fees on OPT in DHS Docket No. ICEB–2026–0100. U.S. research and innovation rely heavily on attracting, educating, and retaining talented students from around the world. Any hindrance placed on the OPT program risks losing our position as a leader in science and engineering on the global stage.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that international students strengthen U.S. institutions and raises concerns about the proposed OPT fees.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security:

I submit this comment as a member of the public. DHS's interest in OPT program integrity is legitimate, and fraud should be addressed. I respectfully ask DHS to reconsider the design of this proposal, which may not achieve that goal and may carry costs the notice does not fully weigh.

1. Fit between problem and remedy. The notice describes fraud mainly through enforcement press releases and individual prosecutions. A uniform $70,000/$30,000 charge falls equally on compliant and noncompliant schools, and the notice does not show how the fee amount relates to any reduction in fraud. DHS considered targeted alternatives, such as extending STEM OPT oversight (site visits, training plans, reporting) to OPT generally, but set them aside as more complex. Agencies must reasonably consider alternatives. Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29, 43, 48 (1983).

2. Costs and benefits. DHS's own analysis estimates primary annualized costs of $4.1 billion (range: $32 million to $8.2 billion) and annualized transfers of about $12.8 billion. The fraud-reduction benefit is not quantified comparably. DHS also assumes limited effects on international enrollment, which is uncertain at this fee level. International students contributed $43.8 billion and supported 378,175 U.S. jobs in 2023–24 (NAFSA).

3. Small institutions. DHS estimates that 56 percent of affected institutions are small entities, yet declines an exemption. The Regulatory Flexibility Act requires consideration of significant alternatives that minimize burden on small entities. 5 U.S.C. § 603(c).

4. Legal authority. The notice relies on INA §§ 103(a) and 214(a), and states that fees would be deposited as miscellaneous receipts under 31 U.S.C. § 3302, with ICE retaining nothing. Neither INA provision expressly authorizes a fee of this size, and courts now interpret statutes without deference to agency readings. Loper Bright Enters. v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024). A charge of this magnitude, unconnected to the cost of a service, may also draw major-questions scrutiny. West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S. 697 (2022). The notice sets the OPT fee to align with the H-1B fee, which a federal court set aside in June 2026 (Forbes).

5. Reliance. Students admitted and enrolled have planned degrees around OPT eligibility. Reliance interests must be weighed. DHS v. Regents, 591 U.S. 1, 30–33 (2020).

6. Comment period. A 30-day period is short for a rule with a projected ten-year transfer of roughly $109 billion.

Requested action. DHS should withdraw the proposal or, at minimum: (a) adopt targeted compliance measures instead of a uniform fee; (b) exempt small and public institutions; (c) grandfather currently enrolled students; and (d) extend the comment period to 60 days.

Sources
- DHS, Optional Practical Training Fees, 91 Fed. Reg. 64566 (Oct. 8, 2026): https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/08/2026-20660/optional-practical-training-fees
- NAFSA, International Student Economic Value Tool (2023–24): https://www.nafsa.org/economicvalue
- Forbes, "DHS Immigration Rule Proposes $100,000 In Practical Training Fees" (Oct. 8, 2026): https://www.forbes.com/sites/stuartanderson/2026/10/08/dhs-immigration-rule-proposes-100000-in-practical-training-fees/
comments.reason: The commenter argues the fee is poorly designed, disproportionately costly, and may harm international student enrollment and the economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To whom it may concern,

I'm writing as a member of the public about one concern with this proposal: how it would affect small schools.

I understand DHS wants to protect the integrity of OPT, and I support that goal. My concern is that a fee of $70,000 for a student's first OPT recommendation, and $30,000 for each one after that, would land very differently on a small college than on a large university.

DHS's own analysis estimates that 56 percent of the regulated schools are small entities. Many of these schools have modest budgets and few ways to absorb a charge of this size. A large research university may be able to pay it or pass it along. A small college, a community-oriented campus, or a specialized institution may not, and could end up recommending fewer students for OPT or enrolling fewer international students at all.

The notice says DHS considered exempting small educational institutions, but decided against it because many schools are small and an exemption could leave fraud vulnerabilities unaddressed. That reasoning is hard to follow. Treating more than half of all schools as a loophole suggests the fee is a poor fit for the schools it covers, not that small schools should be left out of the analysis. Federal rulemaking is also supposed to look for ways to reduce the burden on small entities, as the Regulatory Flexibility Act describes (5 U.S.C. § 603(c)).

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposal, or at least to set lower fees or exemptions for small institutions, and to use targeted oversight where fraud has actually been found.

Sources:
- DHS, Optional Practical Training Fees, 91 Fed. Reg. 64566 (Oct. 8, 2026): https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/08/2026-20660/optional-practical-training-fees

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for subsequent OPT participation.

While preventing immigration fraud and protecting the integrity of the immigration system are legitimate government objectives, these excessive fees risk undermining American universities, scientific research, innovation, and the country's ability to attract and retain highly qualified talent.

**1. International researchers are also essential contributors to America's scientific future**

International PhD students are not merely recipients of an American education. They are an integral part of the academic and scientific community, working alongside American students, professors, and researchers to advance knowledge and innovation.

Throughout their doctoral programs, many spend four to six years or more conducting research, publishing scientific papers, contributing to research projects, mentoring students, and supporting university teaching. Many also serve as Graduate Employees, teaching assistants, and research assistants.

Their work contributes directly to scientific discoveries, technological development, and the advancement of American universities. OPT allows these graduates to continue applying their expertise professionally after years of academic contribution.

**2. The United States risks losing highly qualified talent**

Scientific talent is globally competitive. Countries such as Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Germany actively seek international researchers and professionals.

A $70,000 institutional fee for each initial OPT recommendation could discourage universities and research institutions from retaining international graduates, regardless of their qualifications or achievements.

This could push talented researchers toward other countries, weaken American research institutions, limit employers' access to specialized professionals, and ultimately benefit competing economies.

The United States should remain a destination where scientific excellence and professional merit are encouraged, not made prohibitively expensive.

**3. The impact extends to families and local communities**

International doctoral students often relocate with their spouses and children, making significant personal and financial sacrifices to pursue advanced education.

Their families become part of local communities, participate in schools, support local businesses, and contribute to university life. They build relationships and establish roots while supporting the student's academic journey.

Making post-graduation opportunities financially inaccessible creates uncertainty for entire families who have dedicated years to building their lives in the United States.

These consequences extend beyond immigration policy. They affect communities, universities, local economies, and the country's ability to retain people who have become part of American society.

**4. Universities should make decisions based on merit, not financial capacity**

Although the proposed fees are formally charged to educational institutions, a $70,000 expense could fundamentally change their willingness to recommend international graduates for OPT.

Universities with limited budgets and smaller research programs may be particularly affected. This creates an unequal system in which opportunities depend not on academic merit or professional potential, but on an institution's financial resources.

**5. Fraud prevention must be proportional and targeted**

Immigration fraud must be addressed. However, imposing extraordinary fees on every OPT recommendation does not distinguish fraudulent participants from legitimate graduates who have complied with immigration requirements throughout their academic careers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security:

I respectfully submit that the Department lacks statutory authority to promulgate this rule, and I urge its withdrawal.

An agency may impose a charge only where Congress has authorized it. The notice relies on general provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act, namely sections 103(a) and 214(a), neither of which expressly authorizes a fee of this nature or magnitude. The notice further states that the proceeds would be deposited in the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts under 31 U.S.C. § 3302, and that ICE could not retain them because the statute provides no such authority. The charge therefore corresponds to no service rendered and funds no enforcement activity.

Courts no longer defer to agency interpretations of ambiguous statutes. Loper Bright Enters. v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024). Moreover, a federal court set aside the $100,000 H-1B fee in June 2026, an amount to which this proposal is expressly aligned.

A rule lacking authority cannot be cured by revision. Withdrawal is the appropriate course.

Respectfully submitted.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Jae Conover
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT.

The rule’s stated purpose is to protect U.S. workers, but this misunderstands what OPT is. OPT does not give international students the right to work in the United States permanently. That is a totally different thing. It is temporary practical training directly related to a student’s field of study, a short window for international students to apply what they learned and learn about the U.S. job market. The proposed rule does not explain how charging students tens of thousands of dollars for this training would protect any U.S. worker.

More importantly, this policy is going to hugely discourage international students from coming to study in the United States. International students actually boost local economies by paying high out-of-state tuition and through their everyday spending. According to NAFSA, international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported more than 355,000 jobs in the 2024–2025 academic year. New international enrollment has already fallen sharply, and further losses would hit universities and surrounding communities directly. Before it does anything to “protect” the U.S. labor market, this rule will hurt local economies and university budgets first. At these amounts, the fees would function less as a fee than as a barrier. $70,000 is more than many students pay in a full year of tuition, which would make OPT available only to the wealthiest students and push away talented students from more modest backgrounds.

For these reasons, I oppose this proposed rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly support the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed rule establishing significant fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendations ($70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT, including STEM OPT extensions).

The current OPT program is widely used as a de facto work visa and pathway to H-1B status and eventual permanent residency rather than as genuine practical training tied to a student’s academic program. Many F-1 students, particularly large numbers from India and China, enter the United States on student visas while stating an intent to return home after studies, yet arrive with a clear plan to remain and work long-term. OPT has become a primary vehicle for this strategy: students obtain OPT authorization, often with minimal or non-substantive employment at companies that exist largely to facilitate immigration status, and then use that status to enter the H-1B process and later pursue green cards.

This undermines the integrity of both the F-1 and H-1B programs. It allows individuals who never intended temporary study to bypass the numerical limits, wage protections, and higher scrutiny of the H-1B system. It also disadvantages U.S. workers and well-qualified international students who pursue legitimate training and employment opportunities.

High fees will force educational institutions to be far more selective in recommending students for OPT. Schools will have a strong financial incentive to carefully review each case, verify that the proposed employment is real and related to the student’s field of study, and decline recommendations for students whose primary purpose is immigration rather than genuine practical training. This is a necessary and appropriate step to reduce fraud and abuse.

I urge DHS to finalize the proposed fees without significant reductions or exemptions that would weaken their deterrent effect. The entire OPT-to-H-1B-to-permanent-residence pipeline should be tightened so that only well-qualified students who meet the original temporary-student intent requirements can access OPT. The proposed fees are a meaningful step in that direction and will help protect the integrity of the immigration system and American workers.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly supports the proposed OPT fees to curb the misuse of the program as a de facto work visa.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed OPT fee at 91 FR 64566.

1. This is a program-elimination measure in fee form. A $70,000 charge per student for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT, payable by the SEVP-certified institution before a designated school official may recommend OPT, cannot be absorbed by any institution. The predictable response is not to charge students $70,000; it is to stop recommending OPT. If the intent is to end post-completion OPT, DHS should defend that directly rather than route it through a fee the regulated party cannot pay.

2. Labeling the fee a transfer understates the burden. The regulatory impact analysis treats institutional payments to the Federal Government as transfers rather than costs. But public institutions have no authority to levy a $70,000 per-student surcharge, so the charge cannot be passed through as a price; it lands on the student as a benefit withdrawn. A benefit withdrawn is a cost, and it appears nowhere in the analysis.

3. The fee is not tailored to the harms cited. The rule cites fraud and program integrity, yet the charge is per student and is not tied to employer identity, wage level, or any fraud indicator. A legitimate employer paying a prevailing wage costs the institution the same $70,000 as a fraudulent staffing arrangement. Employer-side fees for serial or related-party filings, expanded site visits, and funded SEVIS audits would target the stated problem without eliminating the benefit for every student.

4. The small-entity analysis does not support the rule. The IRFA invites comment on small-entity impact, so: for community colleges, small liberal arts colleges, and seminaries, $70,000 per student exceeds total tuition revenue per student in many programs. The proposed fee therefore eliminates OPT at exactly the institutions whose students have the fewest alternatives, and the analysis records that outcome as a transfer rather than as the loss it is.

5. Reliance and retroactivity. Students chose programs and took on debt on the documented premise that post-completion OPT exists at the current $470 Form I-765 fee. Any final rule should not apply to students already enrolled.

6. Process. Thirty days, from October 8 to November 9, is not adequate for a change of this magnitude. I ask DHS to extend the comment period by at least 60 days, to publish the fee level at which the program remains viable as against the level at which it is functionally eliminated, and to consider cost-recovery pricing with audit funding instead of a punitive per-student charge.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fee acts as a program-elimination measure that harms students and institutions.

comments.commentText:
I strongly support the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed rule that would impose significant fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendations ($70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT, including STEM OPT extensions).

The current OPT program is widely used as a de facto work visa and pathway to H-1B status and eventual permanent residency rather than as genuine practical training tied to a student’s academic program. Many F-1 students, particularly many from India and China, enter the United States on student visas stating an intent to return home after their studies, yet arrive with a clear plan to remain and work long-term. A significant portion of the problem involves companies that are not legitimate operating businesses but are set up primarily as vehicles to place foreign students on OPT so they can later file for H-1B status. These entities often provide little or no real training or productive work related to the student’s degree. At the same time, employers that hire OPT workers do not pay Social Security (FICA) taxes on their wages. This creates a clear cost advantage over hiring American graduates, who require full Social Security contributions. As a result, companies have a financial incentive to prefer OPT candidates over U.S. workers, further disadvantaging American graduates in the job market.

These practices undermine the integrity of both the F-1 and H-1B programs. They allow individuals who never intended temporary study to bypass the numerical limits, wage protections, and higher scrutiny of the H-1B system, while giving employers an artificial cost advantage that discourages the hiring of U.S. citizens and permanent residents.

Schools will have a strong financial incentive to carefully review each case, verify that the proposed employment is with a real operating company offering genuine training related to the student’s field of study, and decline recommendations that appear designed primarily for immigration purposes. This is a necessary and appropriate step to reduce fraud and abuse.

I urge DHS to finalize the proposed fees without significant reduction or exemptions that would weaken their deterrent effect. The entire OPT-to-H-1B-to-permanent-residence pipeline should be tightened so that only well-qualified students who meet the original temporary-student intent requirements can access OPT, and so that employers no longer have a built-in cost advantage that disadvantages American graduates. comments.commentText:
Comment on DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2)

I am an F-1 student currently on post-completion OPT, and I oppose the proposed fees of $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation.

1. The fee is charged to the school, but its effect falls on students. A fee of this size is larger than the full tuition of many legitimate graduate programs. Faced with a $70,000 charge per student, most SEVP-certified schools — especially smaller institutions and programs serving working adult students — will simply stop recommending OPT, or pass the cost to students through higher tuition. Either way, the practical result is the end of OPT access for students at those schools, regardless of their individual merits or compliance history.

2. The fee is not calibrated to the stated purpose. DHS justifies the fee by fraud prevention and program integrity, but SEVP already has site visits, reporting requirements, and DSO oversight, and schools already pay SEVIS-related fees. A flat $70,000 per recommendation is not tied to the actual cost of oversight for an individual student and does not distinguish schools or students with clean compliance records from bad actors. It punishes compliant institutions and students for the misconduct of others.

3. The fee would harm U.S. employers and local economies. OPT allows U.S. businesses — including small businesses in healthcare, technology, and other shortage fields — to employ graduates of U.S. programs who were educated here. If schools stop recommending OPT because of the fee, employers lose access to these workers and communities lose their spending and tax contributions.

4. The subsequent-OPT fee penalizes educational progression. A student who completes a higher degree level and becomes eligible for a new OPT period — a pathway Congress and DHS regulations expressly allow — would trigger a new $30,000 charge to the school. This discourages students from pursuing further U.S. education and discourages schools from enrolling them.

For these reasons, I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed fees in 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2). If DHS proceeds, it should, at a minimum, set any fee at a level tied to documented oversight costs, exempt or reduce the fee for subsequent OPT following completion of a higher degree level, and provide a longer transition period for students already in F-1 status who planned their education in reliance on the current rules.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Laura Buhs
comments.commentText:
I am writing in opposition to the proposed rule to establish up to $100,000/student in fees for OPT recommendations. As an international education professional, I am very familiar with the current state and the expected impacts of the proposed rule.

1.The proposed fees will not recover the costs of the OPT application or administration of the program including deterring fraud and investigating noncompliance. The fees will go to general Treasury funds, so there is no plan for them to address the issues DHS identifies. In fact, the authority to collect the tax is in question. DHs has not established a rational connection between the fee and the issues it claims the fee will address.

I object to universities, students, or their employers being taxed at an extremely high rate when the money will not even support OPT or the F-1 program in general. This does not mean OPT will only be used by highly talented and qualified students. It will limit it to those with the ability to pay – unrelated to merit. This will not prevent fraud and abuse.

In addition, there are far more efficient and effective ways for DHS to deter fraud and investigate noncompliance with the information it already has within SEVIS to identify fraud and noncompliance.

2.There is lack of clarity in the regulatory language that must be addressed:
•It is not clear if $30,000 will be charged only for the first OPT recommendation after paying the $70,000 fee or for every OPT recommendation after paying the $70,000 fee.
•It is not clear how the fee will work when OPT is recommended by different schools for the same student.
•It is not clear how the fee will work for a student with a break in F-1 status.

3.The analysis by DHS does not reflect the expected impact on F-1 students, postsecondary institutions, domestic postsecondary students, local and national economies, job growth, or innovation and discovery.
a.The number of OPT applications will drop dramatically as very few institutions and students can absorb the exorbitant fees and F-1 students will be deprived of valuable practical experiences that complement their education and that contribute to the employment market and economy.
b.Postsecondary institutions and their communities will lose the economic and cultural/social benefits of F-1 students who choose not to study in the U.S. because of the lack of OPT. This will cause budgetary issues for institutions which will affect domestic students and the opportunities available to them.
c.Study after study shows that immigrant participation in the labor market contributes to job growth and does not take jobs from U.S. workers. Other actions by the current administration are already impacting the economy and job growth. The OPT fee will further exacerbate this.
d.The U.S. will lose out in the marketplace for top global talent, especially in STEM fields, affecting research and teaching, innovation, and leading in top fields such as AI. If the concern is about not enough U.S. workers in critical fields, I suggest the federal government invest in U.S. public education as a complement to keeping int’l talent for maximum benefit.

4.Finally, a 30-day comment period instead of the normal 60-day period is not sufficient to review the impacts and prepare comments on such a major change.
I urge you to reconsider the proposed regulations and devise methods that will actually deter fraud, improve immigration integrity and protect U.S. workers.

Laura Buhs
