comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security:

I respectfully object to the proposed fee structure of $70,000 for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) authorization and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations. I strongly encourage DHS to rescind these fees and maintain affordable access to legitimate practical training that aligns with students' degrees.

I'm a researcher at a public university in the US and work alongside citizens and international colleagues, from interns over grad students to postdocs and beyond. Some of my colleagues are currently able to do groundbreaking and lifesaving science only thanks to the OPT program. These researchers have worked hard to obtain their degrees at US-based universities alongside their citizen peers, all of them have received the world-class education that the US is known for. Keeping OPT an affordable and accessible option means those graduates can put their hard-won knowledge and skills to use directly to the benefit of the US economy and for the US people. Imposing the suggested fees would mean many internationals students will leave the US after graduating, draining precious talent and skills that the US economy desperately needs, as many universities will not be able to pay these fees.

I fully endorse protecting American workers, combating fraud, and upholding immigration system integrity. However, financial capacity to pay high fees does not indicate compliance, nor does inability to pay signal wrongdoing. DHS must justify how these specific fee amounts would effectively differentiate between legitimate educational training and system abuse. A decline in program participation due to high fees cannot be considered proof of successful fraud prevention. I respectfully ask DHS to explain how these fees would effectively combat fraud beyond imposing a large financial burden that inevitably limits legitimate use of the OPT program. The agency should consider less restrictive alternatives, such as focused compliance audits, validation that training relates to degree programs, employer oversight, and enforcement of existing worker protections. Interventions targeting actual misconduct would be more appropriate than imposing financial obstacles that impact law-abiding participants.

I'm concerned about the proposed 60-day implementation timeline. DHS should protect students already enrolled in programs or committed to training under current rules. Prospective application doesn't address impacts on decisions made years earlier. I request explicit protections for current students and existing OPT participants needing future recommendations or extensions.

DHS should assess consequences for universities, hospitals, research institutions, small employers, and underserved communities. The analysis should examine whether these fees could discourage clinical training, disrupt research, or limit essential services, and whether smaller institutions would face disproportionate barriers.

DHS should also consider whether shifting costs to students could increase debt or employer dependence, potentially making participants more financially vulnerable.

I request DHS withdraw this fee structure. Any alternative should be evidence-based, proportionate, and address actual problems without making legitimate training financially unattainable. At minimum, DHS should evaluate substantially lower fees, meaningful waivers, and transition protections.

Protecting American workers and immigration integrity are important goals that should be pursued through effective oversight and evidence-based enforcement, not by restricting lawful educational training to those with exceptional financial resources.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by University of Idaho
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees
The University of Idaho opposes the proposed rule published October 8, 2026, and urges that it be withdrawn in its entirety.
The University of Idaho, in Moscow, is Idaho's public land-grant R1 research university and oldest institution of higher education. With over 50 extension centers, we educate and employ people across Idaho. Fall 2025 enrollment was 12,383, including 709 international students and a record 602 doctoral students. F-1 students are vital to our research, teaching, and operations.
The proposed tax imposes a substantial financial burden
The rule charges $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each later one. The cost is driven by volume, not risk. Applied to our 2020–2026 records, it would have required U of I to pay $19,690,000 for 335 recommendations. Graduate students account for 76% of that total, so the tax falls hardest where practical training is most integral to the degree. Even the 2024 and 2025 cohorts would each cost about $2 million, before the staff time and systems needed to collect, approve, and refund payments.
No budget line can absorb a nearly $20 million tax. We would have to absorb an unfunded cost, charge students, or limit access to practical training, and limiting access is the only realistic option. Access would turn on who can pay, not on who qualifies. Designated School Officials would be left recommending only students with money, which could be seen as bias.
The rule harms enrollment, Idaho's economy, and domestic students
International enrollment fell by 111 students from 2024 to 2025 amid recent federal policies, and each new restriction deepens that decline. According to NAFSA, Idaho's 3,601 international students contributed $85.5 million to the state economy and supported 586 jobs in 2024/25; U of I generated the largest share, $32.3 million and 264 jobs. Our international undergraduates also pay about $3.4 million a year above resident tuition, revenue that helps keep costs low for Idaho students and sustains the courses they take.
Students weigh post-graduation work heavily when choosing where to study. In one recent survey, 37–69% of international students, and 38–70% of STEM students, said they would not have enrolled with these fees in place. They would choose countries that offer that opportunity.
The rule restricts access to practical training
OPT is part of a student's education: professional experience tied directly to the field of study. The fees would divide equally eligible students into those who can pay and those who cannot, harming students with fewer resources most. U of I also hires 25 to 40 staff, postdocs, and faculty each year who hold OPT work authorization; losing them would interrupt research projects that serve Idaho.
The rule disrupts research and workforce pipelines
Our OPT authorizations from 2020 through 2026 span 76 majors, with roughly 85% in engineering, computer science, agriculture, and the sciences; computer science alone is 17%. These are fields where Idaho employers need more graduates than the domestic workforce supplies. OPT participants complement, rather than replace, American workers. Losing international graduate students would also put U of I's R1 status at risk: R1 requires 70 research doctorates a year, and we award about 80.
International graduates also stay and pay taxes. We estimate each OPT worker pays about $15,000 a year in federal income tax and $4,200 in Idaho income tax. Nationally, OPT workers pay about $3.6 billion a year in federal income tax plus $1.2 billion in payroll taxes. If OPT participation fell about 80%, federal tax losses of roughly $3.8 billion a year would exceed the fees collected.
Additional concerns
We are committed to OPT compliance and have invested in dedicated advising staff, SEVIS reporting, and eligibility reviews. DHS has not explained why ability to pay would deter misconduct better than these safeguards, especially when the revenue goes to the Treasury rather than to OPT oversight. Nor has it justified the amounts, or explained how often the $30,000 fee applies, how refunds work, or how fees apply to transfers and later degrees.
Together with recent limits on practical training, visa processing, and duration of status, the rule compounds the deterrent to studying in the U.S. DHS should analyze these cumulative effects and narrower alternatives, such as targeting employers linked to fraud. The 30-day comment period is too short for a full institutional response; we request an extension.
For these reasons, we urge the Department to withdraw the proposed rule in its entirety.
Respectfully submitted,
C. Scott Green, President, University of Idaho, 875 Perimeter Drive, Moscow, ID 83843

International students add to this country, to the fields they participate in, and this change would have terrible impacts on so many different fields. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anna Kovtunova
comments.commentText: As written, the rule is ambiguous in both its scope and application. It does not clarify whether the $70,000 fee is a one time, flat, fee or whether it must be paid each time a student changes institutions. Moreover, the fee is directed to the Treasury rather than DHS, which is the department responsible for administering the OPT program. Fees are compulsory payments to offset an agency’s cost of providing a good or service. If the fee is not going to the agency providing the service, it cannot be considered a fee, but a tax. Ultimately, the proposed fee is a huge financial barrier to participation in the OPT program, potentially discouraging international students from studying in the US. If enacted, this rule will disrupt research teams, employer partnerships, and workforce pipelines, and it would impact learning, mentorship, and career opportunities for both international and domestic students. We need more, not fewer, international students coming to the US, and this rule would really hinder that goal.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fee creates a financial barrier that will harm international students and workforce pipelines.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Frank Cobia
comments.commentText:
I support the proposed rule in Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100. It would set a $70,000 fee for an initial Optional Practical Training period and $30,000 for each later one, including the STEM OPT extension (proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(ii) and 214.13(i)(1)).

I am a U.S. citizen and an IT executive in Roswell, Georgia. I have hired and managed IT teams for a long time. OPT and STEM OPT let employers hire recent foreign graduates for up to three years without the labor certification, prevailing wage attestation, or annual cap that apply to H-1B. Those graduates compete directly with American IT workers. They cost the employer less, and U.S. workers get fewer protections.

It makes no sense to bring in more foreign IT workers while American IT workers are being laid off. Technology companies announced 165,925 job cuts through September 2026, more than any other industry, according to Challenger, Gray & Christmas. Recent graduates in computer engineering and computer science have some of the highest unemployment rates of any major, 7.8 percent and 7.0 percent, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

The fee level is justified. DHS should not lower it in the final rule, and a higher fee would also be justified. I ask DHS to finalize the fee as proposed and apply it to the STEM OPT extension. Please don't add exemptions that let large employers or staffing firms get around it. Congress never authorized OPT by statute. It exists only by regulation, and it should ultimately be ended.

Thank you for considering my comment.
Frank Cobia, Roswell, GA
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly supports the proposed OPT fees and asks DHS to finalize them as proposed.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Bulent Altay
comments.commentText:
I am an international Ph.D. researcher at Texas A&M University, and I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT applications.

During my doctoral studies, I have contributed to federally supported engineering research at the Texas A&M Transportation Institute, focusing on computational modeling, material failure, and fatigue crack propagation in railroad infrastructure. Research like mine contributes to improving the safety, reliability, and durability of critical American infrastructure. It also represents years of investment by American universities, research institutions, and federal funding agencies.

Optional Practical Training provides an essential opportunity for researchers like me to apply the specialized knowledge developed through American graduate education to real-world engineering challenges. The proposed fees would create an extraordinary financial barrier at precisely the point when the United States could begin benefiting more directly from that investment.

Although the proposed rule places the payment obligation on educational institutions, universities may transfer these costs to students or employers. Neither recent Ph.D. graduates nor most academic research groups and early-career employers can reasonably absorb such expenses. A $70,000 fee would make many otherwise qualified international graduates financially ineligible for employment opportunities, regardless of their academic achievements, technical expertise, or potential contributions.

I am particularly concerned about the long-term consequences for American scientific and technological competitiveness. International graduate researchers contribute to federally funded projects, collaborate with American colleagues, and develop specialized expertise in fields such as advanced manufacturing, materials science, computational mechanics, and infrastructure engineering. Preventing these researchers from remaining in the United States after graduation risks transferring the benefits of American research investments to other countries.

I recognize the importance of preventing fraud and ensuring compliance with immigration regulations. However, imposing an excessive financial burden on legitimate students and research institutions is neither a targeted nor a proportionate solution. As acknowledged in Section IV.C, the proposed fee revenue would be deposited into the general U.S. Treasury rather than specifically allocated to OPT oversight or enforcement. Strengthening employer verification, compliance monitoring, and targeted investigations would be a more reasonable approach.

After years of rigorous doctoral research and contributions to American engineering, international graduates should have a fair opportunity to continue supporting the country's scientific and technological progress. The proposed fee structure would effectively eliminate that opportunity for many qualified researchers based on financial resources rather than merit or compliance.

I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw the proposed OPT fee increases and instead pursue targeted, evidence-based measures that protect program integrity without undermining American research, innovation, and economic competitiveness.

Respectfully,

An International Ph.D. Researcher
Texas A&M University
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed high OPT fees create financial barriers and harm researchers and institutions.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: As written, the proposed rule by DHS is justified on the basis that HS "this proposed fee would incentivize educational institutions to exercise greater oversight and selectivity when recommending students for OPT, thereby reducing fraudulent authorizations and curbing “visa mill” activities. By establishing a financial obligation through a fee, this proposed rule would encourage schools to ensure that OPT opportunities provide genuine educational value that aligns with the original intent of the practical training program, thereby promoting shared responsibility and accountability." It is not clear to me how this rule would increase the safety and security of the USA or its citizens, so I would like to see more explanation. From my perspective, the opportunity that American institutions of higher education have given to foreigners to experience life in the US as they receive an education here has been a tremendous source of American prestige, stability, and soft power. Some talented foreign students seek to extend their time here, or even to immigrate, in order to take advantage of the tremendous opportunities for individual prosperity and flourishing, and political and intellectual freedom, that America has traditionally afforded. Others opt to go back to their home countries, but they take their knowledge of US culture and the relationships (of intellectual collaboration, friendship, etc) with them. Both outcomes provide great benefits to the USA, and it would be a great loss to our country to curtail them. Moreover, I don't see an adequate justification for the AMOUNT of these fees, which I believe might prove ruinous to most institutions, even if some remedies for refunds etc. are implemented. Why not stick with the much simpler scheme of just keeping the expense to institutions of sponsoring foreign students for OPT very low, rather than introducing some difficult and expensive bureaucratic process that may or may not be effective in alleviating the egregious cost of the new policy?

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Jundong  Song
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Opposition to Proposed Optional Practical Training Fees

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. These fees would create an extraordinary financial barrier to legitimate practical training and could undermine the value of an American education for international students.

My objections concern the proposed fee levels, the transition provisions, and the treatment of students who have already invested in U.S. degree programs.

1. The proposed fees would make practical training financially inaccessible.

Requiring universities to pay does not eliminate the economic burden. Universities could refuse to recommend eligible students or pass the costs to students or employers. Access to practical training would then depend heavily on financial resources rather than academic qualifications, compliance with immigration rules, or the educational value of the training.

DHS should provide a transparent justification for these amounts, including their relationship to actual administrative and enforcement costs.

2. Students already enrolled deserve meaningful transition protection.

Current students have committed substantial tuition, time, and effort under rules allowing eligible graduates to apply for OPT. Although employment authorization is not guaranteed, the opportunity to pursue practical training is a meaningful consideration in choosing a U.S. education.

A 60-day transition would not adequately address commitments made over several years. If DHS adopts any new fee, it should exempt students enrolled before the final rule takes effect, including their post-completion OPT and associated STEM OPT extensions.

3. The proposal could harm U.S. employers and universities.

The fees could discourage employers, particularly small businesses, from hiring otherwise qualified graduates. They could also reduce the attractiveness of U.S. universities and encourage students educated here to take their skills elsewhere. DHS should evaluate these consequences explicitly before proceeding.

4. Fraud prevention should focus on misconduct.

Protecting program integrity is a legitimate objective. However, imposing prohibitive fees on all participants would burden compliant students, institutions, and employers alongside those who violate the rules. DHS should assess targeted investigations, institutional oversight, and proportionate, cost-supported fees as alternatives.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw this proposal. If the agency proceeds, it should substantially reduce the fees, explain their cost basis, and provide clear protection for students already enrolled and their associated OPT and STEM OPT opportunities.

Thank you for considering my comments.
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposed high OPT fees, arguing they create unfair financial barriers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee.

These fees would not meaningfully distinguish legitimate students and employers from fraudulent actors. Instead, they would create an enormous financial barrier for law-abiding F-1 students who have already invested heavily in U.S. education and are seeking temporary, degree-related practical training exactly as OPT was designed to provide.

If the goal is to prevent fraud and protect U.S. workers, DHS should target the actual sources of abuse through employer verification, audits, site visits, stronger reporting requirements, E-Verify, and penalties for sham employers or fraudulent participants.

A legitimate student graduating from an accredited U.S. university should not face the same financial burden as a fraudulent case simply because both seek OPT authorization. Ability to pay $70,000 is not evidence of compliance, merit, or legitimacy.

The proposed fees could also discourage international students from choosing U.S. universities, weaken the competitiveness of American higher education, and deprive U.S. employers of graduates trained in this country.

I strongly request that DHS remove these proposed OPT fees and adopt targeted, evidence-based enforcement measures instead. Fraud should be punished directly; compliant students should not be priced out of lawful practical training.
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposed high OPT fees because they create financial barriers for students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Comment 1 of 10: Student affordability.
All ten topic-specific comments in this series come from the same anonymous individual. I do not claim to represent any institution or stakeholder group.

I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw them. Sections IV.C and V.A would make schools pay $70,000 before an initial OPT recommendation and permit the burden to be passed to students. Moving the bill between a school and a student does not make the barrier disappear.

It is deeply troubling to make access to legitimate educational training depend on finding an additional sum of this size. A student's honesty, academic preparation, and the educational value of a placement cannot be measured by family wealth. A school that cannot finance the payment could refuse a qualified student's recommendation even when every substantive requirement is satisfied.

DHS should assess who would lose access at different income levels and explain how payment capacity identifies fraud. If additional oversight needs funding, DHS should evaluate proportionate alternatives supported by documented administrative costs. Legitimate students should not have to finance a prohibitive barrier in order to demonstrate that they deserve a lawful educational opportunity. Please withdraw the proposed fees.

Reference: Optional Practical Training Fees, 91 FR 64566, sections IV.C and V.A (October 8, 2026).
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw them due to financial burdens.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Comment 2 of 10: Talent and scientific continuity.
All ten topic-specific comments in this series come from the same anonymous individual. I do not claim to represent any institution or stakeholder group.

I strongly oppose this proposal. Section V.A would impose an additional payment for subsequent OPT, including STEM extensions. Repeated financial hurdles can interrupt legitimate training after a graduate has already developed specialized knowledge and begun contributing to a team.

From a talent-development perspective, the relevant question is whether training is lawful, supervised, and educationally valuable. A large payment does not establish any of those facts. It may instead make continuation depend on the wealth of the sponsoring institution or access to a third-party payer.

I am concerned that the United States could train promising graduates and then make their lawful practical training financially inaccessible. The resulting loss could extend beyond an individual placement to unfinished experiments, interrupted collaboration, and recruitment decisions. These are risks to evaluate, not outcomes I claim to have personally observed.

DHS should analyze retention and project-continuity effects by field and institution and compare targeted compliance measures. The agency should also reject the alternative that would reimpose the initial fee at higher educational levels. Talent and integrity deserve substantive evaluation. Please withdraw this financial gatekeeping proposal.

Reference: NPRM, sections V.A and VII.A.5.b.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposal, arguing that financial hurdles on OPT extensions harm talent retention and continuity.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Comment 3 of 10: Faculty mentorship and research.
All ten topic-specific comments in this series come from the same anonymous individual. I do not claim to represent any institution or stakeholder group.

I strongly oppose the proposed fee structure because it risks replacing educational judgment with a funding test. Section III.D describes OPT as training related to the student's major. That relationship should be evaluated through the work, supervision, and learning objectives, rather than inferred from an institution's willingness to make a large payment.

Consider a hypothetical graduate whose technical knowledge is useful to a supervised research project. The project may be academically valuable without having unrestricted funds available for an OPT fee. Refusing the graduate a recommendation in that situation would establish a budget constraint, not a lack of educational value or evidence of misconduct.

The possibility that years of instruction and mentorship could end at such a financial barrier is deeply frustrating. DHS should examine research continuity, grant restrictions, and the ability of departments with different resources to support legitimate training. It should compare direct verification of supervision and educational relevance against the proposed payment mechanism.

Protect program integrity by examining the training itself. Please withdraw the prohibitive fees and preserve access to legitimate, supervised learning.

Reference: NPRM, sections III.D, IV.C, and V.A.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed fees, arguing they create financial barriers and do not reflect educational value.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Comment 4 of 10: University budgets.
All ten topic-specific comments in this series come from the same anonymous individual. I do not claim to represent any institution or stakeholder group.

I strongly oppose the proposed institutional payment obligation. Calling a school the payer does not create new resources. Administrators would have to choose among absorbing the cost, finding outside funding, transferring it, or declining otherwise legitimate recommendations.

For illustration only, 100 initial recommendations at the proposed $70,000 rate would require $7 million before subsequent fees and administrative expenses. This is arithmetic, not a claim about any specific university. DHS should evaluate such budget scenarios against unrestricted resources and operating margins, rather than treating gross revenue as freely spendable cash.

Section IV.C expressly allows costs to be passed to all students. That possibility deserves particular scrutiny: domestic students could bear higher charges or reduced services without having participated in OPT at all. It is unacceptable to treat this shifting of burdens as though it solves the underlying economic harm.

Please assess effects on tuition, aid, student services, and institutions with limited reserves. A policy intended to improve oversight should not force universities to ration lawful educational opportunities according to their capacity to finance a new charge. Withdraw the proposed fees.

Reference: NPRM, sections IV.C, V.A, and VII.B.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed institutional payment obligation and fees, arguing it causes economic harm.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Comment 5 of 10: Employer planning.
All ten topic-specific comments in this series come from the same anonymous individual. I do not claim to represent any institution or stakeholder group.

I strongly oppose this proposal because it could disrupt legitimate recruitment without directly testing employer compliance. Section V.A makes payment depend on a school's OPT recommendation, rather than a particular employer. A careful, law-abiding employer could therefore lose access to a qualified candidate because of an independent institution's funding decision.

Section VII.A.5.b acknowledges possible productivity losses when employers cannot replace OPT participants with qualified workers. DHS should investigate that risk by occupation, location, recruitment lead time, and training needs. The existence of another lawful hiring category does not by itself establish that a suitable replacement is immediately available.

The practical cost of an interrupted placement may include delayed projects, repeated recruitment, and additional work for existing staff. These are potential mechanisms that require evidence, not personal experiences I am asserting.

I support meaningful verification of genuine jobs, supervision, and lawful working conditions. Those checks address conduct directly. A substantial payment imposed upstream does not demonstrate that a particular job is legitimate. DHS should withdraw the proposed fees and evaluate targeted oversight that preserves compliant employers' ability to plan and train responsibly.

Reference: NPRM, sections V.A, VI, and VII.A.5.b.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states they strongly oppose the proposal and argues it disrupts recruitment and harms employers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Comment 6 of 10: Small-business access.
All ten topic-specific comments in this series come from the same anonymous individual. I do not claim to represent any institution or stakeholder group.

I strongly oppose a policy that could make lawful training opportunities depend on the financial strength of a school or potential employer. A small business can offer serious supervision and meaningful work while having far less cash available than a large corporation. Access to capital is not a reliable measure of compliance or training quality.

Although schools would formally owe the fees, section IV.C allows costs to be shifted to employers. If that occurs, smaller employers could face pressure to abandon a placement that a better-funded competitor could finance. Even without a direct charge, they could lose candidates when schools decline recommendations.

Section VII.B requests alternatives that minimize small-entity impacts. DHS should examine these financing constraints and downstream effects separately from its analysis of directly regulated schools. It should compare risk-based inspections, verification of genuine supervision, and enforcement against documented misconduct.

It is deeply concerning to create an entry barrier that may favor institutional wealth over a valuable learning opportunity. The agency should withdraw the proposed fee structure and develop an approach that tests integrity rather than purchasing power.

Reference: NPRM, sections IV.C, V.A, and VII.B.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed fee structure because it harms small businesses and creates entry barriers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Comment 7 of 10: Public-interest training.
All ten topic-specific comments in this series come from the same anonymous individual. I do not claim to represent any institution or stakeholder group.

I strongly oppose the proposed fees because an educational placement's public value cannot be judged by its capacity to finance a large upfront payment. Legitimate degree-related training in community research, environmental work, public policy, or nonprofit services may produce benefits that are not fully reflected in a starting salary or an organization's available cash.

Section VII.A.5.b suggests that parties could share costs when the benefits exceed the fees. That reasoning needs a much more careful examination. A project can benefit the public without giving the student, school, or host organization a way to capture those benefits as money available for payment. Benefits spread across a community do not automatically become a funding source.

I find it troubling that financially constrained public-interest placements could be excluded even when their educational merit and compliance are clear. DHS should analyze these settings separately, including restricted funding and benefits received by people outside the paying parties.

Please withdraw the proposed fees. Preserve meaningful oversight while evaluating training through its educational content, supervision, and actual compliance, rather than its ability to produce an immediate payment.

Reference: NPRM, sections IV.C and VII.A.5.b.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly asks DHS to withdraw the proposed fees due to negative impacts on public-interest placements.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Comment 8 of 10: U.S. workers and labor standards.
All ten topic-specific comments in this series come from the same anonymous individual. I do not claim to represent any institution or stakeholder group.

I strongly oppose the proposed fees and take the protection of U.S. workers seriously. Section IV.B should establish how this particular payment mechanism would improve wages and employment after accounting for different occupations, local conditions, and effects on employers' output.

A reduction in OPT participation does not, by itself, establish an equal increase in suitable jobs for U.S. workers. DHS should examine whether roles are filled, remain vacant, move elsewhere, or disappear when projects are reduced. It should also evaluate possible effects on U.S. colleagues whose work depends on a team's combined skills. I do not assume that every OPT placement is beneficial or that displacement never occurs; that is precisely why careful evidence is necessary.

Where exploitation, false employment, or unlawful working conditions are found, enforcement should address those practices directly. A large payment to the government does not by itself raise a worker's wage or improve supervision.

Workers deserve protections that can be shown to work. Please withdraw these fees and compare targeted labor-standard and anti-fraud measures using measurable outcomes and transparent assumptions.

Reference: NPRM, sections IV.B, VII.A.5.b, and VII.A.6.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states strong opposition to the proposed fees and asks DHS to withdraw them.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Comment 9 of 10: Effective fraud prevention.
All ten topic-specific comments in this series come from the same anonymous individual. I do not claim to represent any institution or stakeholder group.

I strongly oppose the proposed fees while supporting serious enforcement against OPT fraud. Section IV.A identifies misconduct that deserves investigation. The critical question is whether a universal financial barrier detects or prevents it more effectively than direct, risk-based controls.

GAO-19-297 recommended improvements involving fraud-risk assessment, data analysis, school oversight, and DSO training. The report's online updates describe implementation of several recommendations and continuing work on training. These recommendations provide concrete oversight measures to evaluate; I am not claiming that every earlier deficiency remains unresolved.

Payment is not verification. A well-funded dishonest participant could still seek to evade requirements, while an honest participant with limited resources could lose access. DHS should show why the proposed amounts are necessary, compare less burdensome controls, and publish measurable criteria for success, such as confirmed violations detected and corrected.

It is profoundly frustrating to see legitimate educational access put at risk without a convincing demonstration that the chosen barrier addresses the actual misconduct. Withdraw the fee proposal and strengthen investigation, verification, and accountability directed at evidence of fraud.

References: NPRM, section IV.A; U.S. GAO, GAO-19-297, https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-19-297.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states they strongly oppose the proposed fees and asks DHS to withdraw the fee proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Samantha Green
comments.commentText: Secretary Markwayne Mullin,By submitting this comment, I am expressing my opposition to this proposed rule. America’s higher education programs are considered among the best in the world and attract the best and brightest from across the globe. During the program or after graduating, F-1 scholars who utilize Optional Practical Training (OPT) make major contributions to US innovation in many areas from medical breakthroughs to advancements in agriculture and energy that improve quality of life, create jobs and grow the economy. The proposal to increase OPT fees to $70,000 for initial approvals and $30,000 for renewals is unreasonable and harmful to workers. International and domestic workers alike are in need of policies that protect and lift standards for all workers, safeguard their rights in the workplace, and prevent employers from suppressing wages and benefits or pitting workers against each other. The proposed rule does nothing to achieve these ends – instead it punishes students and workers. I am concerned the rule could  damage the ability for the United States to attract and retain top-tier global talent, limit important professional and academic opportunities to only the wealthy, and negatively impact the academic and professional experiences for all students and workers. This is a step in the wrong direction and would harm the nation’s higher education system, global leadership in science, and the economy. I ask you to rescind this proposed rule. Samantha Greensgreen47@calpoly.eduSan Luis Obispo, California 93405

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT authorization.

Internships and other forms of experiential learning are a central part of modern higher education and early-career preparation. NACE reports that 67% of Class of 2024 bachelor’s graduates completed at least one internship and 86% participated in some form of experiential learning. Employers also use internship experience to distinguish otherwise similarly qualified candidates.

Internationally, access to work experience while studying is common. OECD research shows that international students in competing higher-education systems generally have access to part-time work, and study-related internships and work-based learning are often regulated separately from ordinary student employment.

The proposed OPT fee should also be considered together with the recent restrictions and uncertainty surrounding CPT. Under the government’s 2026 interpretation, many optional but academically relevant internships may no longer qualify for CPT if they are not required for all students in a curriculum. If students also become effectively priced out of pre-completion OPT, they may graduate from U.S. universities with substantially less practical experience than domestic classmates holding the same degree.

A U.S. degree alone does not necessarily make a graduate equally competitive. Domestic students may graduate with the same degree plus internships, industry experience, professional references, and employer networks. Restricting both major pathways to pre-graduation practical training could therefore disadvantage international graduates for reasons unrelated to academic ability or merit.

The fee itself is also extraordinary. DHS proposes $70,000 for the first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for a subsequent recommendation. A student who uses pre-completion OPT and later post-completion OPT could therefore trigger $100,000 in fees even though standard pre- and post-completion OPT share the same 12-month aggregate limit. DHS itself anticipates that this structure will reduce participation in pre-completion OPT. This means the fee is not merely administrative; it is expected to change students’ educational and career decisions.

A financial deterrent also does not distinguish between fraud and lawful participation. A student with a legitimate degree, a genuine degree-related job, and a compliant employer faces the same $70,000 barrier as a higher-risk case. DHS should explain why these amounts are reasonably related to the actual administrative and enforcement costs attributable to an individual OPT participant.

The proposal may also create inequities among institutions and students. Two equally qualified students could receive different opportunities simply because one attends a university willing and able to absorb a $70,000 charge while the other does not. DHS estimates that the rule could generate approximately $12.4 billion annually under its primary scenario, demonstrating that the economic effects are substantial.

If DHS is concerned that F-1 employment could displace U.S. workers, less restrictive alternatives should be considered. At minimum, students should have a clear pathway to participate in academically relevant internships while physically outside the United States without jeopardizing F-1 status or future OPT eligibility. Overseas employment generally does not require U.S. CPT or OPT authorization, so this would allow students to gain professional experience without occupying U.S.-based internship positions.

DHS could also use more targeted anti-fraud measures, such as risk-based audits, stronger employer verification, enhanced reporting, and penalties for demonstrated violations. These approaches would address misconduct directly rather than imposing the same extraordinary financial barrier on every legitimate participant.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw or substantially revise the proposed fee structure and to evaluate its combined effects with recent CPT restrictions on practical training, graduate employability, university competitiveness, and the United States’ ability to attract and retain international talent.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed high OPT fees, arguing they harm students' early-career preparation.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Optional Practical Training Fees

I submit this comment in opposition to the proposed rule requiring schools to pay $70,000 for a student's initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal.

1. The fee exceeds DHS's fee-setting authority. Immigration fees are authorized to recover the cost of adjudication services. Reviewing a school's OPT recommendation and issuing an employment authorization document is a routine administrative act costing a fraction of the proposed amount. DHS's own estimate that the rule would collect $12.4 billion per year confirms the fee is not calibrated to cost recovery. A charge of this magnitude functions as a revenue measure, not a service fee, and therefore exceeds the authority Congress granted DHS to set fees.

2. The rule would effectively terminate OPT, contrary to its legislative purpose. OPT exists so F-1 students can obtain practical training related to their field of study. Schools that cannot absorb a $70,000 fee will either pass it on to students, most of whom cannot afford it, or stop recommending OPT altogether. Either way, OPT becomes unavailable to the overwhelming majority of students it was designed to serve. An agency may not use a fee schedule to accomplish indirectly what it has no authority to do directly. If OPT should be narrowed or eliminated, that is a decision for Congress, not for a fee rule.

3. The rule harms the American public interest. International students choose the United States in large part because OPT offers post-study work experience. If OPT becomes unaffordable, many will study in Canada, the United Kingdom, or Australia instead. The United States would lose tuition revenue that sustains its universities, research contributions in university laboratories, and the companies and jobs these graduates would otherwise create here. American employers, especially startups and small businesses that cannot compete with large firms for experienced workers, would also lose a critical entry-level pipeline.

4. DHS has not provided evidence that a fee of this size is needed. The proposal does not demonstrate that fraud or abuse in OPT is of a scale that could justify $70,000, nor does it connect the size of the fee to any identified problem. Its figures describe the revenue the rule would generate, not the harm it would prevent. A fee imposed without an evidentiary basis linking its size to a documented problem is arbitrary: it burdens students, schools, and employers while the agency has not shown that those costs purchase any improvement in program integrity.

5. The burden will fall hardest on public universities and students of modest means. Well-resourced private institutions may absorb or subsidize the fee; public universities under tight budgets cannot, and will be forced to restrict OPT recommendations or shift the cost to students. This undermines the breadth of American higher education and one of its principal attractions to talented students worldwide.

For these reasons — unlawful fee-setting, inconsistency with OPT's purpose, lack of evidence, and damage to the American public interest — DHS should withdraw the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees. Schools would have to pay them before recommending a student for practical training. DHS has not shown that it has authority to charge them, or that payments this large would separate legitimate training from fraud.

DHS relies on INA § 214(a)(1), which lets it set the time and conditions of nonimmigrant admission.[1] That provision says nothing about fees. DHS set the amounts to match the H-1B payment, not to recover a cost. The money would go to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, and ICE could neither keep nor use it.[2] Skinner requires Congress to speak clearly before an agency imposes financial burdens, "whether characterized as 'fees' or 'taxes,'" even to recover costs that do not benefit the payer.[3] A charge that recovers no cost at all needs at least as clear an authorization. When Congress authorizes immigration fees, it says so expressly and specifies how the money is collected and used. Examples include the H-1B/L fraud fee, adjudication fees, the SEVIS fee, and the 2025 visa integrity fee.[4] Section 214(a)(1) has nothing comparable. In July, the First Circuit relied on that pattern, on Skinner, and on Learning Resources. It held that the government had not made a strong showing of authority to require the $100,000 H-1B payment, which is the benchmark DHS used here.[5] Washington Alliance upheld DHS's authority over OPT; it did not consider any fee.[1]

The fraud DHS describes involves shell companies and fake worksites. Yet the school pays before recommending OPT, possibly before the student has a job offer, and the payment "would not be tied to a specific employer."[2] A school's willingness to pay says nothing about whether a future employer is legitimate. DHS rejected broader site visits, training plans, and reporting partly because enforcing them would take "substantial time and resources."[2] The fees would not fund that enforcement either. DHS's main evidence is also inconsistent. The text describes more than 10,000 students working for suspect employers, while footnote 56 describes 10,000 suspect employers. Both cite a video.[2] DHS should release the underlying data.

DHS's primary estimate after the transition year is $12.4 billion a year in fees from 2,478 schools, an average of about $5 million per school. Its low-participation scenario still assumes about 88,000 initial OPT participants a year, mostly STEM students, plus about 74,000 STEM extensions.[6] DHS does not explain why schools would keep paying at that scale. Using the unpaid fee as a proxy for lost opportunities does not capture enrollment lost over whole degree programs.[6] The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act discussion says in one paragraph that the rule would not reach the statutory threshold, and in the next that it would exceed it.[6]

DHS should also weigh this proposal together with its pending H-1B fee proposal. If both take effect, one graduate who uses OPT, receives a STEM extension, and is then sponsored for a cap-subject H-1B could trigger $203,265 in new payments by the school and the employer.[7]

Under the transition rule, if a student began OPT before the effective date, the school would owe $70,000 for a STEM extension recommended afterward, because no initial fee was ever paid.[8] DHS acknowledges that current students are differently situated from prospective ones,[2] but gives them no protection. Students enrolled before the final rule takes effect should be exempt for OPT and STEM extensions tied to their current degree.

I ask DHS to withdraw the proposal. Any new proposal should cite specific statutory authority, disclose the fraud data, and support its participation and cost assumptions.

References:

[1] 8 U.S.C. § 1184(a)(1); Wash. All. of Tech. Workers v. DHS, 50 F.4th 164 (D.C. Cir. 2022).

[2] DHS, ICE, [Optional Practical Training Fees](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/08/2026-20660/optional-practical-training-fees), 91 Fed. Reg. 64566 (Oct. 8, 2026), pp. 64570–71 & n.56, 64574–78 & n.124.

[3] Skinner v. Mid-America Pipeline Co., 490 U.S. 212, 224 (1989); see Nat'l Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336, 340–43 (1974).

[4] 8 U.S.C. §§ 1184(c)(12), 1356(m), (v), 1372(e); Pub. L. 119-21, § 100007, 139 Stat. 370 (2025).

[5] California v. Mullin, No. 26-1699, order at 4–6 (1st Cir. July 24, 2026) (denying stay pending appeal); Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, 607 U.S. 229 (2026).

[6] 91 Fed. Reg. at 64582–83, 64587–89, 64597.

[7] $70,000 + $30,000 here, plus $103,265 under DHS, Fee for Certain H-1B Petitions, 91 Fed. Reg. 54817 (Aug. 25, 2026) (proposed).

[8] Proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(3), 91 Fed. Reg. at 64599–600.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Dear Acting Director Venturella:

I submit this comment in strong opposition to the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for an F-1 student’s initial OPT recommendation and a $30,000 fee for any subsequent recommendation, including STEM OPT extensions. The proposal would impose a prohibitive barrier that effectively dismantles a longstanding program without clear congressional authorization. I urge DHS to withdraw it for the reasons below.

1. The fees exceed statutory authority and function as a general revenue tax.

Under the Independent Offices Appropriations Act and established precedent, a user fee must reasonably relate to the cost of a specific service and the proceeds should support that program. The NPRM states that the projected $8.4 to $16.5 billion in annual collections would go to the general Treasury, not to SEVP compliance or anti-fraud work. The preamble also indicates the amounts were set as a deterrent, aligned with proposed H-1B fees, rather than calculated from the marginal cost of a DSO recommendation in SEVIS. Using a prohibitive price to reduce participation, and suggesting the program might otherwise be shut down, amounts to an attempt to curtail a regulatory program and raise general revenue without an Act of Congress.

2. The FICA tax rationale is mathematically implausible.

In the NPRM, DHS points to the FICA exemption (7.65% combined employee Social Security and Medicare) as creating an incentive for employers to prefer F-1 OPT students. For a 7.65% savings to equal the $70,000 initial fee over a 12-month OPT period, an entry-level graduate would need to earn more than $915,000. Typical OPT salaries are far lower. Treating a statutory payroll tax differential that Congress itself created as justification for a $70,000 to $100,000 per-student charge is arbitrary.

3. Requiring universities to pre-pay $70,000 before a DSO recommendation is unworkable.

The obligation falls on the school before any OPT recommendation is entered in SEVIS. At that stage, a student seeking initial post-completion OPT is not required to have an employer. Nonprofit universities are educational institutions, not staffing agencies. Forcing them to front $70,000 per graduate, or to build escrow and pass through arrangements with students or prospective employers before USCIS even adjudicates an EAD, creates an unnecessary administrative and financial burden. Grant-funded labs and early-stage employers often cannot absorb an additional $30,000 to $100,000 surcharge within existing budgets.

4. The rule harms U.S. STEM capacity while failing to target actual fraud.

International graduate students contribute substantially to research and innovation in fields such as artificial intelligence, biomedical engineering, and other critical STEM areas. OPT and STEM OPT provide a bridge from graduate training to practical work. DHS has identified concerns about shell companies and other abuse, but ICE and USCIS already have targeted tools such as SEVIS reporting, Form I-983 reviews, and site visits to address bad actors. Applying a six figure charge across all certified institutions and compliant students, rather than focusing enforcement on fraudulent employers, is not a reasoned response.

5. Reliance interests and less burdensome alternatives were not adequately considered.

Hundreds of thousands of current F-1 students entered multi-year programs in reliance on the existing OPT framework. Even with grandfathering of prior recommendations, students who have not yet graduated, and those on initial OPT who will need a subsequent recommendation for a STEM extension after the effective date, face sudden disruption. DHS has not meaningfully evaluated more targeted measures, such as cost based compliance fees or strengthened employer verification, that could address integrity concerns without broadly reducing access to practical training.

For these reasons, the proposed rule is arbitrary, capricious, and in excess of statutory authority. I respectfully request that DHS withdraw Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100.

Respectfully submitted.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations. Preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers are legitimate goals, but the proposed approach imposes broad costs without adequately establishing that these particular fees are necessary or effective. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal and evaluate more targeted alternatives.

1. A high fee is not a reliable fraud screen.

DHS expects these fees to deter bad actors and encourage schools to scrutinize OPT requests. Yet ability to pay is not the same as compliance. A legitimate school could be priced out while a well-funded fraudulent operator could pay. DHS should provide evidence linking the proposed dollar amounts to reductions in fraudulent authorizations and distinguish that outcome from a reduction in legitimate participation. What proportion of discouraged applicants is expected to be fraudulent, and on what evidence is that estimate based?

2. The projected costs require a stronger accounting of benefits.

DHS's regulatory impact analysis estimates annualized economic costs of about $4.1 billion in its primary scenario, with substantial uncertainty [1]. The agency should compare these modeled costs with quantified estimates of avoided fraud, enforcement savings, and measurable gains for U.S. workers. Lower OPT participation alone is not proof of better wages or employment outcomes. Without such a comparison, the public cannot assess whether the fees are proportionate to the stated objectives.

3. The fees do not directly finance stronger oversight.

DHS states that fee receipts would go to the U.S. Treasury rather than be earmarked for SEVP enforcement [1]. The agency proposes deterrence and stronger school incentives, but it should demonstrate why those indirect mechanisms would outperform risk-based school audits, employer verification, data-driven fraud detection, and mandatory DSO training. GAO identified specific SEVP oversight vulnerabilities and recommended stronger fraud-risk controls [3]. DHS should compare these alternatives using estimated effectiveness and cost rather than assume a uniform fee is preferable.

4. The effects on U.S. education and research deserve fuller analysis.

OPT can influence where students pursue degrees and where graduates develop their skills. Research on earlier STEM OPT expansions found increases of approximately 14–15% in STEM degree completions, including gains among domestic students [2]. That finding does not directly predict the effect of this proposal, but it cautions against assuming that opportunities for international graduates necessarily disadvantage U.S. students. DHS should evaluate impacts on university enrollment, research capacity, domestic STEM training, and innovation.

5. A uniform charge creates uneven burdens and reliance concerns.

A $70,000 obligation may have vastly different effects on large universities, smaller colleges, and the students they recommend, irrespective of compliance history. Students and institutions also make multi-year educational commitments under existing OPT expectations. DHS should examine these distributional and reliance effects and explain why its proposed 60-day transition is adequate.

For these reasons, I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fees and instead evaluate evidence-based, risk-targeted oversight measures, including their expected fraud-reduction benefits, costs, and effects on U.S. workers and universities. An effective rule should target misconduct rather than treat financial capacity as a proxy for program integrity.

Thank you for considering this comment.

References

[1] DHS (2026), “Optional Practical Training Fees,” 91 FR 64566–64600, Docket ICEB-2026-0100. https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-10-08/html/2026-20660.htm

[2] Amuedo-Dorantes & Shih (2026), “OPT Reforms and the Relative Supply of STEM Skills,” AEA Papers and Proceedings 116:351–355. https://doi.org/10.1257/pandp.20261100

[3] U.S. GAO (2019), “Student and Exchange Visitor Program: DHS Can Take Additional Steps to Manage Fraud Risks,” GAO-19-297. https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-19-297

comments.title: Comment Submitted by the Associated Students of the University of California (ASUC)
comments.submitterName: the Associated Students of the University of California (ASUC)
comments.commentText:
Submitted electronically via Regulations.gov
Docket No.: ICEB-2026-0100
RIN: 1653-AB01

October 21, 2026

To:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Department of Homeland Security

Re: Public Comment in Strong Opposition to the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Proposed Rule: Optional Practical Training Fees (91 FR 64566)

This comment is submitted on behalf of the Associated Students of the University of California. As the student government representing all students at the University of California, Berkeley, we strongly oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training Fee, as we are deeply concerned about its potential consequences for the international student community. We respectfully urge DHS to consider and provide further explanations regarding the following concerns:
We are concerned about the rationale behind this proposed rule. In the Summary, DHS’s main justifications are to combat fraud, strengthen the integrity of the immigration system, and protect U.S. workers. However, in Section VI, DHS’s own evidence suggests that most students do not come to the United States with employment as the ultimate goal of their education. Therefore, we question whether this proposed rule would effectively address the aforementioned goals, as it may not only undermine the attractiveness of U.S. higher education, to which international students contribute billions of revenue, with approximately $43 billion during the last academic year, but also fail to achieve its primary purpose. This directly raises questions about DHS’s justification mentioned in footnote 124. We therefore urge DHS to provide a detailed accounting of the proposed rule’s potential economic losses in other sectors of the U.S. economy.
We question whether the proposed rule provides a reasonable amount of time for transition. In Section V.C, DHS provides DSOs and international students with only 60 days after the final rule is published. However, particularly at a time when most of the U.S. universities and colleges have already begun their semesters or quarters, some students may have decided to pursue higher education in the United States specifically because of the practical training opportunities offered by specific businesses they are interested in that are primarily operating in the United States. Therefore, we urge DHS to explain what measures it would take to accommodate these students and how it intends to address the harm to their reasonable expectations.
We demand calculations and accounting of how DHS determined the $70,000 initial OPT authorization fee and another $30,000 for each subsequent or STEM authorization. What mathematical reasoning supports such a substantial fee, and how would it effectively achieve the objectives stated in the proposal? We noticed in section V.A compares the proposed fee amounts with the tuition costs that international students pay for one or two years of education in the United States. However, the fact that international students already pay substantial tuition fees does not necessarily make the proposed fees economically reasonable or effective, and we would like to kindly remind DHS of its own stated objectives to “combat fraud, strengthen the integrity of the immigration system, and protect U.S. workers.” We do not see how the proposed fee would effectively address these objectives, instead, such high costs could potentially favor wealthier institutions and students with greater financial resources while disadvantaged students who lack financial support, especially for public universities such as UC Berkeley.
With these in mind, ASUC respectfully urges DHS to respond to the concerns raised above and reconsider the proposed rule.
Sincerely,
Associated Students of the University of California
comments.reason: The student government strongly opposes the proposed OPT fee due to negative impacts on international students.

comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule, Optional Practical Training Fees, published on October 8, 2026 (91 FR 64566). The proposal would impose a fee of $70,000 for an initial period of Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for each subsequent OPT period. I respectfully urge the Department to withdraw this proposal.

1. Disproportionate financial burdens on international students and universities

OPT is an important component of the F-1 student program, allowing international graduates to apply their academic knowledge and skills in professional settings. The proposed fees are so substantial that they risk making OPT practically inaccessible. Although educational institutions would formally bear the payment obligation, these costs could ultimately be passed on to students, employers, or other members of university communities. This would create significant financial barriers for international students, many of whom have already made substantial investments in their education in the United States.

2. Insufficient justification and lack of proportionality

The Department identifies fraud prevention, immigration system integrity, and the protection of U.S. workers as justifications for the proposed fees. While these are legitimate governmental objectives, the Department should demonstrate how fees of this extraordinary magnitude are reasonably related to the actual administrative and enforcement costs of the OPT program. The proposal raises serious questions about the methodology used to calculate these amounts and whether they are necessary to achieve the stated objectives. The Department should provide a transparent, evidence-based justification before imposing such substantial financial obligations.

3. Negative consequences for U.S. higher education and research

International students contribute significantly to American universities, research institutions, and the broader economy. They participate in academic research, support innovation, contribute specialized expertise, and enrich the intellectual life of university communities. OPT provides an important pathway through which these contributions extend beyond the classroom. By imposing prohibitive fees, the proposed rule could discourage universities from facilitating OPT and employers from recruiting international graduates. In the long term, this could weaken the competitiveness of U.S. higher education and undermine the country's ability to attract and retain international talent.

4. Unequal access to professional opportunities

The proposed fees would disproportionately disadvantage international students with limited financial resources and institutions unable to absorb additional costs. For many graduates, OPT provides an essential opportunity to gain professional experience and establish careers after completing their degrees. Making access to this opportunity dependent on an institution's or employer's capacity to absorb extraordinarily high fees risks creating unequal access to professional development and employment opportunities.

5. Less restrictive alternatives are available

The Department's objectives of preventing fraud and ensuring program integrity do not necessarily require prohibitive fees. More targeted measures, including strengthened institutional oversight, improved verification procedures, risk-based compliance reviews, and enhanced reporting requirements, could address documented abuses without undermining access for otherwise eligible students. The Department should meaningfully consider these less burdensome alternatives.

Conclusion

I respectfully urge the Department to withdraw the proposed rule. Its extraordinarily high fees are insufficiently justified and risk imposing disproportionate burdens on international students, universities, and employers. The objectives of protecting U.S. workers and maintaining immigration system integrity are important, but they should be pursued through proportionate, evidence-based, and carefully tailored regulatory measures.

OPT should remain an accessible pathway for international graduates to contribute their knowledge, skills, and professional expertise to American society. A regulatory framework that effectively restricts access on the basis of institutional or financial resources would undermine the educational, economic, and research interests that OPT helps advance.

Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges the Department to withdraw the proposal.

I strongly oppose the proposed increase in Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees. This policy would create a significant financial and operational burden not only for international students but also for U.S. companies that depend on highly skilled international talent.

I strongly oppose the proposed fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT) and STEM OPT.

The United States was founded on the principles of opportunity, ambition, and the belief that talented individuals from anywhere in the world should have the opportunity to contribute to its success. Throughout its history, the country has benefited enormously from attracting ambitious, highly educated and talented people from across the globe.

This proposal moves in the opposite direction.

Imposing substantial fees on universities for recommending international students for OPT will make it significantly more difficult for graduates to enter the US workforce. Universities may be forced to limit their support for international students, employers may become less willing to recruit them, and talented graduates may choose to pursue their careers in other countries instead.

These are individuals who have already invested years in American universities, contributed to the US economy through tuition, research and spending, and developed skills that American employers need. Preventing them from contributing professionally after graduation makes little economic sense.

The United States competes globally for talent. Countries such as the United Kingdom, Canada and Australia actively seek to attract highly educated international graduates. Making the US less accessible risks driving precisely the kind of ambitious, highly skilled people that have historically helped make America successful towards its international competitors.

If the objective is to strengthen the American economy, encourage innovation and maintain global competitiveness, the country should be making it easier for talented graduates to contribute, not introducing substantial financial barriers to their employment.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal. The United States should continue to be a country where talent, ambition and hard work are rewarded, regardless of where someone was born. Preserving meaningful opportunities for international graduates is not simply beneficial to those students; it is an investment in America's own economic future.

comments.commentText:
Dear Department of Homeland Security:

I am a doctoral student in biostatistics, and I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for an initial Optional Practical Training recommendation and $30,000 fee for subsequent recommendations. Protecting U.S. workers and preventing fraud are important objectives. However, the proposed fees could undermine American research, weaken employers’ access to qualified graduates, and restrict legitimate training opportunities without adequately distinguishing them from fraudulent activity. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal.

My training focuses on statistical methods used to evaluate health interventions and improve the reliability of medical evidence. In biostatistics, the value of a researcher’s work extends beyond an individual position: rigorous study design and analysis help researchers determine whether treatments are effective, identify safety concerns, and draw reliable conclusions from clinical data. These contributions benefit American patients, clinicians, and research teams. A substantial financial barrier to retaining U.S.-trained graduates could interrupt this work and reduce the future domestic benefits of investments in their education and training.

I am particularly concerned about the economic reasoning in Section VII.A.5.b of the proposal. DHS assumes that, when the benefits of OPT exceed the proposed fees, affected parties could collectively share the costs to preserve participation.[1] This assumption overlooks the distinction between social value, private financial returns, and the availability of funds. Patients who may benefit from better medical evidence cannot readily finance a researcher’s employment authorization. A university or nonprofit may recognize the value of a graduate’s contributions while lacking unrestricted funds to cover the fee. An inability to pay therefore does not demonstrate that an opportunity offers insufficient value to the United States. DHS should explicitly evaluate these financing constraints and the benefits of research that extend beyond the student, institution, and employer.

The proposed fee would also make financial resources a major determinant of access to practical training. Two equally qualified graduates pursuing equally legitimate opportunities could face different outcomes because one has access to a wealthy employer or personal resources and the other does not. A flat fee does not directly measure competence, compliance, or educational value. It could disadvantage smaller employers and nonprofit research organizations even when they offer appropriate supervision and competitive compensation.

Protecting American employment also requires examining whether international graduates complement U.S. workers, rather than assuming that excluding one graduate creates one job for an American. A 2024 study by Guo, Gong, and Pang found that an expansion of STEM OPT increased domestic employment in STEM occupations, with stronger effects in information technology.[2] This finding does not establish that every worker benefits or predict the effects of the proposed fee. It does, however, demonstrate why DHS should assess potential effects on team productivity, business expansion, and demand for American workers before imposing a substantial barrier to participation.

Fraud should be addressed through measures that identify and penalize misconduct. Payment of a large fee does not establish that an employer exists, that appropriate training occurs, or that wages and working conditions comply with applicable requirements. DHS should compare the proposal with targeted employer verification, risk-based inspections, and enforcement against documented violations. Reducing legitimate participation alongside fraudulent participation is not sufficient evidence that a policy improves program integrity or benefits the country overall.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed fees and evaluate proportionate alternatives supported by evidence. Any future proposal should account for effects on American research, smaller employers, domestic workers, and students already investing years in U.S. education. Preserving legitimate practical training while enforcing meaningful safeguards would better serve the interests of the United States.

Thank you for considering my comment.

References:

[1] Department of Homeland Security. “Optional Practical Training Fees.” Proposed rule, October 8, 2026, particularly Section VII.A.5.b.
https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-10-08/html/2026-20660.htm

[2] Guo, X., Gong, J., and Pang, M.-S. (2024). “Creation or Destruction? STEM OPT Extension and Employment of Information Technology Professionals.” MIS Quarterly, 48(2), 715–730.
https://aisel.aisnet.org/misq/vol48/iss2/15/
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fees harm research, employers, and students, and urges DHS to withdraw the proposal.
