comments.title: Comment Submitted by AAMC
comments.commentText:
The AAMC welcomes the opportunity to comment on the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule: Optional Practical Training (OPT) Fees. The introduction of a new fee of $70,000 for initial OPT per F–1 nonimmigrant student, and $30,000 for any subsequent OPT would have a negative impact on the biomedical research workforce, the advancement of biomedical research, and ultimately the health of the American public. We strongly urge DHS to not finalize this proposed rule.

International visa holders contribute to the biomedical research workforce
International visa holders make up a significant portion of biomedical research learners in the United States (U.S.). National Science Foundation (NSF) data show that in 2023, 24% of research doctorate (PhD) recipients and 59% of postdoctoral scholars in the biological and biomedical sciences were temporary visa holders. Many international biomedical PhD students use the F-1 visa mechanism and the majority subsequently participate in Optional Practical Training (OPT) to further their training as a postdoctoral scholar or to get some employment experience. Participating schools must be certified by the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP). All AAMC-member institutions utilize SEVP and are eligible to have students engage in OPT. Therefore, many international biomedical graduate students would be impacted by the proposed OPT fee.

As we have stated in previous comments to DHS, for decades, the U.S. has attracted talented international students and postdoctoral scholars to train in our biomedical research facilities; the proposed policy will further deter international PhD students from training in the U.S. International scholars contribute to the intellectual and cultural vibrancy and scientific preeminence of the U.S. biomedical research enterprise. Losing international talent would also lead to a reduction in U.S. competitiveness. Most scientists who are international visa holders remain in the U.S. after their training and contribute to our goal of improving health through discovery.

The fee will lead to increased costs, including loss of investment
The proposed rule states that “DHS believes that the OPT fees are on par with the educational costs that foreign students incur for one or two years of education in a program of study in the U.S.” However, unlike most undergraduate and master’s students, who pay tuition, most biomedical PhD students receive waived tuition and are paid a stipend. This is because biomedical PhD students serve a dual role as trainee and researcher which improves the health of the American people. Most academic institutions do not have the financial resources to cover this proposed fee. They also may not be the employer of those on OPT. Should the new fees be passed on to the students, as allowed in the proposed rule, it would severely limit the number of students who could afford to participate in the OPT program.

In addition to the fee itself, the proposed rule will lead to other financial costs for the institution as they will need to comply with the new rule and adapt their processes for selecting students to recommend for OPT and establish new processes for funding the new fees. The proposed rule also recognizes the various opportunity costs due to reducing OPT, including lower training program enrollment. Those institutions that have a higher percentage of international students will be disproportionately impacted.

Most importantly, the proposed OPT fees could potentially lead to a loss of U.S. investment in biomedical research should international students and scholars not have this pathway to contribute the skills that they acquire during their training to the U.S. biomedical research enterprise. From several perspectives, the proposed fee is prohibited and unworkable.

Combined with other recently enacted visa policies, this new fee has a substantial cost and will have a deeply negative impact on researchers and learners in academic medicine. Therefore, the AAMC asks DHS not to finalize this proposed rule.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the fees harm the biomedical workforce and strongly urges DHS not to finalize the rule.

To the Department of Homeland Security,

I am writing to express my concerns regarding the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees. I ask DHS to kindly withdraw this proposal and maintain affordable access to degree-related practical training.

My primary concern is that these high fees would shift the focus of practical training from educational merit and regulatory compliance to financial capability. Although the proposal assigns payment to educational institutions, it notes that these costs may be passed on to students or employers. This financial burden could lead universities to withhold recommendations for qualified students, prompt employers to retract training opportunities, and prevent eligible students from gaining necessary professional experience.

While I definitely support protecting American workers and preventing immigration fraud, a high fee is not an indicator of compliance, nor is the inability to pay evidence of misconduct. Because these funds would go to the U.S. Treasury rather than directly funding ICE oversight, DHS should clarify how this structure improves program integrity beyond acting as a financial deterrent. The agency should instead consider alternatives, such as targeted compliance reviews, degree verification, and employer accountability measures that address actual misconduct.

The proposed 60-day implementation timeline also creates significant uncertainty for currently enrolled students who made long-term financial and educational plans under the existing framework. I request explicit protections and grandfathered exemptions for current students and active OPT participants who will need future recommendations or extensions.

Lastly, DHS should fully analyze the broader consequences of this policy on universities, employers and the population of immigrant students currently in the US. This fee structure risks disproportionately impacting smaller institutions, increasing student debt, and making participants more financially vulnerable.

I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fees and evaluate lower cost structures, meaningful waivers, and transition protections that support the immigration system without making lawful training inaccessible.

Thanks

comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement:

I am an international student, and I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees of $70,000 for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for subsequent OPT. For me, this proposal could take away the chance to gain experience in my field after investing in a U.S. degree. It would be a serious career and financial setback at the point when I am trying to turn my education into a livelihood.

The chance to put what I learn into practice is a major part of why a U.S. education is worth the investment to me. As AI changes what employers expect from entry-level hires, I am concerned that there are fewer openings where new graduates can learn on the job. That makes practical training more important. In a real workplace, I can learn how to use new tools responsibly, verify their output, and take responsibility for work that other people depend on. Those skills will matter wherever I build my career, including if I return to my home country.

Under Section V.A, schools would have to pay before recommending a student for OPT. Putting the payment obligation on the school still leaves students exposed. If my university asks me to cover the fee, I would face an enormous new expense before earning anything through OPT. If my university cannot afford to pay, I could lose access to training even if I meet the eligibility requirements. And if access depends on finding an employer willing to cover the cost, I could lose opportunities with employers that can offer good training but cannot absorb a fee of that size. For students already enrolled, that uncertainty arrives while we are still paying for our degrees and trying to focus on finishing them.

I take DHS’s concerns about fraud and worker protection seriously. A school’s ability to pay $70,000 tells DHS little about whether a placement is genuine, whether the work relates to the student’s degree, or whether the employer follows applicable labor rules. Section IV.C also explains that the fees would go to the U.S. Treasury. The payments themselves would provide no dedicated funding for the oversight DHS says the program needs. I ask DHS to address the conduct it has identified through targeted employer verification, reviews of suspicious placements, and enforcement where there is evidence of abuse.

DHS’s own regulatory analysis recognizes that the fees could reduce OPT participation. Before adopting any policy that would restrict access this sharply, DHS should assess how many eligible students would lose legitimate training opportunities because their schools, employers, or families cannot pay. It should also account for students who have already committed to tuition and years of study under the existing rules. I urge DHS to withdraw both proposed fees and preserve meaningful access to practical training for students who follow the rules.
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees, stating it would be a severe financial setback.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an F-1 student in a STEM field. I plan to apply for OPT after graduation and later for the STEM OPT extension. Under this proposal, I would not be grandfathered, so the rule would decide whether I can use the practical training my program is designed to include.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal for three reasons.

First, the fee is not based on any real cost. Processing an OPT application does not cost $70,000, or $30,000 for an extension. DHS estimates the rule would collect $8.4 to $16.5 billion a year, deposited into the general Treasury rather than used to run the program. Few schools can pay this for every eligible student. In practice, the rule would end OPT for most students without Congress or DHS ever openly deciding to end it. A policy change of this size should be debated directly, not carried out through a fee.

Second, the rule would deepen a funding crisis at American public universities. I study at a public university. Our professors have told us that enrollment in our graduate program has fallen by half in recent years as policies toward international students have worsened, and that the department is struggling to pay faculty salaries. Most of my friends who considered studying in the U.S. have chosen the UK, Australia, and other countries instead, citing costs and policies like this one. International students pay tuition that supports programs, faculty, and research for American students. When they go elsewhere, public universities and the communities they serve lose that support.

Third, existing rules already address fraud and worker protection. STEM OPT requires a formal training plan on Form I-983, employers enrolled in E-Verify, wages comparable to U.S. workers, and regular reporting. If specific abuses exist, targeted enforcement against bad actors is the right tool. A blanket fee punishes every compliant student and school.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. If DHS has evidence of specific fraud, I ask it to address that through targeted enforcement or a fee set at the actual cost of processing.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly urges DHS to withdraw the proposal, arguing the excessive fees would end OPT for most students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule, *Optional Practical Training Fees* (91 FR 64566), published October 8, 2026. The proposed $70,000 fee for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT recommendations, including STEM OPT extensions, would create an unprecedented financial barrier to a program that benefits international students, American universities, employers, and the U.S. economy.

DHS relies on its authority under the Immigration and Nationality Act to regulate F-1 student status. However, that authority should not be interpreted as permission to impose extraordinary financial penalties unrelated to the actual cost of administering OPT. Under the Independent Offices Appropriation Act (31 U.S.C. § 9701), federal user fees should generally reflect the cost of providing a specific government service. DHS has not adequately demonstrated why fees of $70,000 and $30,000 are necessary to administer OPT or prevent fraud.

Furthermore, DHS acknowledges that the proposed amounts were partly benchmarked against H-1B fees to discourage employers from using OPT as an alternative. Discouraging lawful participation through prohibitive charges is not the same as addressing program integrity.

Disproportionate Impact on Students and Universities:

The proposed fees would make OPT inaccessible to many qualified international graduates, regardless of their academic performance or compliance history. Because universities must pay before recommending students, institutions with limited financial resources may stop supporting OPT altogether. This would disproportionately affect public universities, smaller institutions, and students who cannot afford additional costs. It would also create financial and administrative burdens for Designated School Officials, who must verify payments and update SEVIS records.

A student's financial resources should not determine whether they can access legitimate practical training opportunities after completing a U.S. degree.

Economic and Workforce Consequences:

OPT provides an important connection between American higher education and the U.S. workforce. International students contribute to research, innovation, entrepreneurship, and industries such as artificial intelligence, healthcare, biotechnology, and semiconductor manufacturing. According to NAFSA, international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported more than 355,000 jobs during the 2024–2025 academic year. Making post-graduation employment opportunities prohibitively expensive risks reducing international enrollment, university revenue, and the availability of highly skilled graduates. It also places American employers at a disadvantage compared with competitors in countries such as Canada, the United Kingdom, and Germany, which offer post-study employment pathways. The consequences would extend beyond international students to universities, American workers, research institutions, and local economies.

Less Restrictive Alternatives to Prevent Fraud:

DHS has legitimate reasons to protect the integrity of OPT. However, the proposed fees do not distinguish between legitimate students and fraudulent employers. Financial barriers are not reliable indicators of academic merit, employer legitimacy, or regulatory compliance.

Instead, DHS should:

Strengthen targeted investigations of employers and staffing agencies associated with fraudulent employment arrangements.
Use SEVIS data and risk-based monitoring to identify suspicious employer patterns and irregular student placements.
Increase employer accountability through audits and verification of training arrangements.
Establish reasonable administrative fees based on documented processing and enforcement costs, rather than imposing arbitrary amounts.

These measures would address fraud more directly without restricting legitimate participation.

Request for Reconsideration:

Given the significant economic, educational, and administrative consequences, DHS should withdraw the proposed rule in its current form. At a minimum, the Department should reconsider the proposed fee amounts, provide stronger evidence supporting their necessity, evaluate less restrictive alternatives, and allow sufficient time for universities, employers, and students to assess the implications. OPT is not simply an immigration benefit; it is an important component of the relationship between American higher education, workforce development, and national competitiveness. Policies intended to protect U.S. workers and prevent fraud should strengthen this system rather than undermine access to legitimate educational and professional opportunities.
I respectfully urge DHS to reject the proposed fees and pursue targeted, evidence-based measures that preserve program integrity while protecting the interests of students, universities, American employers, and the broader U.S. economy.

Respectfully submitted,
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they create prohibitive financial barriers for students and the economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I write to strongly oppose the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule establishing a $70,000 initial fee (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)) and a $30,000 subsequent fee (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(2))—totaling $100,000 per student—for Designated School Official (DSO) recommendations for F-1 Optional Practical Training (OPT) and STEM OPT under proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11). DHS should withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.

1. The Proposed $70,000 and $30,000 Fees Exceed DHS’s Statutory Authority and Constitute an Unlawful Revenue Tax
Congress authorized SEVP fees under Section 641(e) of IIRIRA (8 U.S.C. § 1372(e)) and the Independent Offices Appropriation Act (31 U.S.C. § 9701) solely to recover the reasonable costs of operating and maintaining the SEVIS information-collection system. Likewise, USCIS already recovers the full cost of adjudicating Employment Authorization Documents through the Form I-765 filing fee ($470 online / $520 paper) under 8 U.S.C. § 1356(m). Entering an OPT recommendation into SEVIS is a routine electronic record update performed by a university DSO that imposes virtually zero marginal cost on ICE. Charging $70,000 to $100,000 per student to collect an estimated $12.4 billion annually for deposit into the general U.S. Treasury bears no rational relationship to agency service costs. Under National Cable Television Ass’n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974), an agency may not levy punitive, policy-driven taxes disguised as user fees without explicit congressional authorization.

2. Equating F-1 Experiential Training with H-1B Petitions Is Arbitrary and Capricious Under the APA (5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A))
DHS’s stated rationale—setting OPT fees “comparable to the fee for H-1B visas” to deter employment—ignores the fundamental legal and economic reality of OPT. Post-completion OPT is limited to 12 months (with a 24-month STEM extension requiring a formal Form I-983 training plan). A $100,000 fee for 1 to 3 years of entry-level postgraduate training frequently exceeds the trainee’s entire annual compensation. Even more irrationally, under proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2), a student who completes a short summer internship on pre-completion OPT and later applies for post-completion OPT triggers both the $70,000 initial fee and the $30,000 subsequent fee—$100,000 total for a single 12-month statutory OPT allowance. This punitive structure effectively abolishes pre-completion OPT and hands-on experiential training.

3. Severe Harm to U.S. Innovation, Universities, Small Businesses, and Domestic Students
U.S. technological competitiveness depends on retaining graduates trained at American colleges and universities.
- Universities and research institutions operating on federal grants and fixed budgets cannot legally or financially absorb $70,000–$100,000 per graduate for postdoctoral or research positions.
- Small businesses and early-stage U.S. startups cannot afford a $100,000 upfront surcharge to hire a recent graduate, entrenching market concentration among a handful of large corporations while driving talent and innovation outside the United States.
- DHS’s suggestion that schools may pass this $12.4 billion annual burden onto “all students” would directly inflate tuition for U.S. citizen and permanent resident students, while non-refundable payment rules (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)) expose educational institutions to unrecoverable losses even if a graduate never works a single day.

4. Opposition to the $140,000 Multi-Degree Alternative
DHS specifically requested comment on an alternative that would charge the full $70,000 initial fee again whenever a student advances to a higher degree level (e.g., $70,000 after a bachelor’s degree and another $70,000 after a master’s or doctoral degree, totaling $140,000+). This alternative should be rejected, as it directly penalizes students for pursuing advanced degrees at U.S. institutions.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed exorbitant fees and asks DHS to withdraw the rule in its entirety.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an international student studying in the United States. I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee, and I urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw this rule.

OPT is temporary, field-related practical training, recommended by a designated school official and approved by USCIS, for up to 12 months, with a 24-month extension only for qualifying STEM degrees. It is the bridge between a U.S. degree and work in the field a student studied. A $70,000 fee does not regulate that bridge. It prices it out of existence.

The fee bears no reasonable relationship to adjudication cost. The current I-765 filing fee is $470 online. A $70,000 school fee is roughly 149 times that amount, and a student who uses pre-completion OPT, post-completion OPT, and a STEM extension could trigger $130,000 in fees. DHS projects $8.4 billion to $16.5 billion per year across 2,478 schools. That is revenue extraction, not cost recovery. If fraud is the concern, the proportionate response is targeted enforcement, audits, and employer verification, not a blanket charge on every eligible student.

Calling this a school fee does not protect students. The proposal allows schools to pass the cost to the F-1 student, to all students, or to employers, with no limit on how it is collected. No ordinary entry-level research, nonprofit, healthcare, or teaching job can justify a $70,000 upfront payment before a graduate earns a dollar. In practice, schools, especially public and smaller institutions, will stop recommending OPT, and employers will stop considering OPT candidates. Only students whose families or employers can pay five figures will get training, even though they meet the same eligibility requirements as everyone else.

This is also a direct burden on schools in the United States. Schools would have to front $70,000 per student before a DSO can even make a recommendation, build new billing and collection systems, decide which students are worth recommending, and absorb the cost when no one pays. That diverts money and staff time from teaching, advising, research, and financial aid. Public and smaller schools, which cannot absorb this cost, will lose students, tuition revenue, and programs, and will face pressure to raise tuition and fees for American students to cover the shortfall.

The rule also harms the American economy it claims to protect. In 2024-25, international students contributed $42.9 billion and supported 355,736 jobs, according to NAFSA, roughly one U.S. job for every three international students. NAFSA and JB International estimate that the 17 percent fall in new international enrollment in fall 2025 already cost about $1.1 billion and nearly 23,000 jobs. In an IDP Education survey cited by NAFSA, 66 percent of students said they would go elsewhere or consider going elsewhere without post-study work opportunities. Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Germany all offer post-graduation work routes. That loss would fall on local communities, not just campuses.

The rule harms American innovation. The Peterson Institute for International Economics has found that eliminating OPT would cause permanent losses to innovation, productivity, growth, and job opportunities for native workers. About 72 percent of foreign graduates use OPT. A 10 percent rise in foreign graduates is associated with a 2.0 to 3.6 percent rise in new patents in the average state. Twenty percent of U.S. venture-capital-financed startups have an immigrant founder, and 75 percent of those founders first arrived on a student visa. One quarter of U.S. billion-dollar unicorn companies have a founder who arrived as an international student. The National Foundation for American Policy found immigrants founded or co-founded 455 of 775 U.S. unicorns. Cutting OPT does not keep those companies and patents in American hands. It moves them abroad.

The evidence does not support the claim that OPT systematically displaces U.S. workers. NAFSA cites a 2023 Niskanen Center analysis finding that experiential learning like OPT leads to increased innovation and higher average earnings, without costing U.S. workers jobs or decreasing wages, and a 2019 National Foundation for American Policy study finding no evidence that OPT reduces job opportunities for U.S. workers. OPT is time-limited, field-restricted, and school-recommended, unlike an uncapped, permanent guest-worker program.

Fewer international students also means strained university budgets, greater tuition pressure on American students, smaller classes, and research labs with fewer researchers. DHS should withdraw this rule. At a minimum, it should not finalize a fee untethered to adjudication cost, passable to students without limit, that effectively ends practical training for most students.

Respectfully,
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security:

I support stricter oversight of Optional Practical Training (OPT) and the proposed effort to make institutions more accountable. My support is not rooted in opposition to international students or skilled immigration. It rests on a distinction that immigration policy too often obscures: educating international talent is not the same as granting access to the domestic labor market.

F-1 status is intended for study, not as a general employment or immigration pathway. OPT can provide legitimate, degree-related practical training, but the expansion of STEM OPT has also created functional overlap with employment-based visa programs such as H-1B. These programs are legally distinct, yet their purposes should remain distinct in practice. Those seeking long-term U.S. employment should pursue the appropriate employment authorization or immigration process, subject to its requirements, rather than rely on student status as a substitute.

This distinction need not undermine American universities. The United States can welcome students from around the world without promising that graduation leads to employment here. Indeed, separating academic admission from expectations of post-graduation work could allow F-1 adjudication and university recruitment to focus more clearly on educational merit and genuine academic purpose. It could also reduce incentives to use enrollment mainly as an entry point into the U.S. job market. These are potential benefits to evaluate, not guaranteed increases in visa approval rates.

Nor should international education be judged by how many graduates remain in America. The United States has a remarkable ability to train researchers, engineers, and future faculty from across the world. When graduates take that expertise to other countries, they carry with them American research practices, professional networks, and collaborative traditions. That can expand American academic influence while strengthening research institutions elsewhere. Talent circulation is not necessarily talent loss. The United States can be a global educator rather than treating every international graduate as someone it must retain.

There is equally no contradiction between academic openness and protecting American workers. Domestic labor-market rules should govern employment; university admissions should govern education. Academic openness need not imply unrestricted labor-market access, just as protecting domestic workers need not mean closing academic doors. Clearer boundaries could reduce opportunities to circumvent employment-specific safeguards and could encourage graduates to consider a genuinely global range of career opportunities.

I also recognize the documented concerns about fictitious OPT employment, shell companies, and false reporting. I support stronger verification, institutional responsibility, and enforcement against abuse. But financial capacity is not a measure of honesty or merit. If DHS adopts the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent fees, it should demonstrate that these specific amounts address fraud and program misuse rather than merely exclude legitimate students and institutions unable to pay. I support the regulatory goal while expecting the proposed instrument to withstand scrutiny.

I write as an international student pursuing an engineering PhD in the United States. I came from one of the leading universities in my home country to an American university with an outstanding engineering research program. My doctoral training gives me the opportunity to participate in global research and learn from the rigor, openness, and collaborative methods of American academia. After graduation, I intend to return to my home country and pursue a professorship, bringing those scientific methods, international connections, and perspectives into my teaching and research.

If I leave the United States after earning my degree, I will not regard that as a failure of American education. I will regard it as evidence of its reach. An American degree is an academic achievement, not a promise of U.S. employment. International education is an exchange of knowledge, not an entitlement to immigration. Protecting American workers does not require diminishing America's role as an educator of the world.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Respectfully,

An International PhD Student
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly supports stricter oversight and fees on OPT to separate student status from the labor market.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: The government justifies its proposal by citing the need to combat fraud and protect American workers, while also explicitly acknowledging an intent to curb what it deems "abusive" practices by raising the cost of participation. However, there is a critical logical flaw here: the ability to pay does not prove a program is legitimate, nor does an inability to pay prove that a student is acting improperly. If the core issues are fraudulent schools, sham employment, or exploitation, the government should explain why targeted oversight and enforcement are insufficient—and why it is necessary to impose such high financial barriers on all participants, including those acting in good faith. When choosing a study-abroad destination, students weigh factors such as tuition, educational quality, and post-graduation practical opportunities. If access to these practical opportunities hinges on whether someone is willing to pay an additional $70,000 to $100,000, rational students may simply choose to apply to other countries instead. Consequently, schools could lose both students and revenue, while employers might lose access to talent already trained within the United States.

comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed $70,000 fee for international students applying for Optional Practical Training (OPT).

International students make significant financial, academic, and cultural contributions to the United States. Beyond paying substantial tuition fees, often without access to the financial assistance available to domestic students, they contribute to local economies through housing, transportation, and everyday expenses. They also bring diverse perspectives, skills, and knowledge that enrich American universities and communities.

Studying in the United States already requires an enormous financial and personal commitment. International students must navigate complex immigration regulations, maintain strict compliance with their visa requirements, and face significant limitations on employment opportunities throughout their education. Imposing an additional financial burden of this magnitude would make an already challenging process even more inaccessible.

It is also important to recognize that the United States has been profoundly shaped by generations of immigrants. Immigration has played a fundamental role in the country's economic development, innovation, cultural identity, and global influence. Creating further financial barriers for educated individuals who have invested years in American institutions seems inconsistent with that history and risks discouraging talented students from choosing the United States as their educational destination.

International students should be recognized for the value they bring to this country, rather than continually facing additional obstacles to their academic and professional development. OPT provides an important opportunity to apply the knowledge acquired through an American education, gain practical experience, and contribute to the U.S. workforce.

I respectfully urge policymakers to reconsider this proposal and recognize its potential consequences for international students, American universities, and the country's ability to attract international talent.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am a Designated School Official at a large public research university in the Southeast and am opposing the proposed rule for multiple reasons:

1-What is presented as a fee is actually a tax. Fees are collected by USCIS to cover the cost of adjudicating the application. I have a very hard time understanding that this cost went from $470 to $70k overnight.

2-In the proposal, DHS requests that the “fee” be paid by the school before recommending OPT. “DHS believes this proposed fee would incentivize educational institutions to exercise greater oversight and selectivity when recommending students for OPT, thereby reducing fraudulent authorizations and curbing “visa mill” activities.”
Under the OPT regulation, 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii), the issuance of the OPT recommendation by the school’s DSO is based on the DSO checking that the student is eligible: “Prior to making a recommendation, the DSO at the educational institution of the student's most recent enrollment must ensure that the student is eligible for the given type and period of OPT and that the student is aware of the student's responsibilities for maintaining status while on OPT.” See: 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)
It is not the responsibility of the DSO or the school to determine who is worthy of the opportunity to apply for OPT work authorization. Moreover, how would DHS suggest we proceed without risking lawsuits from students who are not selected?

3-The reasons for the new rule are described as combating fraud and abuse of OPT and protecting American workers.
a.Combating fraud and abuse; USCIS has access to an extensive database of information through SEVIS and the SEVP portal, and schools and students are required to update it with any changes during the student’s program of study and during their OPT/STEM OPT work authorization periods. I suggest that they use these tools more effectively to identify, in a targeted way, which students, employers, and schools may be committing fraud, rather than punishing everyone for potential abuse. The same examples are periodically cited to demonstrate fraud issues; it is unclear how many issues there really are.
b.Protecting American workers: Numerous studies have shown that “there is no evidence that foreign students participating in the OPT program reduce job opportunities for U.S. workers. Instead, the evidence suggests that U.S. employers are more likely to turn to foreign student workers when U.S. workers are scarcer” (International-Students-STEM-OPT-And-The-US-STEM-Workforce.NFAP-Policy-Brief.March-2019.pdf).
Moreover, F-1 students are a major boost to our research and development sector: “Immigrants make up nearly half of U.S. recipients of the world's most prestigious STEM awards, yet little is known about how this talent first arrives in the country”. “Most foreign-born U.S. awardees first arrived as students, postdoctoral researchers, or visiting scholars” (How Global Talent Pathways Shape U.S. STEM Award Achievement | Center for Security and Emerging Technology). Several of the students I recommended for OPT over the past few years are now engaged in medical research, AI development, environmental conservation, astrophysics research, and more. I am in awe of their accomplishments.

The proposed rule would, in effect, ravage the OPT/STEM OPT programs (leading to very low or nonexistent "fee" income) and have a dramatic impact on the F-1 program. If that is the ultimate goal, please consider that F-1 students and those on OPT/STEM OPT have a significant positive financial impact on the U.S. economy through the tuition fees and taxes they pay, as well as their living expenses (IIE Open Doors / Research Special Reports and Analyses). Moreover, they are not eligible for any financial support in the U.S. Furthermore, international students bring diverse backgrounds, experiences, perspectives, and characteristics that lead to more creative and innovative ideas. They are a huge asset to our country; they challenge us and make us stronger and better. They save us from intellectual inbreeding.
comments.reason: The commenter argues against the proposed rule, stating the fee is an unjustified tax and incorrectly shifts oversight duties to schools.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Opposition to Proposed OPT Fees: Fairness, Justification, and Proportionality

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee. These extraordinary charges raise serious concerns about fairness, proportionality, and the legal and economic justification for restricting access to lawful practical training.

1. Financial capacity is not academic merit.

In Section IV.C, DHS suggests that high fees would encourage schools to recommend only the "most promising students." However, universities do not necessarily have funds allocated for such fees. An excellent student at a public university could lose access to OPT because their school cannot afford $70,000, while a less qualified student at a wealthy institution might receive a recommendation.

This would select for financial resources, not necessarily academic ability. DHS should explain what evidence connects an institution's capacity to pay with a student's merit or potential.

2. Shifting fees to students and employers compounds inequality.

In Section VI, DHS suggests that schools may pass the fees to students or employers. This does not solve the fairness problem; it transfers the burden to family wealth or employer budgets.

Graduates in humanities, arts, social sciences, education, public service, and nonprofit work may be especially affected. A large corporation might afford $70,000, while a museum, school, or nonprofit cannot, regardless of the graduate's qualifications or contribution.

Initial post-completion OPT generally does not require a job offer. It may therefore be unrealistic to expect an employer to finance a fee before the student even has work authorization or a confirmed position. Passing the cost to students would favor those from wealthy families over equally qualified peers.

3. Different fields create value in different ways.

Financial capacity and immediate market returns cannot capture the value of all disciplines. Basic biology may take decades to yield treatments. Mathematics and theoretical physics may lack immediate commercial applications. Environmental science can produce public benefits without direct revenue. Pharmaceutical research entails substantial costs and uncertain outcomes. Technology research may commercialize more quickly, but its long-term impact is also uncertain.

A rare-disease researcher may not produce a profitable product for years. That does not make the research less valuable than a highly paid software position. DHS does not explicitly price each individual's worth, but using willingness to pay as a screening mechanism risks favoring well-funded, commercially profitable work over equally valuable public-interest activities.

4. The specific fee amounts require justification.

In Section IV.C, DHS links the $70,000 amount partly to H-1B-related fees and deterrence, not to a demonstrated calculation of OPT processing costs. DHS also states that collected fees would go to the U.S. Treasury rather than directly fund ICE's OPT administration.

Why $70,000 rather than $5,000 or $10,000? What independently justifies the additional $30,000? Why should fees associated with another immigration category determine OPT charges?

If these are not cost-recovery fees, DHS should identify the statutory basis for imposing fees of this magnitude and provide a transparent explanation for why these particular amounts are reasonable and proportionate. Regulatory authority alone does not establish that every possible fee level is justified.

5. Uniform fees can impose unequal burdens.

Charging everyone the same amount creates formal equality, but not necessarily substantive fairness. A $70,000 fee may be manageable for a wealthy institution yet prohibitive for a smaller university or nonprofit. It could exceed a legitimate OPT worker's annual salary.

The proposed charges are not adjusted for institutional resources, individual income, discipline, or the nature of the training. Equally qualified students could face radically different outcomes for reasons unrelated to eligibility. DHS should evaluate these distributional consequences and justify imposing the same threshold across such different circumstances.

Conclusion

Eligibility for practical training should depend on lawful qualifications and legitimate educational opportunities, not principally on institutional wealth, employer profitability, or personal financial privilege. DHS has not adequately justified these specific fee amounts or their unequal effects. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and reconsider its fairness, legal and economic basis, and proportionality.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Kubra Yigit
comments.commentText:
Comment on DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100: Optional Practical Training Fees

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. This proposal would impose an unreasonable financial burden on educational institutions and effectively eliminate practical training opportunities for many international students, including highly qualified PhD graduates who have spent years contributing to scientific research and innovation in the United States.

I am a sixth-year PhD student at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, conducting research in microbiology and molecular biology. Throughout my doctoral training, I have contributed to scientific research addressing fundamental questions in microbial stress responses and biotechnology. My work has involved developing experimental approaches, novel therapies for antibiotic resistant microbes, conducting advanced biochemical and molecular biological research, and generating knowledge that contributes to the broader scientific community.

OPT is an essential bridge between academic training and professional employment. It allows international graduates to apply their specialized knowledge in U.S. industries, research institutions, and biotechnology companies. Many employers recruit PhD graduates specifically because of the expertise developed during their doctoral training.

The proposed fee would create several serious problems:

1. It would disproportionately harm U.S. universities and employers. The proposed fee is charged to educational institutions rather than directly to students, but institutions are unlikely to absorb such an extraordinary expense. Universities may instead restrict OPT recommendations, effectively preventing graduates from accessing employment opportunities. Employers would lose access to highly trained scientists, engineers, and other specialized professionals.

2. It would undermine U.S. competitiveness in science and technology. The United States has invested substantial resources in educating international doctoral students through research grants, university facilities, and collaborative scientific projects. Preventing these graduates from entering the U.S. workforce would diminish the return on these investments and encourage talented researchers to pursue opportunities in other countries.

3. The proposed fee is disproportionate to its stated objectives. DHS identifies fraud prevention and protection of U.S. workers as the primary justifications for this rule. However, a $70,000 fee is not a targeted fraud-prevention measure. It would indiscriminately affect legitimate students who have maintained their immigration status, completed rigorous academic programs, and secured employment directly related to their fields of study. Existing mechanisms for verifying student eligibility and employment could be strengthened without imposing such an excessive financial barrier.

4. The proposal would negatively affect small businesses and biotechnology companies. Many innovative companies, particularly startups and smaller biotechnology firms, rely on highly specialized scientific talent. Restricting access to international graduates would increase recruitment difficulties and reduce the ability of these companies to compete and innovate.

5. The proposal would create significant uncertainty for students and institutions. International PhD students make educational and career decisions years in advance, often relying on the expectation that OPT will provide an opportunity to gain practical experience after graduation. Introducing an extraordinary fee would disrupt these plans and undermine confidence in the U.S. higher education system.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. If DHS believes additional measures are necessary to prevent fraud, it should consider proportionate, evidence-based alternatives that target fraudulent practices without penalizing legitimate international students, educational institutions, and U.S. employers.

International students are not simply temporary participants in the U.S. education system. Many contribute directly to research, technological advancement, economic growth, and the training of future scientists. Policies governing OPT should recognize these contributions while addressing fraud through reasonable and targeted measures.

Thank you for considering my comments.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule imposing a $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT). These excessive fees would effectively eliminate practical training opportunities for many qualified international graduates, damage American universities and businesses, and weaken U.S. economic competitiveness without adequately addressing the underlying causes of immigration fraud.

1. The proposed fees are excessive and would disproportionately burden American universities.

DHS estimates that the rule would generate approximately $12.4 billion annually in fee payments under its primary scenario. Its own analysis projects that 841 of 1,389 affected small educational institutions (60.5%) would experience costs exceeding 1% of annual revenue during the transition year, with 116 facing costs exceeding 20%.

These burdens could force institutions to reduce OPT recommendations, increase costs for students, or divert resources from education and research. Smaller universities would be particularly disadvantaged.

2. The proposal would discourage international enrollment and harm the U.S. economy.

According to NAFSA, international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported more than 355,000 jobs during the 2024–2025 academic year. Meanwhile, the Institute of International Education reported a 17% decline in new international student enrollment among surveyed institutions in fall 2025.

A September 2026 IZA research paper by Michael Clemens modeled a $100,000 OPT-related tax and estimated that OPT participation could decline by at least one-third, and substantially more under certain scenarios. Although these are model-based projections rather than measured effects of this specific rule, they demonstrate the substantial risk to university enrollment and finances.

Making practical training prohibitively expensive would further discourage talented students from choosing American universities, reducing tuition revenue and local economic activity.

3. The proposal would harm American workers and businesses.

OPT allows U.S. employers to recruit graduates trained by American universities, supporting innovation, productivity, and business growth.

A 2024 study published in MIS Quarterly found that STEM OPT extensions increased employment among domestic STEM workers, particularly in information technology. Additionally, research published in the American Economic Association Papers and Proceedings in 2026 found that OPT expansions increased STEM degree completions by 14–15%, with increases among domestic students as well.

These findings challenge the assumption that restricting OPT necessarily benefits American workers. Instead, reducing access to skilled graduates could hurt American employers, limit innovation, and weaken job creation.

4. The fees are poorly targeted toward preventing fraud.

DHS identifies fraud prevention as a primary justification but does not sufficiently demonstrate why charging legitimate educational institutions $70,000 or $30,000 per recommendation is necessary or proportionate to that objective.

A blanket financial barrier does not distinguish fraudulent activities from legitimate academic and employment opportunities. Instead, it risks excluding qualified students and institutions based primarily on financial resources rather than compliance.

More targeted measures, including employer verification, risk-based audits, stronger enforcement against fraudulent organizations, and improved institutional oversight, would address misconduct without imposing extraordinary costs on legitimate participants.

5. The proposal undermines fairness and reasonable expectations.

International students make substantial financial commitments to American universities with the understanding that OPT may provide an opportunity to gain practical experience after graduation.

Imposing fees of this magnitude would fundamentally change those expectations, potentially making practical training inaccessible after years of tuition payments and academic investment.

The rule would disproportionately favor wealthy students and institutions, rather than selecting participants based on qualifications, academic achievement, or professional merit.

Conclusion

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal. The proposed fees would impose substantial costs on American educational institutions, businesses, workers, and communities while jeopardizing U.S. competitiveness and providing insufficiently demonstrated fraud-prevention benefits. DHS should instead pursue targeted, evidence-based enforcement measures that preserve legitimate practical training opportunities.

Subject: Formal Opposition to Proposed Optional Practical Training Fees — Docket ICEB-2026-0100

To the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement:

I respectfully submit this comment in strong opposition to the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee.

While I fully support protecting American workers, preventing immigration fraud and maintaining the integrity of the U.S. immigration system, I believe the proposed fee structure could produce significant unintended consequences for American workers, businesses, universities and the broader economy.

1. Protecting American economic competitiveness

American universities educate talented individuals who contribute to scientific research, engineering, technology, healthcare, manufacturing and other important industries. OPT provides a structured opportunity for graduates to apply their academic knowledge in practical employment settings.

2. American businesses and workers could also suffer

Many U.S. companies, particularly startups, small businesses and research organizations, operate with limited financial resources. Additional substantial costs could discourage legitimate hiring, delay business expansion and reduce the resources available for training American employees.

3. The proposal should be supported by meaningful economic evidence

DHS should explain how the proposed fee amounts were calculated, how they relate to actual administrative and enforcement costs, and what evidence demonstrates that these fees will effectively prevent fraud.

A blanket financial burden is not necessarily an effective fraud-prevention mechanism. Targeted investigations, employer verification, SEVIS oversight and enforcement against fraudulent organizations would be more directly connected to the identified concerns.

4. Protecting American taxpayers and educational institutions

Universities contribute to local economies through employment, research, tuition revenue and partnerships with American businesses. Policies that discourage international enrollment and research collaboration could negatively affect these institutions and the American communities that depend on them.

Withdraw the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 fee structure.
Conduct a transparent economic impact assessment.
Establish reasonable, evidence-based administrative fees.
Strengthen targeted enforcement against fraudulent employers and institutions.
Evaluate effects on American workers, small businesses, universities and research organizations.
Provide appropriate transition protections for students and institutions that have relied on existing regulations.
Protecting American workers should remain a priority, but that objective should not come at the expense of American innovation, educational competitiveness and legitimate economic growth.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Opposition to Proposed Optional Practical Training Fees

I am writing to oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee, particularly because of their consequences for U.S.-trained STEM doctoral researchers and American scientific innovation.

1. Doctoral and postdoctoral research form a connected scientific training pathway

A PhD degree is a major milestone, but it does not necessarily mark the end of a scientist's training or the full realization of that training's value. Postdoctoral research often enables scientists to develop greater intellectual independence, enter new fields, learn complementary techniques, and build interdisciplinary collaborations. It can be among the most productive and innovative career stages, when doctoral expertise generates broader advances.

For F-1 graduates of U.S. doctoral programs, OPT and STEM OPT offer a vital bridge into postdoctoral research. J-1 and H-1B status may be possible alternatives, but they are not automatically interchangeable. Universities have different sponsorship policies; H-1B petitions involve institutional costs and processing, while J-1 eligibility and potential two-year home-residence requirements create distinct constraints. Qualified universities may sponsor cap-exempt H-1B petitions, so academic OPT cannot simply be characterized as evasion of the H-1B numerical cap. DHS should assess whether these alternatives are actually accessible.

2. The proposal may export returns on American research investment

Research PhD training commonly takes five or more years and entails stipends or salaries, tuition support, benefits, mentoring, facilities, equipment, and materials. Total costs vary substantially, but the investment across a doctorate can reach hundreds of thousands of dollars, including support from federal research grants.

A $70,000 fee could interrupt the transition into postdoctoral work for graduates whose institutions cannot fund it. Researchers may instead join laboratories in Europe, Asia, or elsewhere, carrying expertise developed through American research investment. This could interrupt ongoing projects and shift future publications, inventions, patents, and startups abroad. The loss includes scientific continuity and potential returns on U.S. investment.

3. DHS's opportunity-cost assumptions may undervalue scientific research

In Section VII.A.5.b, DHS uses unpaid OPT fees as a proxy for opportunity costs when participation declines, while acknowledging that actual societal benefits can differ. It also suggests parties can share fees when OPT benefits exceed the cost. But the benefits of basic research are uncertain, may emerge years later, and often accrue to patients, companies, and the public rather than to the university making an immediate payment. Federal grant budgets can also limit the use of funds for immigration-related expenses.

A laboratory's inability to pay $70,000 does not show that retaining a researcher is worth less than $70,000. DHS should model research-specific losses, including disrupted grants, retention of U.S.-trained scientists, and downstream innovation, rather than rely solely on the fee as a proxy.

4. Financial capacity is not evidence of academic merit or compliance

DHS argues that a large fee would make institutions recommend only the most promising students and deter fraud. But payment capacity reflects budget constraints and access to funds, not necessarily scientific excellence or an employer's legitimacy. Genuine university researchers may be excluded while well-funded entities can still afford the fee. DHS cites real instances of shell employers and fraudulent employment, but does not establish that academic postdoctoral laboratories carry the same risks.

The proposal should distinguish legitimate university-based research from high-risk employment arrangements, report fraud rates by employer and degree type, and compare targeted employer verification and risk-based audits with a universal fee.

5. DHS should assess the national research interest separately

NSF's 2024 Survey of Earned Doctorates reports that temporary visa holders earned approximately 38% of U.S. science and engineering doctorates. International researchers are therefore a major component of the U.S. scientific pipeline. A policy that discourages graduates from continuing research here could harm the country's ability to turn doctoral training into discoveries and economic activity.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and evaluate its effects on PhD-to-postdoc transitions, public research investment, and scientific competitiveness. Fraud should be addressed through proportionate, evidence-based enforcement, not a financial barrier that may drive legitimate researchers abroad.

Reference: NSF NCSES, Survey of Earned Doctorates 2024: https://ncses.nsf.gov/pubs/nsf26315/

comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking regarding Optional Practical Training (OPT) Fees (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100), published on October 8, 2026. The proposal to require SEVP-certified educational institutions to pay a $70,000 fee prior to an initial OPT recommendation and a $30,000 fee for each subsequent recommendation (totaling $100,000 for students completing both post-completion OPT and a STEM OPT extension) is economically destructive, disproportionate to administrative costs, and counter to the national interest of the United States.

As an graduate student in Texas, I witness firsthand how vital international talent is to our local economy and research institutions.I urge DHS and ICE to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety for the following reasons:

1. The Proposed Fees Constitute a De Facto Ban on Practical Training
Requiring a $70,000 to $100,000 outlay per student before a Designated School Official (DSO) can enter an OPT recommendation in SEVIS does not regulate the program; it functionally dismantles it. Public and private universities operate on tight educational budgets and cannot absorb billions of dollars in new federal charges. If institutions pass these costs on to F-1 students or prospective employers, the financial barrier will exceed the typical starting salary of an entry-level graduate, Pricing out nearly all students and small-to-medium-sized businesses while restricting experiential learning only to the wealthiest applicants or largest corporations.

2. Arbitrary and Disproportionate Fee Structure
Under established administrative principles and user-fee statutes, federal agency fees connected to immigration and student oversight must reasonably reflect the actual cost of administering the service or providing oversight. A $70,000 charge for a DSO to record an OPT recommendation in SEVIS bears no rational relationship to the administrative cost of adjudicating or overseeing that student's practical training. Furthermore, depositing up to $16.5 billion annually into the general Treasury rather than dedicating reasonable fees to SEVP oversight demonstrates that this rule operates as a punitive tariff on international education rather than a legitimate regulatory fee.

3. Severe Harm to U.S. Higher Education and Local Economies
International students contribute tens of billions of dollars annually to the U.S. economy through tuition, housing, and local spending, often subsidizing domestic tuition rates and funding critical university labs. Experiential learning through OPT and STEM OPT is a primary reason top global students choose U.S. universities over competitors in Canada, the United Kingdom, Europe, and Asia. Eliminating realistic access to post-graduation training will trigger a sharp decline in international enrollment, starving U.S. universities of vital revenue, shrinking research capacity, and harming college-town economies across the country.

4. Disruption of the U.S. STEM and Innovation PipelineU.S. employers rely on OPT and STEM OPT to evaluate and train early-career talent trained at American institutions. Rather than protecting domestic workers, driving international graduates out of the country immediately after they complete their degrees exports U.S.-trained innovators directly to foreign competitors. If DHS seeks to address program oversight or fraud, targeted enforcement, clear reporting standards, and reasonable, cost-based SEVIS fees are far more effective and lawful alternatives than imposing a prohibitive $70,000–$100,000 financial wall.

5. Unfairness to Currently Enrolled F-1 Students
Thousands of F-1 students currently enrolled in multi-year degree programs invested their savings and selected U.S. institutions in good-faith reliance on existing OPT regulations. Triggering a $70,000 fee for any DSO recommendation made 60 days after a final rule is published unfairly penalizes students who are already mid-degree and have no way to alter their educational investments.

For these reasons, I strongly urge DHS and ICE to withdraw Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 and preserve accessible, fair pathways for international students to complete their practical training in the United States.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly expresses strong opposition to the OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the proposed rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for an initial OPT recommendation.

My concern is not simply who ultimately pays the fee. The more fundamental issue is that a fee of this magnitude would function as a barrier to lawful employment rather than as a reasonable administrative charge. The government should not use an extraordinarily high fee as a mechanism to restrict international students’ access to employment opportunities for which they are otherwise legally eligible.

OPT is designed to allow international students to obtain practical experience related to the education they received in the United States. Students who satisfy the applicable academic, immigration, and employment requirements should be evaluated under those requirements, rather than effectively excluded from the labor market because of an extremely large financial barrier.

A $70,000 fee would create an unfair system in which access to employment opportunities could depend heavily on financial resources rather than qualifications, skills, education, and compliance with immigration rules. Students with the same degree, the same qualifications, and the same legitimate employment opportunity could face very different outcomes simply because one is able to overcome this financial barrier and another is not.

If the government believes that additional oversight or enforcement is necessary for the OPT program, those concerns should be addressed directly through reasonable verification, compliance requirements, and enforcement mechanisms. Imposing a $70,000 fee is not a proportionate way to address such concerns. A regulatory fee should reflect legitimate administrative and enforcement needs, not operate as a de facto restriction on lawful employment.

International students invest years in obtaining U.S. degrees and developing skills that can contribute to American universities, businesses, research institutions, and the broader economy. After completing those educational requirements, they should not face an extraordinary financial barrier simply to pursue temporary practical training that is already authorized under the immigration system.

I therefore respectfully urge DHS not to adopt the proposed $70,000 OPT fee and instead consider reasonable, proportionate measures that protect program integrity without using financial barriers to restrict legitimate employment opportunities.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed $70,000 OPT fee, arguing it creates an unfair financial barrier to employment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an F-1 student who began a Master of Science in Data Science at Northeastern University in Fall 2026. I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee, and I urge DHS to withdraw this rule.

1. The rule changes the terms after students have already committed. I chose to study in the United States, paid tuition, and relocated my family based on the existing rules, including OPT as part of my STEM education. Before my program even started, new restrictions affecting CPT were announced. Now this proposal would add a fee larger than many students' total annual tuition. Students who followed every legal requirement cannot reasonably plan their education when the rules keep changing mid-program. DHS should at minimum exempt students who were already enrolled before a final rule takes effect.

2. The fee amount has no stated relationship to the cost of administering OPT. A $70,000 charge per recommendation is far greater than any plausible cost of processing a DSO recommendation or monitoring compliance. A fee of this size functions as a barrier, not a cost-recovery charge. I ask DHS to explain how these amounts were calculated and whether it has the legal authority to impose them.

3. The rule punishes all students for the misconduct of a few. DHS says the goal is to combat fraud. Fraud should be addressed through targeted enforcement against bad-actor employers and schools, not by charging every lawful student. Most of us, like me, are pursuing legitimate training in our field of study.

4. The fee will in practice fall on students and their families. The proposal allows schools to pass the cost to students or employers. For most international students, this would make OPT financially impossible, which effectively closes the practical training pathway that STEM education depends on.

5. The rule harms U.S. competitiveness. International students contribute tuition, research, and skills in STEM and AI fields where the U.S. competes globally. Making OPT unaffordable will push talented students to choose other countries.

I respectfully request that DHS (a) withdraw the proposed fees; (b) if any fee is retained, set it at a level tied to actual administrative cost; and (c) exempt students already enrolled or admitted before a final rule is published.

Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.commentText:
I am an F-1 student in computational biology at a U.S. university. I am submitting this comment to strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees.

1. The rule is unclear for students already on OPT, and those students should be fully exempt. I have already applied for post-completion OPT and plan to apply for a STEM OPT extension soon. I made my education, career, and financial decisions based on the current rules. The proposed rule does not clearly say whether a STEM extension for a student whose initial OPT began before the effective date would carry a $30,000 fee, a $70,000 fee, or no fee. I urge DHS to clearly exempt every OPT and STEM OPT period for students whose initial OPT was recommended before any final rule takes effect.

2. The fees would cut off a pipeline the U.S. depends on. Computational biology connects biomedical research, drug discovery, and data science. Skills like AI/ML for biology are exactly what U.S. research labs, biotech companies, and hospitals are trying to hire. STEM OPT already has safeguards: E-Verify employers, a formal training plan (Form I-983), and regular reporting. Raising the cost from roughly $500 today to $70,000 adds no protection. It only pushes schools to limit or deny OPT recommendations.

3. Placing the fee on schools will distort academic decisions. Universities would face a six-figure cost for each student they recommend. They may ration OPT, favor students who can afford to repay them, or discourage valuable pre-completion training. Fields like computational biology, where internships and research positions often come before graduation, would be hit especially hard.

4. The fee is far out of proportion to any administrative cost. DHS should publish the actual cost of administering OPT and set any fee at that level.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw this proposed rule. At a minimum, it should exempt current OPT holders and their future STEM extensions, and limit any fee to actual administrative cost.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they disrupt current students and harm the STEM pipeline.
