comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Requiring OPT fees does not address the root concerns presented in this proposed rule about OPT. Furthermore, the proposed rule lacks data that shows the number of “bad actors” who have been found amongst those on OPT.

The proposed rule describes the $70,000 and $30,000 fees as deterrent in nature to protect against fraud. But, imposing such a fee not only deters those who have misleading employment, but also the majority of students engaging in OPT with legitimate interest in practical training. To deter OPT also deters general international enrollment, which will significantly impact higher education institutes and the economy. International student tuition helps to fund U.S. universities, services, and staffing, of colleges and universities across the U.S. According to NAFSA’s latest analysis*, international students studying at U.S. colleges and universities contributed $42.9 billion and supported 355,736 jobs to the U.S. economy during the 2024-2025 academic year.

A $70,000 fee is exorbitant when students have no guarantee they will find practical training opportunities. Even if the fee is refunded if OPT is not approved, there’s no refund if the student does not find employment on OPT. That the proposed rule compares the cost of this fee with the cost of 1-2 years of education in a U.S. program of study is not comparable because educational programs provide educational deliverables (right to attend class, engage in student life activities, etc). Applying for OPT does not guarantee a deliverable, particularly in challenging job markets. So, a student may invest $70,000 and be approved for OPT, but never receive a job offer. Comparing the OPT fee with the H-1B fee is also notably different as H-1B offers have guaranteed employment, whereas OPT employment adds a risk of whether a student will find employment or not.

The proposed rule states that “DHS believes this proposed fee would incentivize educational institutions to exercise greater oversight and selectivity when recommending students for OPT.” This does not align with previous responsibility delineations that it is DHS’s job to determine appropriate employment, not the DSOs responsibility. It calls for schools to be subjective in choosing the best students to have practical training opportunities, as opposed to allowing access to all students who DHS deems are eligible. And since it is permitted for students to pay the educational institution for the OPT fee, it selects only those who have enough funding to apply for OPT, creating inequity in who may apply for OPT. The rule states “Furthermore, the financial commitment of this fee may encourage schools to apply a heightened level of scrutiny when reviewing an F–1 nonimmigrant student’s request for OPT to ensure that the student is engaging in a legitimate OPT opportunity.” However, the sense that schools would be able to subjectively determine whether a student’s OPT intention is legitimate or not is neither in the DSO’s responsibilities/scope, nor increased by the addition of a fee for OPT recommendations.
The conclusion that SEVP-certified educational institutions would be able to identify and make judgments for “high achieving eligible F-1 nonimmigrant students who are pursuing OPT directly related to the F-1 nonimmigrant student’s major program of study” is the same basis that we recommend OPT without a fee. Including a required fee does not lead schools/DSOs to have better judgment. DSOs already present the OPT eligibility requirements to F-1 students interested in OPT prior to the OPT recommendation, including that the employment must be related to their major area of study. The addition of a fee will not help me as a DSO become more discerning about whether a student intends to follow these requirements or not.
The proposed rule states “those seeking to abuse the program are less likely to invest in participation when faced with a tangible cost, making engagement in OPT for nefarious purposes less attractive to bad actors.” However, a fee does not eliminate the “nefarious purposes” of “bad actors” but instead limits them to those who can afford to pay such a fee. DHS needs to determine uniform qualifications, as opposed to a fee that adds bias against those who have fewer funding sources available to them. A student’s wealth/financial resources should not be the basis of whether they are permitted to apply their education practically in a training setting.

Finally, the court has already criticized the government for providing the minimum 30-day public comment period with the proposed rule to eliminate Duration of Status. It is difficult for institutions to pull together the quantifiable evidence and thorough responses needed to respond to such a rule as this in such a short time frame.

*https://www.nafsa.org/policy-and-advocacy/policy-resources/nafsa-international-student-economic-value-tool-v2
comments.reason: The commenter argues that the high OPT fees are exorbitant, lack supporting data, and will harm students and the economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Manufacturing is not just about having enough people on the production floor. Modern factories also need engineers who understand automation, industrial software, quality control, and equipment reliability.

These positions require specialized training, and the transition from an engineering degree to working in a manufacturing facility takes time.

OPT provides eligible international graduates with an opportunity to develop practical experience in these environments. That training can involve diagnosing equipment failures, improving production processes, or helping manufacturers implement new technologies.

My concern with the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee is that they could make this pathway significantly less accessible.

For manufacturers, particularly smaller suppliers, recruiting specialized engineers is already challenging. A delayed automation project or an unfilled quality engineering position can affect production schedules and customer commitments.

Reducing access to qualified graduates does not necessarily result in an equivalent increase in employment for American workers. In some cases, existing employees may simply be asked to manage additional responsibilities.

The proposed fees also raise questions about proportionality. A university's ability to pay a substantial amount does not establish whether an engineering graduate has a legitimate training opportunity.

I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee provisions under 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2) and examine their potential effects on domestic manufacturing capacity.

Any alternative policy should focus on verified compliance risks while preserving lawful, degree-related practical training.

Strengthening American manufacturing requires investment in workforce development, equipment, and technical expertise. The consequences for all three should be considered before implementing a policy of this scale.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees make the pathway less accessible and harm manufacturers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Cybersecurity is an area where workforce capability directly affects the reliability of American businesses and essential services.

Security teams must continuously monitor networks, investigate suspicious activity, test systems, and respond to vulnerabilities. These responsibilities require both academic knowledge and practical experience.

Graduates in computer science, cybersecurity, and information systems may use OPT to develop relevant professional skills under applicable employment authorization rules.

The proposed fee structure creates several concerns.

Workforce availability. Substantial fees imposed on educational institutions may reduce the number of graduates able to obtain practical training authorization. Employers with specialized technical requirements could face a smaller candidate pool.

Operational resilience. Some organizations, particularly smaller businesses and service providers, have limited cybersecurity staffing. Persistent vacancies can increase the burden on existing personnel and delay security improvements.

Regulatory effectiveness. A $70,000 payment does not establish whether a training position is legitimate or whether an employer maintains appropriate security practices.

These are potential consequences, not demonstrated outcomes. They nevertheless warrant analysis because cybersecurity staffing affects more than the individual employer.

I request that DHS evaluate the proposed fees under § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2) against their potential effects on cybersecurity workforce development.

The Department should also compare the proposal with targeted employer verification, compliance audits, and enforcement against fraudulent training arrangements.

Immigration integrity and cybersecurity workforce development are both legitimate public interests. A complete regulatory analysis should account for both.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fees create workforce concerns and requests DHS to evaluate the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
When a hurricane approaches the Gulf Coast, families don't care where the engineer who helped develop a flood prediction model was born. They care whether the forecast is accurate and whether their community has enough time to prepare.

That is why I believe the proposed OPT fees deserve serious consideration beyond immigration policy.

Disaster preparedness relies on professionals trained in meteorology, environmental engineering, geographic information systems, hydrology, and data science. Universities provide the academic foundation, but applying these skills to real emergency planning requires practical experience.

OPT can help qualified international graduates make that transition.

A graduate trained in flood modeling, for example, may gain practical experience analyzing drainage systems, processing geographic data, or supporting infrastructure risk assessments. These skills have direct applications in communities vulnerable to hurricanes, flooding, and other natural disasters.

My concern is that the proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee could discourage universities from supporting these training opportunities.

Local governments, engineering consultants, and smaller research organizations may already face difficulty recruiting people with specialized technical backgrounds. Reducing access to trained graduates could make that challenge more difficult.

I recognize that not every OPT participant works in disaster preparedness, and I am not suggesting that this proposal would immediately weaken emergency response systems.

However, workforce development in these fields is a long-term process. Decisions that affect the availability of specialized graduates should account for possible consequences to public safety and infrastructure planning.

I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed fees under § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2) and evaluate more targeted compliance measures.

Protecting American communities requires more than responding to emergencies after they occur. It also requires maintaining the scientific and technical expertise needed to anticipate and reduce risks.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed high fees would harm recruitment of trained graduates for disaster preparedness.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Everything seems to cost more these days. Housing, groceries, insurance, repairs, and basic services are already expensive for American families.

So I have a simple question: Has anyone seriously examined whether these proposed OPT fees could make certain services even more expensive?

Businesses need trained employees to operate efficiently. Accountants, engineers, data analysts, and technical specialists help companies manage costs, improve processes, and serve customers.

Some international graduates develop those skills through OPT after completing their education at American universities.

If the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 fees discourage schools from supporting OPT, employers could face additional difficulties filling specialized positions.

Businesses do not operate in a vacuum.

When staffing problems delay projects or reduce productivity, companies may experience higher operating costs. Depending on market conditions, some of those costs may eventually be passed on to customers.

I am not claiming that OPT fees would automatically raise consumer prices. The relationship depends on the industry, labor market, and availability of alternative workers.

But that is exactly why DHS should study the issue before adopting such substantial fees.

The Department should explain whether it has evaluated the potential effects on business operating costs, service availability, and consumer prices.

It should also demonstrate why these fees are necessary to prevent fraud when more targeted enforcement methods may be available.

I oppose the proposed fee provisions under 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2) and request their withdrawal pending a fuller economic assessment.

American consumers should not be overlooked when evaluating the indirect consequences of immigration policy.
comments.reason: Argues the proposed OPT fees could increase business operating costs and consumer prices.

Although the payment obligation would fall on educational institutions, the effects could extend to American employers seeking individuals with specialized international knowledge.

Large corporations may have multiple ways to recruit internationally experienced employees. Smaller exporters and growing businesses often have fewer resources and less flexibility.

The potential consequence is not simply a reduction in OPT participation. It may also include lost opportunities for American companies to develop new customer relationships and compete effectively in foreign markets.

The proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee under § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2) should therefore be evaluated in the context of American export competitiveness.

I request that DHS withdraw these fee provisions and conduct an assessment of their potential effects on businesses engaged in international trade.

The Department should also consider targeted anti-fraud measures that address actual compliance violations without imposing broad financial restrictions on legitimate practical training.

A regulatory approach intended to protect American economic interests should consider how American companies compete, grow, and create opportunities in international markets.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees of $70,000 and $30,000 and urge DHS to withdraw them.

I am a PhD student researching efficient, optimized cooling systems. This work matters because Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimates data centers could consume 11.8% of U.S. electricity by 2030. I came to the United States because its universities, national laboratories and industry can turn research like mine into working infrastructure, and OPT is the step that makes that possible. This rule would shut that door for the very people the country needs to solve its AI and energy challenges.

The fee does not fit the fraud it claims to address. DHS's evidence involves shell companies, staged worksites and document brokers (91 FR 64571). Those are identifiable bad actors, and DHS found them using site visits and data analysis, without any fee. Yet the rule charges a student in a university research group or national laboratory exactly the same $70,000 as a student at a shell company. No school can know in advance which employer will prove fraudulent, so the only reliable effect is that schools recommend far fewer students. A policy that punishes thousands of lawful students for the conduct of a few is not fraud prevention. It is collective punishment.

The fee also does not fund the oversight DHS says is needed. The money goes to the Treasury, and ICE cannot use it (91 FR 64576). DHS chose the amount by comparing it to H-1B fees, not by measuring what oversight costs. A charge unrelated to cost, funding no enforcement, and priced to deter participation is a barrier, not a safeguard. DHS also rejected proven tools such as STEM OPT-style site visits and training plans because they take effort (91 FR 64576). Convenience for the agency cannot justify closing a pathway for hundreds of thousands of people.

The harm is large, and DHS admits it cannot measure it. Its own analysis projects $8.4 to $16.5 billion in annual fees and $8.07 to $8.92 billion in annual opportunity costs, yet states it "cannot precisely quantify" them (91 FR 64584, 64588-89). It concedes that employers may lose productivity and schools may lose enrollment revenue. The rule's costs rest on a guess, while its claimed benefits rest on an assumption that fewer students means less fraud.

The damage to STEM talent would be severe. The Peterson Institute for International Economics (Policy Brief 26-10) estimates that a one-third decline in foreign STEM graduates entering the labor force would shrink the PhD-level STEM workforce by 11.5% and cut GDP by 0.8% to 1.6% after a decade, and that most such graduates enter the workforce through OPT. DHS's own model expects schools to pay only for students with STEM OPT eligibility, leaving others without access (91 FR 64583). Doctoral researchers face a total of $100,000, which pushes institutions away from pre-completion OPT and removes research-integrated training (91 FR 64584).

The burden falls unequally. DHS finds that 56% of regulated institutions are small entities and that nearly one in ten small entities would face costs above 5% of revenue (91 FR 64576, 64595). Public universities and small colleges cannot match wealthy private ones. Access to OPT would then depend on the size of a school's endowment, not on a student's talent or work.

DHS's invitation to charge $70,000 again at each education level (91 FR 64577) is especially damaging. A PhD student who used OPT after a master's degree would face a second $70,000 bill, ending OPT for those with the deepest training.

DHS dismisses reliance as "speculative" and tells employers to recruit U.S. citizens (91 FR 64578). In specialized fields, qualified candidates often do not exist. Students and families spent years and substantial savings choosing the United States over Canada, the U.K., Australia and Germany, which are eager to welcome them. Changing the terms at the final step breaks the trust that makes the U.S. the top destination for talent.

The country has two choices: pursue the fraudsters directly, or tax every honest student to deter them. The first protects American workers and keeps the talent that builds American industry. The second drives that talent and its tuition away. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal and target enforcement at the employers and brokers it has already identified.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw them.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to withdraw the proposed rule establishing $70,000 in fees for an initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations. OPT is a critical component of the international student educational experience in the United States, and imposing fees of this magnitude would fundamentally undermine the accessibility, value, and purpose of American higher education.

As someone who works directly with international students at a public university, I see the investment students make in pursuing an education in the United States. These students commit years of study, significant financial resources, and considerable personal sacrifice to develop the knowledge and skills that American institutions provide. OPT represents the opportunity to apply that education in a professional setting, contribute to the U.S. workforce, and gain practical experience that complements their academic preparation. It is not simply an opportunity to obtain employment; it is an extension of the educational experience that makes studying in the United States valuable.

In his September 2026 NAFSA International Educator interview, economist Michael Clemens challenges the assumption that immigration is a zero-sum economic exchange. His research and discussion emphasize that immigrants and U.S.-born workers create opportunities together through innovation, entrepreneurship, investment, and specialization. He also highlights the important role international students play in the American research and innovation ecosystem. This perspective is particularly relevant to OPT. When an international student applies the skills developed at a U.S. university, the benefits are not limited to that individual. Employers gain specialized knowledge, colleagues gain new perspectives, research teams strengthen their capacity, and communities benefit from economic activity. Restricting these opportunities does not necessarily create opportunities for American workers; it can diminish the conditions that allow new opportunities to emerge.

The proposed fees would place universities in an untenable position. A $70,000 fee for each initial OPT recommendation is not a reasonable administrative cost. It is a financial barrier that could force institutions to make decisions about which students receive access to practical training based on institutional resources rather than academic merit, educational preparation, or legitimate employment opportunities. Public universities, particularly those already operating under significant financial constraints, would face difficult choices about whether to absorb these costs, pass them on to students, or discontinue recommending students for OPT altogether.

The consequences would be especially significant for students who have already invested in a U.S. education. Many international students make decisions about where to study based on the availability of practical training opportunities. As Clemens explains, the possibility of gaining professional experience in the United States influences whether students choose to pursue their education here in the first place. If OPT becomes financially inaccessible, the United States risks discouraging talented students from enrolling, reducing the value of their educational investment, and weakening the international competitiveness of its universities.

I recognize the importance of maintaining the integrity of the immigration system, preventing fraud, and ensuring that OPT is used for legitimate educational and professional purposes. However, a substantial fee is not a substitute for targeted oversight. If the government identifies specific vulnerabilities within the program, it should pursue measures that directly address those concerns through appropriate monitoring, compliance requirements, and enforcement. Such measures should be proportionate to the problem and should not create an overwhelming financial burden for institutions and students who are complying with the law.

OPT should remain an accessible, educationally grounded opportunity for eligible international students. The United States benefits when students are encouraged to study, develop their expertise, and contribute their skills to the communities and industries that helped educate them. Preserving OPT is not simply about supporting international students; it is about protecting the long-term educational, economic, and innovative capacity of the United States.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed OPT fee rule and preserve a practical training pathway that supports legitimate educational outcomes, strengthens the U.S. workforce, and allows international students and American communities to continue creating opportunities together.
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposed rule, arguing the high fees undermine accessibility and higher education.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by John Thompson
comments.commentText:
Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees (RIN 1653-AB01)
I oppose this proposed rule and ask DHS to withdraw it. I spent more than forty years in enrollment leadership at four private liberal arts colleges (Furman, Centre, Rhodes, and Gettysburg) and served as president of the Common Application board of directors. I now advise private colleges on enrollment and financial aid. These views are my own.
A private college that recommends twenty graduates for OPT in one year would owe $1.4 million before any of them could apply for work authorization. If ten go on to the STEM extension, another $300,000 comes due. Under section IV.C, ICE could not keep the money. It would go to the Treasury as a miscellaneous receipt, and none of it to SEVP or to oversight of OPT.
DHS is right that OPT fraud deserves enforcement. The site-visit findings in section IV.A describe real abuse. My objection is to who would pay for stopping it.
1. Burden on small private colleges (Section VII.B). DHS treats all 1,294 private nonprofit institutions as small entities. In the transition year it estimates that 841 of 1,389 small institutions (60.5 percent) would bear costs above 1 percent of revenue, and 116 above 20 percent. Those figures likely understate the burden. DHS estimated revenue from published room, board, and tuition, and private colleges do not collect published tuition. In NACUBO's finalized 2024-25 study, institutional grant aid equaled 50 percent of gross tuition revenue for all undergraduates. DHS should rerun Table 17 using net tuition revenue, which IPEDS already reports.
2. The rejected small-institution exemption (Section VII.B.6). DHS rejected an exemption because 56 percent of regulated institutions are small, so "fraud could still continue." That is a count of institutions. It is not evidence of where the fraud occurs. The abuse in section IV.A centers on employers: shell companies, staged worksites, and residential addresses with no employees present. I could find no case in the proposal involving an accredited private nonprofit college recommending its own graduates for OPT.
3. The enrollment effect (Sections VI and VII.A). DHS says only about 20 percent of F-1 students used OPT in 2024, a figure that divides one year's participants by every enrolled student, including first-year students years from eligibility. The Institute for Progress, citing SEVIS data, reports that 54 percent of F-1 graduates use OPT, including 64 percent in STEM. DHS concedes that institutions "could also experience declines" in enrollment, but does not quantify them, and every one of its scenarios assumes no change in STEM participation.
4. Pass-through to domestic students (Sections IV.C and VI). DHS says schools may pass the fee to "all students." At a tuition-dependent college, that would mean American families paying a federal immigration fee through their tuition bills. International tuition revenue also helps fund seats for domestic students. The Institute for Progress estimates the fee would mean roughly 46,000 fewer Americans enrolling in bachelor's and master's programs each year. DHS's analysis does not address this.
5. Fee basis (Section IV.C). DHS set the fee to be "comparable to the fee for H-1B visas" and offers no cost basis for it. H-1B status can run six years; OPT runs at most three. Per year of work authorized, $100,000 in OPT fees is twice the H-1B rate. Congress gave DHS cost-based fee authority for this program at 8 U.S.C. 1372, and DHS used it in 2019. A fee set that way would fund the oversight DHS says it lacks.
I ask DHS to take five steps:
(1) Withdraw the proposed rule.
(2) Target employers. Extend the STEM OPT employer requirements (E-Verify and the Form I-983 training plan) to all post-completion OPT, and bar OPT employment at private residences or with employers formed less than a year before hiring.
(3) If a fee is necessary, set it under 8 U.S.C. 1372 at the documented cost of oversight, and exempt or scale it for small nonprofit institutions.
(4) Rerun the small-entity analysis using net tuition revenue, and model the effect on enrollment.
(5) Extend the comment period. Thirty days is short for a rule with a primary estimate of $12.8 billion in annual transfers.
The fraud DHS describes lives at worksites where nobody works. A rule aimed at those worksites should do more about the fraud and far less harm to colleges that have done nothing wrong. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and write that rule instead.

I strongly oppose the proposed rule and respectfully urge DHS to withdraw it.

1. The proposed fees are disproportionate and would make OPT inaccessible.

The proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee could result in $100,000 in additional costs for a student pursuing OPT followed by STEM OPT. Such extraordinary financial barriers would effectively prevent many qualified students from participating in practical training, regardless of their skills, academic achievements, or compliance with immigration regulations.

Access to practical training would increasingly depend on financial resources rather than academic merit or professional qualifications.

3. Broad financial restrictions are not an effective substitute for targeted fraud prevention.

Existing oversight mechanisms already include SEVIS reporting, E-Verify participation and Form I-983 training plans for STEM OPT, employer site visits, and enforcement against fraudulent activities. DHS should strengthen these targeted measures rather than impose extraordinary financial burdens on every legitimate participant. The proposed fees do not adequately distinguish compliant students and employers from those engaging in misconduct.

4. The proposal threatens American economic competitiveness.

International students contribute to American universities, research, technological innovation, and local economies. Practical training opportunities help the United States attract talented students who might otherwise study in competing countries.

Research published by NAFSA and JB International in August 2026 projected that declining international enrollment could result in up to 111,000 fewer students, $3.4 billion in lost economic activity, and nearly 40,000 U.S. jobs at risk. Although these projections predate the proposed rule, they illustrate the economic vulnerability of international education. Restricting OPT would also reduce the opportunities for American employers, particularly startups and smaller businesses, to recruit graduates educated at U.S. institutions.

5. The proposal inadequately protects currently enrolled students.

A 60-day transition period does not adequately address these reliance interests. Imposing major new financial barriers after students have already committed to their educational programs would be unfair and disruptive.

2. If any revised rule proceeds, exempt students who enrolled before its effective date.
3. Limit any additional fees to reasonable, documented administrative costs.

Protecting program integrity and maintaining America’s attractiveness to talented international students should not be mutually exclusive goals.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am submitting this comment in strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed rule, "Optional Practical Training Fees" (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100), published at 91 FR 64566. The proposed imposition of a $70,000 fee for initial OPT recommendations and $30,000 for subsequent extensions is arbitrary, exceeds statutory authority, and threatens irreparable harm to the U.S. higher education system and domestic economic competitiveness.

1. The Proposed Fees Exceed Statutory Authority and Are Arbitrary and Capricious
Under established administrative law principles and the Independent Offices Appropriation Act (IOAA), agency fees must be reasonably related to the direct cost of providing the specific service or adjudication to the recipient. A $70,000 fee for an initial Form I-20 recommendation—and $30,000 for an extension—bears no rational relationship to the minimal administrative processing costs borne by SEVP or the Department. Furthermore, the agency’s acknowledgment that proceeds will be diverted into general Treasury receipts rather than used directly for program integrity functions confirms that this assessment operates not as a cost-recovery fee, but as an unauthorized tax and an effective constructive termination of the OPT program.

2. Disproportionate Financial Devastation on U.S. Academic Institutions
By placing the collection burden directly on SEVP-certified institutions prior to SEVIS entry, DHS imposes an untenable financial and administrative mandate on colleges and universities. Academic institutions, especially smaller colleges and regional universities, lack the capital to front tens of millions of dollars annually. If passed down to students, these fees will eliminate practical training opportunities for all but the wealthiest foreign nationals, triggering catastrophic drops in international student enrollment. This will deprive U.S. institutions of essential tuition revenue that directly funds domestic student aid, faculty positions, and university infrastructure.

3. Harm to the U.S. STEM Pipeline, Healthcare, and Economic Innovation
Optional Practical Training is an integral experiential component of an American degree. Eliminating access to post-graduation training will sever critical pipelines in fields with acute domestic shortages, including biomedical sciences, artificial intelligence, semiconductor manufacturing, and healthcare. Instead of protecting American jobs, this proposal will force top global researchers and technical graduates to bring their innovations, patentable discoveries, and business ventures to competitor nations with welcoming post-study work frameworks.

4. Insufficient Comment Window
Given the profound economic disruption of a rule projected to collect billions of dollars, providing only a 30-day comment window is legally deficient under the Administrative Procedure Act. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Dear Department of Homeland Security,

I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed rule imposing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT authorization.

As an international Ph.D. student conducting research in science and engineering at a U.S. university, I believe this proposal would seriously undermine American scientific competitiveness, discourage highly skilled international talent, and impose an unreasonable financial burden on students and research institutions.

1. Harm to American Scientific Competitiveness

International graduate students play an essential role in American research and innovation. Many Ph.D. students spend five or more years conducting original research, publishing scientific papers, and contributing to projects supported by American universities and federal research funding.

OPT allows these highly trained graduates to apply their expertise in American universities, national laboratories, and technology companies. A $70,000 fee would make this opportunity inaccessible to many qualified researchers, especially those pursuing academic postdoctoral positions.

American institutions invest substantial resources in educating and training international Ph.D. students. Forcing these graduates to leave because of prohibitive OPT fees would effectively transfer the benefits of that investment to competing countries. This outcome directly contradicts the goal of maintaining American leadership in science and technology.

2. Disproportionate and Unjustified Financial Burden

The proposed fees are extraordinarily high compared with the purpose of OPT as a practical training program.

DHS should demonstrate how these specific amounts are justified by actual administrative, oversight, and fraud-prevention costs. Without such evidence, the proposed fees appear to function as a financial barrier rather than a reasonable regulatory measure.

Furthermore, many universities, research laboratories, and early-career researchers cannot afford these costs. The proposal would disproportionately affect academic researchers and graduates from less affluent backgrounds, regardless of their qualifications.

3. Ineffective Approach to Fraud Prevention

I recognize the importance of combating fraud and maintaining the integrity of the OPT program. However, imposing extremely high fees on all participants is not a targeted solution to fraudulent employment practices.

Legitimate students and researchers should not be collectively penalized for misconduct by a small subset of employers or participants.

More effective alternatives include stronger employer verification, targeted investigations, improved compliance monitoring, and stricter enforcement against fraudulent organizations. These measures would address the underlying problems without restricting legitimate professional training.

4. Negative Consequences for American Universities and Employers

The proposed fees would make it significantly more difficult for American universities, research institutions, and companies to recruit and retain highly skilled international graduates.

Academic postdoctoral positions and early-career research jobs generally operate under limited budgets. Requiring an additional $70,000 for OPT could make hiring international graduates financially impractical, even when their specialized expertise is essential.

This would weaken research collaboration, reduce access to specialized talent, and potentially slow scientific discovery and technological innovation in the United States.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee structure and instead adopt proportionate, evidence-based measures to strengthen OPT oversight and prevent fraud.

The United States has benefited enormously from international students who contribute to scientific research, innovation, and economic development. OPT policies should preserve America's ability to attract and retain talented researchers while ensuring appropriate regulatory oversight.

A policy that prevents highly trained graduates from contributing to the American economy because they cannot afford an extraordinary fee would ultimately harm the very national interests it seeks to protect.

Thank you for considering my comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposed rule and to urge DHS to withdraw or substantially revise it. My comments reference Sections IV.B, IV.C, V.A, and V.C of the NPRM.

1. The proposed rule does not provide a reasonable transition period (Section V.C).
DHS proposes that the final rule take effect only 60 days after publication. Many international students chose to enroll in U.S. institutions, and in some cases chose their specific field of study, in reliance on the availability of practical training. Students who are already mid-program have made irreversible financial and personal commitments based on the rules in effect when they enrolled. A 60-day window gives institutions no realistic time to budget for, raise, or allocate funds on the scale proposed, and gives students no time to adjust their plans. I urge DHS to explain what measures it would take to protect the reasonable expectations of students already enrolled, and at a minimum to exempt students who were enrolled before the effective date.

2. DHS has not justified the fee amounts (Sections IV.C and V.A).
The NPRM provides no calculation, cost study, or economic analysis supporting the $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee. The only stated bases are that the amounts are “comparable to” H-1B fees and “on par with” one or two years of tuition. Neither is a justification. OPT is a training component of the F-1 program, not a substitute for H-1B, and the fact that international students already pay substantial tuition does not make an additional six-figure fee reasonable or effective. I request that DHS publish the mathematical reasoning and data behind these specific figures, including why a fee of this magnitude, rather than targeted enforcement against the fraudulent employers DHS itself identifies in Section IV.A, is the appropriate tool.

3. The fee is poorly matched to the stated objectives of combating fraud and protecting U.S. workers (Section IV.A–C).
The fraud described in Section IV.A is committed primarily by shell-company employers and “pay-to-stay” schemes. A fee charged to schools and, as DHS acknowledges, likely passed on to students, punishes legitimate students and institutions while leaving fraudulent employers untouched. Fraudulent actors who already sell fake jobs for a fee are the parties most able to absorb or monetize another fee; honest students at public universities with limited financial aid are the ones who will be excluded. The practical effect is to favor wealthier institutions and wealthier students, which has no relationship to program integrity.

4. The “protecting American workers” rationale is internally contradictory (Section IV.B).
DHS states the fee is meant to ensure that “only highly qualified” students participate in OPT, and at the same time argues that OPT participants displace U.S. workers. If international graduates are winning positions in open competition, that is evidence of exactly the talent the U.S. economy depends on, not a reason to price it out. DHS’s own 2016 rule recognized that STEM innovation and a strong post-secondary system benefit U.S. workers on the whole; the NPRM offers no new quantified evidence to the contrary, only citations to unemployment rates among recent graduates that it does not causally link to OPT. The labor market is not a fixed number of seats: companies that cannot hire the strongest graduates in the United States will move the work, and the teams around it, abroad, which harms U.S. workers far more than competition does. A fee does not screen for ability; it screens for wealth.

5. The fee undermines the F-1 program’s purpose rather than serving it.
DHS asserts in Section IV that without these fees it “may shut down the program entirely.” Presenting a six-figure fee as the only alternative to elimination is not a reasoned choice among options; it is a threat. DHS should analyze and respond to less burdensome alternatives, such as mandatory employer registration and verification, enhanced site-visit funding through a modest employer fee, or caps targeted at the specific high-risk employer clusters it has already identified.

For these reasons, I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule, or at minimum to publish the analysis behind the fee amounts, respond to the concerns above, and provide a transition period and exemption for currently enrolled students.

I am writing to express my concerns regarding the Department of Homeland Security's proposed rule, Optional Practical Training Fees, published on October 8, 2026.
The proposal would require educational institutions to pay $70,000 for an international student's initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent OPT recommendation. These requirements would apply to both pre-completion and post-completion OPT, including STEM OPT extensions.
I am concerned that these fees would create substantial financial barriers to practical training opportunities that are directly relevant to students' academic programs and professional development.
First, the proposed fees could significantly restrict access to internships during graduate school. Recent changes to Curricular Practical Training (CPT) eligibility have already made internships less accessible to students whose academic programs do not require internships for graduation. For these students, pre-completion OPT may be the primary available pathway to gain professional experience outside their universities. Imposing a $70,000 institutional fee for an initial OPT recommendation could make that pathway financially impractical.
Second, the proposal could undermine opportunities for international graduates to apply their specialized training in the United States. OPT enables students to obtain practical experience in fields related to their degrees. Graduate students often develop highly specialized expertise through years of academic research, and opportunities to apply that knowledge in industry, government, or research institutions can be important components of their professional development.
Third, the proposal places a substantial financial burden on educational institutions, with the possibility of costs being transferred to students or employers. Although the rule would require institutions to pay the fees, it does not prohibit them from obtaining funding from other parties. This creates uncertainty regarding who would ultimately bear these costs and whether universities would continue recommending eligible students for OPT.
I recognize DHS's stated objectives of preventing fraud, protecting the integrity of immigration programs, and ensuring compliance with employment authorization requirements. These are legitimate subjects for regulatory oversight. However, I encourage DHS to evaluate whether the proposed fees are proportionate to these objectives and whether more targeted compliance measures could achieve similar results without substantially restricting access to authorized practical training.
I also encourage DHS to consider the combined effects of recent CPT eligibility restrictions and the proposed OPT fees, particularly for students in degree programs where internships are academically relevant but not mandatory.
I respectfully request that DHS reconsider the proposed fee structure, evaluate less financially burdensome alternatives, and fully account for the consequences for students, universities, employers, and the broader research and education community before issuing a final rule.
Thank you for considering this comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100
RIN 1653-AB01

I support DHS's proposed OPT fee structure, including the $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee. My support relates particularly to the NPRM's objectives of strengthening program integrity, deterring fraud, increasing institutional accountability, protecting U.S. workers, and ensuring that OPT remains genuine practical training.

DHS has identified significant program-integrity concerns involving suspected fraudulent employers and arrangements, including nonexistent worksites, "pay-to-stay" schemes, residential addresses represented as worksites, missing employment records, and phantom employees. These documented concerns provide a reasonable basis for stronger safeguards.

OPT should involve bona fide practical training, actual work, a legitimate employment relationship, and work directly related to the student's major area of study. The relevant issue is not whether every OPT participant, school, or employer presents a fraud risk. Many legitimate participants do not. Rather, documented vulnerabilities justify reasonable measures designed to deter artificial arrangements and improve scrutiny.

I support DHS's use of a substantial financial commitment as a screening and deterrence mechanism. A nominal fee may be insufficient to materially change institutional behavior or deter arrangements principally intended to obtain employment authorization. A substantial fee can require institutions and other interested parties to evaluate whether an OPT opportunity provides sufficient genuine educational and economic value to justify participation.

I encourage DHS, in the final rule, to explain clearly why the selected $70,000 and $30,000 amounts are reasonably calibrated to achieve the intended deterrence and institutional scrutiny while preserving bona fide practical training. A clear connection among the documented problems, selected fee amounts, expected behavioral effects, and alternatives considered would strengthen the basis for the final rule.

I also support greater institutional accountability. Schools perform an important gatekeeping function through the DSO recommendation process. An OPT recommendation should reflect meaningful consideration of eligibility and whether the proposed practical training serves the educational purpose of OPT. A substantial institutional financial commitment can encourage schools to distinguish genuine practical training from questionable arrangements.

DHS should also consider the interests of American graduates and workers. American graduates may compete with OPT participants for entry-level professional and technical positions. Immigration policy should, where reasonably possible, avoid creating artificial financial or regulatory incentives for an employer to prefer an F-1 graduate over a similarly qualified U.S. worker.

This does not require assuming that every OPT participant displaces a U.S. worker. The relevant policy concern is whether the program can create incentives that distort hiring decisions in some circumstances. Employers should select candidates primarily based on skills, qualifications, productivity, and legitimate business needs rather than an immigration-related cost advantage.

Fees should complement, not replace, enforcement. DHS should use targeted, risk-based verification where objective indicators warrant additional review. Unusual concentrations of OPT participants associated with particular employers, worksites, addresses, or institutions could appropriately trigger further scrutiny without creating a presumption of wrongdoing.

Where warranted, DHS should verify that employers conduct legitimate operations, that claimed employment actually exists, and that the work is meaningfully related to the student's field of study. This approach can protect legitimate students and employers while concentrating enforcement resources on higher-risk circumstances.

Finally, DHS should evaluate the rule after implementation and publish appropriate aggregate data concerning OPT participation, suspected and confirmed fraud, enforcement actions, institutional compliance, and other measurable program-integrity outcomes. This would provide an empirical basis for determining whether the fees are achieving their stated objectives and whether future adjustments are warranted.

OPT should remain genuine, degree-related practical training rather than simply an alternative pathway into the U.S. labor market. The vulnerabilities identified by DHS provide a reasonable basis for stronger safeguards. I therefore support the proposed fees, together with institutional accountability, targeted enforcement, and transparent evaluation of their effectiveness.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly supports the proposed OPT fee structure to deter fraud and strengthen program integrity.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Allan Lee
comments.commentText:
I graduated this summer and work as a designer in Chicago on post-completion OPT. I strongly oppose the proposed OPT Fees rule.

I will need my school's recommendation for the extension in spring 2027, likely after any final rule takes effect. Under the proposal, my school could not recommend me until someone pays $30,000. The rule allows schools to pass the cost to students, so I expect to be the one paying.

I have already spent more than $110,000 on my education and living expenses in the U.S. As a junior designer, I earn a reasonable salary, but most of it goes to rent and living costs. A $30,000 fee would nearly wipe out my savings. If I cannot pay, I will have to stop working when my EAD expires and leave the country, even though I have followed every rule. The NPRM says the fee is meant to prevent fraud, yet it does not consider what the fee would cost ordinary people like me who are working lawfully.

The STEM extension already has the safeguards DHS says it wants. To get it, my employer must sign a Form I-983 training plan and attest that I am not replacing a U.S. worker. My pay must be comparable to that of similar U.S. workers, I must submit regular self-evaluations, and DHS can visit my worksite. If DHS has evidence of fraud, it can use these tools to investigate and penalize the employers and schools involved. Instead, the rule charges everyone the same fee, whether they are committing fraud or working honestly in an entry-level job.

The money would not even pay for enforcement. Under the proposal it goes to the general fund of the Treasury (31 U.S.C. 3302), and the NPRM does not set aside any of it for OPT oversight. The rule would collect billions of dollars from the honest majority while doing nothing specific about the dishonest few.

The NPRM also has no transition rule for people already on OPT. Because the fee applies to any recommendation made on or after the effective date, people like me would be charged partway through a plan we made in good faith under the current rules. The Supreme Court has held that agencies must consider this kind of reliance (DHS v. Regents, 2020), and the NPRM does not.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw this rule, for my sake and for the students who come after me. It is unfair to charge honest participants for gaps in DHS's own oversight. If fraud in OPT is a serious problem, DHS should target the employers and schools responsible. At a minimum, any final rule should exempt anyone already granted OPT or enrolled before its effective date, and should not apply to STEM extensions, which are already subject to I-983 oversight
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fee would deplete their savings and force them to leave the country.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an international Ph.D. student in Mechanical Engineering nearing graduation, and I oppose the proposed OPT fee rule, especially applied to students who are already enrolled in U.S. degree programs. I chose to pursue my Ph.D. in the United States in part because OPT would allow me to continue developing ideas from my federally funded research toward commercialization after graduation. If a $70,000 OPT fee had been part of the rules when I was deciding where to pursue my Ph.D., it would have materially affected that decision.

DHS itself acknowledges in the proposed rule that current F-1 students are “in a different position” from prospective students, but nevertheless proposes essentially the same cutoff for both groups. The Supreme Court has held that agencies changing established policies must seriously consider reliance interests and reasonable ways of accommodating them. See Department of Homeland Security v. Regents of the University of California, 591 U.S. 1, 30–33 (2020). A 60-day effective-date delay does not meaningfully address the reliance of someone who has already spent four or five years completing a degree. DHS recently recognized a similar transition problem in its 2026 Duration of Status final rule, where F-1 and J-1 nonimmigrants already maintaining status under the prior system received a transition period of up to four years rather than being immediately moved into the new system. A comparable transition for students already enrolled before this OPT rule takes effect would be reasonable.

I therefore respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees or, at minimum, grandfather students who began their current U.S. degree programs before the final rule takes effect, including post-completion OPT and any STEM OPT extension based on that degree. This would allow DHS to apply this policy to new prospective students while protecting students who made years-long educational and financial commitments under the existing framework.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fee rule and argues it harms current students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by lynn Man
comments.commentText:
I am a second-year master's student on an F-1 visa, and I oppose the proposed OPT Fees rule. I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw it.

I chose to study in the United States after comparing offers from several countries. One of the main reasons was that U.S. law and regulations allowed graduates to gain practical training after completing their degrees. By graduation, my family and I will have paid more than $100,000 in tuition, fees, and living expenses. I receive no federal financial aid and no institutional scholarship.

Some comments on this docket, such as ICEB-2026-0100-0018, claim that international students take scholarships away from American students. My experience is the opposite, and it is typical. International students are not eligible for federal grants or loans, and most international students rely mainly on personal and family funds. Most of us pay full tuition, and that tuition helps support the same programs domestic students attend. The proposed fee would not change this, because it goes to the general fund of the Treasury (31 U.S.C. 3302), not to scholarships for anyone.

The proposed rule would require my school to pay $70,000 before it could recommend me for OPT, and another $30,000 for a STEM extension. The rule allows schools to pass these costs on to students. If my school does, I would suddenly face an extra $100,000 that did not exist when I enrolled. That is deeply unfair to me, since I have not even started working yet, and to my family, which is not wealthy. If my school decides not to pay at all, I would lose the chance to build my career here after graduation entirely, even though I have complied with every requirement of my status.

I made a multi-year financial commitment relying on the rules in place when I enrolled. The NPRM does not analyze the reliance interests of students who are already enrolled, and it offers them no transition protection. When an agency changes a long-standing policy, it must consider serious reliance interests like these (DHS v. Regents of the University of California, 2020). At a minimum, DHS should exempt students who were enrolled before the effective date of any final rule.

The rule's stated purpose is to combat fraud. I support enforcement against fraudulent employers and schools. But nothing in my case involves fraud, and the fee does not distinguish me from a fraudulent actor. The only thing it tests is whether my school, or I, can pay $70,000. That is a test of wealth, not of integrity or educational value. Targeted enforcement against the employers and schools that actually commit fraud would serve DHS's stated goal without penalizing students who follow the rules.

I also oppose the alternative in Section V.A, which would charge the initial fee again at each degree level. It would penalize students for continuing their education in the United States, for example a master's graduate who goes on to a Ph.D.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule, or at least to exempt currently enrolled students and pursue targeted enforcement instead.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and asks DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed $100,000 fee associated with Optional Practical Training (OPT). This policy would impose substantial financial burdens on international students and U.S. universities while doing little to address the stated concern of protecting employment opportunities for American workers.

**First, shifting the financial burden to universities would ultimately undermine the competitiveness of American higher education.**

If universities are expected to pay this fee on behalf of international students, the cost will not simply disappear. Universities will likely have to absorb it through reduced research funding, fewer available positions, increased tuition, or other budget adjustments. International students already contribute significantly to the U.S. economy through tuition payments, living expenses, research, and innovation. Making it prohibitively expensive for universities to recruit and retain international talent would discourage qualified students from choosing American institutions and encourage them to pursue educational and professional opportunities in other countries. This would be a counterproductive outcome for a country whose scientific leadership and economic competitiveness depend in part on attracting global talent.

**Second, targeting OPT is a poorly targeted response to concerns about competition for American jobs.**

International students participating in OPT represent only a limited segment of the U.S. labor market. A policy that imposes an extraordinary financial barrier on this group is unlikely to meaningfully address the broader challenges facing American workers. If the objective is to protect domestic employment opportunities, policymakers should focus on the actual sources and scale of labor-market displacement rather than disproportionately burdening recent graduates who have studied and trained at U.S. institutions.

**Third, OPT participants already face substantial disadvantages in the job market compared with domestic candidates.**

OPT is a temporary work authorization, generally limited to 12 months, with eligible STEM graduates potentially qualifying for an additional 24-month extension. This temporary status creates uncertainty for both employees and employers. International graduates must find positions compatible with their work authorization and may need to navigate the additional uncertainty of future H-1B sponsorship. Employers, in turn, may be reluctant to recruit candidates whose long-term employment prospects are uncertain. If an international graduate cannot transition to another appropriate work authorization, employment must end when OPT expires. These constraints already make international graduates less attractive to some employers than otherwise equally qualified domestic candidates.

Adding a $100,000 fee would further discourage employers from hiring international graduates, regardless of their qualifications or productivity. It would make it particularly difficult for universities, research laboratories, startups, and other organizations that depend on highly skilled talent but operate under limited budgets to recruit these graduates. The result could be the loss of valuable scientific expertise and human capital that the United States has already invested substantial resources in educating.

**In conclusion, this proposal risks imposing significant costs on universities, international students, and the broader U.S. research and innovation ecosystem without establishing a proportionate benefit to American workers.** It could weaken the competitiveness of U.S. higher education, discourage international talent from remaining in the country after graduation, and push valuable skills and innovation toward competing economies.

I urge the relevant authorities to reconsider this proposal and reject the imposition of a $100,000 OPT-related fee. Immigration and employment policies should be proportionate to their objectives, grounded in evidence, and designed to protect domestic workers without unnecessarily undermining the institutions, research capabilities, and talent pipeline that contribute to America's long-term prosperity.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed $100,000 OPT fee, arguing it burdens universities and harms U.S. competitiveness.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
This proposal makes absolutely no sense.

So let me get this straight. International students come to the US legally, pay thousands of dollars in tuition, spend years studying at American universities, and graduate with American degrees. Then the government wants to make it nearly impossible for them to work here?

These are people who could be working, paying income taxes, renting apartments, buying cars, and spending money in American communities.

And for those who eventually transition to H-1B status, their employers are already required to pay at least the prevailing wage or the wage paid to similarly employed workers, whichever is higher. These are legitimate jobs with wage protections, not some loophole for hiring people for pennies.

Why would we spend years educating talented people just to push them to work for our competitors overseas? Other countries would be happy to welcome graduates trained by American universities.

And how exactly is charging a university $70,000 to recommend a student for OPT supposed to prevent fraud? Does paying $70,000 suddenly make someone more honest?

If fraud is the problem, investigate fraud. If employers are breaking the rules, investigate those employers. Stop punishing people who followed the law.

This proposal hurts American universities, American businesses, and ultimately the American economy. I strongly oppose it.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
American universities are already facing serious financial pressures. Many are dealing with budget cuts, declining public funding, and rising operating costs. International students, especially those pursuing master's degrees, are an important source of tuition revenue for many institutions.

For many international students, the opportunity to work in the US through OPT after graduation is a major reason they choose American universities. Unlike PhD programs, many master's programs offer limited scholarships or assistantships. Many students pay substantial tuition out of pocket, helping support American universities, faculty, research, and educational programs.

If OPT becomes practically inaccessible, international students will have much less incentive to pursue expensive degrees in the US. Universities could lose an important source of revenue at a time when many are already struggling financially.

And the economic contributions do not stop at graduation. Many OPT participants work legally for American employers, earn W-2 wages, and pay applicable taxes. They rent apartments, buy groceries, purchase cars, eat at restaurants, and spend their earnings in American communities. Their wages and spending contribute to local businesses and the American economy.

I also find the justification for these proposed fees very difficult to understand.

OPT applicants already pay USCIS $470 to apply online for employment authorization, or $520 for paper applications. Premium processing costs another $1,780, bringing the total to $2,250 for an online application. Despite these existing fees, regular processing can still take months.

Now DHS proposes charging universities an additional $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations.

What exactly justifies these amounts? If the existing processing fees are insufficient, why? What has changed so dramatically that a university must now pay $70,000 simply to recommend a student for practical training?

DHS also argues that these fees are intended to prevent OPT from being used to circumvent the H-1B program. But this argument overlooks why many international graduates rely on OPT in the first place.

H-1B visas are subject to annual numerical limits and a selection process. Even when an American employer is willing to sponsor a qualified graduate, that person may not be selected.

OPT, especially STEM OPT, provides a lawful period of employment while graduates pursue opportunities to transition to H-1B or another appropriate immigration status.

Are these graduates really trying to avoid H-1B, or are they simply unable to obtain H-1B status because of a selection process outside their control?

In fact, DHS previously recognized that limited H-1B availability created difficulties for American technology companies and universities trying to attract international talent. That was part of the original justification for the STEM OPT extension.

Why is a system originally intended to address this problem now being characterized as an attempt to circumvent immigration rules?

Moreover, ordinary H-1B government filing fees are generally only several thousand dollars, depending on the employer and circumstances. Even with premium processing, a common filing fee combination totals approximately $6,500. DHS should explain why a $70,000 OPT recommendation fee is appropriate, rather than using an exceptional and legally contested H-1B payment policy as its benchmark.

DHS also acknowledges that its own resources for reviewing OPT cases and investigating potential fraud are limited. Yet these proposed fees would not directly fund additional OPT enforcement activities.

Why should American universities bear enormous new financial burdens because the federal government lacks sufficient resources to enforce its own regulations?

Universities already have immigration reporting and compliance responsibilities. Their primary mission is to educate students, conduct research, and develop talent. Their limited funding should support those purposes.

If fraud is the problem, investigate fraudulent employers and institutions. Legitimate employment by authorized graduates should not be treated as evidence of fraud.

This proposal risks damaging American higher education, reducing legitimate economic activity, and transferring substantial costs to universities without adequately demonstrating how those costs would improve enforcement.

I hope DHS will reconsider the proposed fees and provide a much stronger justification for both the amounts and the assumptions underlying this rule.
comments.reason: Argues the proposed fees make OPT inaccessible, harming university revenue and the economy.
